#3065. Brian Sullivan: Why the 'real' price of oil is likely $30-$40 higher than where it is now

Oil, in reality, is $125 per barrel or higher.

That's the real cost of a barrel of oil because buying the physical commodity is a very different story from a number on traders' screens.

Oil futures are just that: paper contracts indicating a price today, tomorrow, next month or further out.  If you want to buy the physical commodity, it may be a totally different story — and price.

As I've reported, prices for oil delivery have skyrocketed. Last week, a VLCC (aka a "supertanker" in non-shipper parlance) was chartered from the U.S. Gulf Coast to China for $76 million. Another very large crude carrier went for $77 million from the U.S. to South Korea. That's 10 times more than the price of the same trip less than one year ago.

Assuming these ships hold about 2 million barrels of oil, that charter price means each barrel on the ship costs about $38 over the price of the oil itself.

I'm certainly not saying to avoid looking at oil futures prices, but you need to know that the price on the CNBC screen or CNBC.com isn't always the full price being paid. These days, any company that needs oil shipped by sea, rail or truck will pay a hefty premium over the price of the oil itself. So, while the volume of oil moving through Hormuz is closing in on pre-war levels, costs are not. And there's no sign that they're going anywhere but up.

You know what else is up? The stocks of the shipowners. Look at their moves this month and this year.

On a more serious note, I want to express my condolences for the awful attacks on the airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The cowardly strike on civilians—some of whom were religious pilgrims—took the lives of at least 14 people and injured more than 300.

The airport was attacked at least three times as travelers and energy industry professionals from around the world were flying into Riyadh for the World Petroleum Council conference. I was scheduled to fly in on Saturday, but the trip was canceled because of the strikes. The WPC went on as planned — here's one panel that took place Tuesday — and I look forward to seeing all my global energy friends again soon.

Thanks for reading—and watching. Be safe in these crazy and often scary times.

The supercap oil and gas stock to watch right now is Shell (SHEL). Shell is not a shell of its former self. It's back to being what energy investors wanted: a major player in global energy, focused on what it does best. Shareholders are being rewarded.

Shell hit a new high this week. While analysts remain bullish, the stock is getting close to its target price.

Shell may be underappreciated for its huge liquefied natural gas business. RBC analyst Biraj Borkhataria writes: "Without a sustained resumption in Qatari volumes and with European storage levels below seasonal lows heading into winter, European gas prices continued on an upward trajectory in 3Q26. With HH broadly unchanged throughout the summer, export margins have increased to the widest levels seen since 2022, on our estimates nearly double the level in 2Q26 (~$13/mmbtu vs. $7/mmbtu)."

Borkhataria expects Shell and other companies with huge U.S. LNG positions — TotalEnergies (TTE) and BP (BP) — to benefit from wider margins on exports to Europe.

Speaking of RBC and energy, the firm lists ConocoPhillips as one of its top 30 global stock ideas. The company is covered by analyst Scott Hanold, who believes it has a "returns-focused value proposition, a strong balance sheet, and peer-leading distributions." He loves its "global and diverse" asset base and management's clear "investment propositions." Hanold has a $152 target on COP. That's more than 20% upside.

In oil and gas, refiners and big energy stocks are generating cash for investors, and Morgan Stanley is optimistic more is coming.

The firm says the diesel shortage is now spilling over into gasoline, potentially marking another leg of the "golden age" for refiners. Morgan Stanley has been revising its earnings estimates higher for companies including ExxonMobil (XOM), Valero (VLO), Phillips 66 (PSX) and PBF (PBF).

First, Truist says you have to buy First Solar (FSLR). The analyst upgrades it to Buy with a $270 target. Another call on the Power Insider radar: TD Cowen is starting coverage of TeraWulf (WULF) with a Buy rating and a $21 target. That indicates about 50% upside for the stock, but it's actually one of the Street's lower price targets. TeraWulf and other AI power companies have seen their stocks hit hard following months of big gains, but Cowen analyst Michael Elias says the valuation is now attractive and a likely lease in the second half of 2027 at a Kentucky location could be a catalyst.

In the wake of the terror attacks on Saudi Arabia, we spoke with RBC Capital Markets' Helima Croft about the attacks, energy and more.

The entire energy world is watching Europe's natural gas storage levels. The question is whether the continent will have enough gas to make it safely through the winter. Power Insider wrote about the topic in the last issue.

The fact that JPMorgan highlights expected weather patterns should tell you how much temperature matters when it comes to gas storage. The early forecast calls for October and November to be average or slightly warmer than the 10-year average. The red line represents the 10-year average.

Europe has been largely "saved" by mild temperatures over the past few years. Natural gas storage levels are lower this year than in years past, so the thermometer will matter a lot when it comes to how well countries can, ahem, weather the winter. Random, but interesting.

#3064. Geron: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Operating expenses fell 9% year to date, and $339 million in cash leaves Geron room to pursue hematology deals.

On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Geron (GERN +16.13%) announced that full-year net revenue will reach the mid- to high end of its guidance range of $220 million to $240 million. Growing commercial adoption of RYTELO (imetelstat), an enzyme-inhibiting drug approved for lower-risk myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), a group of bone marrow disorders, provides expanding cash flow from community oncology practices. Three things management said stand out.

Community oncology clinics drive the majority of patient prescriptions, giving Geron a growing footprint in second-line blood disease treatment. Net product revenue reached $60.1 million in the third quarter, representing a 27% increase year over year.

An independent monitoring committee found the Phase III IMpactMF trial unlikely to hit its primary endpoint for overall survival, prompting management to stop the study. Ending the trial avoids future clinical trial spending and sharpens focus on existing commercial priorities.

Geron is launching RYTELO in Germany by the end of 2026 without spending heavily on international sales teams. This staged approach maintains drug pricing overseas while leaving room to sign regional distribution partners later.

Operational efficiency is helping reduce total costs, and management is openly pointing to improved expense controls. Operating expenses year-to-date fell 9% following earlier workforce reductions, while cash reserves reached $339 million. Management is watching commercial adoption rates, European reimbursement milestones, and disciplined capital allocation.

With a self-sustaining U.S. commercial footprint and substantial liquidity, management intends to leverage its existing infrastructure by acquiring additional hematology assets.

#3063. As Democrats Take Control of Congress, Warren Buffett Has a Timely Warning for Investors

The Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate following the 2026 midterm elections.

The 2026 midterm elections was a decisive victory for Democrats, who won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. With Republicans retaining the White House, the election results bring a period of divided government starting in January.

Wall Street's initial reaction has been enthusiastic. As of this writing (Nov. 4), the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI +3.03%) surged more than 1,500 points during morning trading, while the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.58%) and Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +1.44%) also rallied.

Beneath the broader market's gains, investors are undoubtedly repositioning their portfolios. Artificial intelligence (AI) hyperscalers like Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta Platforms are surging, while many semiconductor stocks and data center operators are plunging.

The contrasting performance reflects uncertainty about how the election could affect AI and adjacent industries. For investors wondering whether to change their portfolios following the election, Warren Buffett's advice about mixing politics and investing is particularly relevant.

Warren Buffett: Image source: Getty Images.

During an interview in 2019, Buffett discussed how investors frequently allow their political views to influence financial decisions. The "Oracle of Omaha" noted that he had invested through 14 presidencies -- seven Republicans and seven Democrats. Despite the different administrations and their economic policies, Buffett continued investing.

His message was straightforward: "You do not want to have a political view in investing."

Buffett's point is that some investors become so concerned about election outcomes that they abandon otherwise attractive investments. Making portfolio decisions based primarily on which political party holds power can mean missing lucrative opportunities for long-term wealth.

In Berkshire Hathaway's 2016 annual shareholder letter, Buffett highlighted how the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced from 66 to 11,497 during the 20th century, representing a capital gain exceeding 17,000%! That growth occurred despite wars, recessions, financial crises, and changes in political leadership.

Buffett's underlying message is that American businesses will continue innovating, generating profits, and creating shareholder value across different political administrations. While government policies certainly matter, investors shouldn't confuse political uncertainty with the disappearance of long-term economic growth.

Following the Democratic sweep, investors began to reassess the potential implications for AI infrastructure in particular. Shares of the cloud computing hyperscalers surged during morning trading on Nov. 4, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index declined about 4%. Data center operators and neoclouds endured even steeper losses, with Iren falling roughly 9% and Hut 8 plunging nearly 17%.

This divergence highlights an interesting development. Investors seem concerned that tighter oversight of AI infrastructure -- particularly data center construction and electricity consumption -- could complicate the industry's expansion.

However, big tech might benefit from a different dynamic. If expanding computing capacity becomes more difficult, companies with enormous infrastructure networks could gain a competitive advantage over smaller rivals attempting to enter the market.

This helps explain why investors are treating different pockets of the AI ecosystem so differently.

Buffett's investment philosophy provides a useful framework for investors navigating the post-election volatility. Consider semiconductor companies such as Nvidia and Micron Technology. Both companies are exposed to AI infrastructure spending, meaning delays in data center build-outs could affect demand for their products.

However, one election will not automatically eliminate the long-term need for advanced computing processors, high bandwidth memory (HBM), or networking equipment. Investors should examine whether these companies' earnings expectations, competitive moats, and valuations still justify their stock prices.

Similarly, data center operators experiencing plummeting stock prices could eventually offer attractive value opportunities. Of course, a falling stock doesn't necessarily mean it's undervalued. This is where Buffett's discipline becomes especially valuable.

Throughout his career, Buffett repeatedly observed that investors can benefit when widespread pessimism or emotionally charged selling pressure creates opportunities to purchase quality businesses at prices below their intrinsic value.

This is all to say that a political transition isn't a compelling reason to change a long-term investment strategy. Rather than panic-selling or blindly following momentum, investors should concentrate on business fundamentals, reasonable valuations, and diversification. That's the ultimate lesson Buffett reinforced through decades of consistent investing under both political parties.

#3062. Exclusive: Aina’s Smart Ring Wants to Be a Remote Control for Your AI Agent

Apoorv Shankar believes that in the very near future, humans will interact with technology through a series of approvals and rejections. AI agents will proactively come to us to complete tasks, and humans will say, “Yes, order that Uber,” or “No, don't get lunch from that spot.”

But if you get multiple pings from an AI agent throughout the day, taking out your phone to say yes or no every single time will be a “bottleneck,” he says. That's why he made the Aina Ring. It has a small display and a joystick-like button that lets you quickly accept or reject an AI agent's actions with your hands. Your phone can stay in your pocket.

Aina has been in stealth for the last 15 months, though the company debuted a few experimental products at CES 2026 under a different name: Project Mirage. One was called Dune—think of it as the precursor to the Aina Ring. Connect it to your Mac and the three buttons become context-aware controls based on what you're doing. In a meeting? The buttons can turn into shortcuts for mute, camera off, or record.

Aina studied how people used Dune and developed the Aina Ring, which it’s announcing today. Preorders are live now, and the ring costs $399 for a limited time before the retail price rises to $499 when it starts shipping in January 2027.

“Approvals are going to be the future of interfaces and interaction, and we wanted to build a device that just made it easy to approve stuff,” Shankar says.

This isn't Shankar's first time with a smart ring—he previously was the vice president of hardware at Ultrahuman, a fitness- and health-tracking ring that competed with Oura. (Ultrahuman was briefly banned in the US after a patent dispute with Oura.)

The team explored other gadgets like smart glasses and pendants, but ultimately decided the ring was the most convenient way to interact with agents. The titanium Aina Ring connects to Macs or iPhones, and at any moment, the onboard assistant is looking for the three things you need next. It learns your routines from your personal data, like location, calendar, and email, and after you connect various third-party services in the Aina app, like Uber or Spotify.

If you usually go for a run at 6 am, as soon as you put on your running shoes, it will suggest continuing the podcast you started last night, or play music—the ring's joystick doubles as a music-playback controller. If it's 8:30 am and you usually take an Uber to work, it'll suggest the ride—flick yes on the ring, and it'll handle the task right away. If you're running late for a Zoom meeting, Aina will ask if you want the assistant to send an email saying you'll be late. Shankar calls these “Aina Cues,” powered by the ring's Context Aware Operating System.

Many of these actions will likely be limited based on what apps and features are supported, though Shankar says users can create their own Cues using natural language. So if you want the ring to prompt you about turning on the coffee machine every morning at 8 am, you can configure that. If your favorite app or service doesn't work through Aina, you can connect your preferred AI agent—like Muse or Instinct—to Aina, and they will handle the task through virtual browsers.

The display is crucial to make sure the user knows whether an action went through. “Agents today don't respond immediately,” Shankar says. “For us to trust these devices—that what I said actually just happened—you need display confirmation.”

These Cues aren't the only capability on the Aina Ring. Aina Voice lets you quickly talk to your AI agents by pressing the center button, or ask Aina to take notes, similar to smart rings like the Sandbar Stream or Pebble Index 01. The ring also has a tiny speaker, so you can take phone calls—initiate the call with a voice command, then bring your hand to your ear, like you're James Bond talking through an earpiece. (Bond would strongly advise against the gesture.)

Like the experimental Dune gadget, the ring also turns into a context-aware remote based on what you're doing. If it knows you're in a Zoom call on your Mac, it will offer up Zoom controls on the ring. If you're watching TV and can connect your TV system to Aina, it can act as a TV remote.

Many companies have tried and failed to be the next gadget for the AI revolution. Humane and Rabbit are two notable examples, but nothing has stuck so far. OpenAI is developing such a product with ex-Apple designer Jony Ive. But many of these devices claimed to replace your phone, and some, like the Rabbit, just felt awkward to carry around alongside the smartphone.

The Aina Ring isn't trying to replace anything—Shankar says phones are “too perfect.” Instead, it's just a means to stop you from being a bottleneck, so your AI agents can keep working on your behalf.

“We are seeing a major shift in how we operate with things—agents are able to do so much, and everything is waiting on us," he says. "I don't have an easy way to approve—we're going to see that a lot more once we see what the potential of proactive AI is.”

#3060. These 6 Stocks Make Up a Big Share of the S&P 500

Six tech stocks make up nearly a third of the S&P 500. Here's how AI spending is shaping each one's results.

Nvidia (NVDA -3.17%), Microsoft (MSFT +6.68%), Apple (AAPL +5.31%), Amazon (AMZN +6.12%), Alphabet (GOOG +3.25%) (GOOGL +3.18%), and Meta Platforms (META +1.44%) walk into an index fund. They take up about a third of the room.

As of Nov. 2, 2026, these six stocks make up 30.8% of the S&P 500 (^GSPC +1.58%). Line up the index's 428 smallest companies, and their combined weight still looks small by comparison.

That share has held roughly steady in recent years. In October 2024, the same six stocks made up about 30.2% of the S&P 500. Most of the added concentration since then has come from further down the list, as Broadcom, Tesla, and Eli Lilly gained ground. The index's 10 largest companies now account for 39% of its weight, up from about 36.4% two years ago.

The group of six mega-techs has still outperformed, though. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS +2.24%) owns these six plus Tesla in equal doses and rebalances every quarter. It gained 41.9% over the last two years. The Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO +1.62%) managed a 31.7% increase. That's a respectable result, just not a particularly magnificent one.

Here is a closer look at each tech titan at the top of the S&P 500 index.

Every gold rush needs someone selling shovels, and Nvidia makes the sharpest and shiniest ones. Its AI chips sit inside the data centers the other five companies keep building, and the stock rose 49.3% over two years. That's good enough for a 7.1% slice of the S&P 500.

That position cuts both ways. Nvidia's best customers are the four big spenders on this list, and several of them design their own chips. That's a bit like each of your biggest clients opening a shovel factory in their backyards. Guidance points to roughly 89% year-over-year sales growth in the upcoming Q3 2027 report. That's down from 106% in Q2 but still an impressive velocity. Nvidia is fine as long as the digging for AI gold continues.

Microsoft got to the AI party early, and now it's stuck with the catering bill. The stock gained 23.6% in two years, trailing the index, and its weight slid from 6.4% to 5.5%.

Azure remains one of the largest cloud platforms, and the OpenAI partnership gave Microsoft an early lead in AI software. But investors have grown more cautious about the cost. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion on capital expenditures last quarter, largely on AI data centers and the computing hardware in them. On the upside, the company is financing it with incoming cash flows rather than new debt or stock sales. The open question is how quickly Copilot subscriptions and Azure AI revenue can justify that spending.

Apple, meanwhile, essentially skipped the AI spending spree and still ended up as the biggest company in the S&P 500, at 7.2%. The stock rose 51.9% over two years. Believe it or not, that's a slightly better showing than Nvidia's over the same period.

This company's capital spending is pocket change next to its peers', at just $3.2 billion in Q4 2026. It has partnered with others for some AI features rather than building every artificial brain in-house. I admire the thrift. Still, if AI reshapes how people use their phones, Apple could end up renting key AI technologies from the same rivals it competes with.

Amazon's 24.2% gain in two years is within shouting distance of the S&P 500's increase. Its weight crept from 3.5% to 3.9%.

Amazon Web Services rents computing power to everybody else, which makes Amazon both a big AI spender and a landlord to other AI spenders. It even builds its own chips, called Trainium, so it doesn't have to buy every shovel directly from Nvidia. Capital spending hit $77.3 billion last quarter. That's a lot of shovels in three months, and Amazon is taking on costly debt to pay for them. AWS growth tells you whether the landlord is filling the units.

Two years ago, many investors thought AI chatbots would eat Google Search for lunch. Alphabet apparently didn't get the memo. In last week's Q3 2026 report, Search posted 12% year-over-year revenue growth amid the highest query growth in five years. The stock has risen 63% since November 2024, the best on this list, and its S&P 500 weight climbed from about 3.6% to 4.9%.

Alphabet builds its own AI chips, runs a growing cloud business, and spends like the rest of them, with $51.4 billion in capital spending last quarter. But all that spending pushed free cash flow to negative $9 billion, and the stock fell about 10% after the Q3 report. Investors liked the receipts right up until they started showing more cash going out than coming in. Even so, Alphabet remains the clearest case on this list of AI spending that has paid off for shareholders.

Meta Platforms trails the group. The stock rose just 7% over two years, and its index weight fell from 2.5% to 2.3%. Tesla now ranks ahead of it in the S&P 500.

Meta is spending heavily on AI, at $34.9 billion last quarter, but it has no cloud business to rent that capacity to other companies. The returns have to come from Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, mainly through better ad targeting and new AI products. The ads are still working, judging by Meta's double-digit growth in both ad impressions and average ad prices. Investors just aren't sure the rest of the bill makes sense yet.

#3059. The Most Undervalued Asset In Critical Infrastructure

Christopher Guttman-McCabe leads Anterix‘s regulatory and spectrum agenda, advancing private broadband for critical infrastructure.

Over the past 18 months, tens of billions of dollars in announced transactions have involved spectrum licenses. Yet most conversations about spectrum focus on what it costs rather than what it enables. ​That’s a mistake.

Spectrum is no longer simply a communications input. For more and more organizations, it’s become a strategic infrastructure asset that shapes resilience, operational control and long-term flexibility.

I’ve watched this conversation change dramatically. What has not changed is that we still tend to think about spectrum too narrowly. We debate auction results, compare license valuations and measure holdings in megahertz. Those metrics tell us surprisingly little about what spectrum is actually worth to the organizations that depend on it.

Spectrum has monetary value. It also has strategic value. Owning spectrum determines how much control an organization has over its own communications and, increasingly, over its own operations.

The buyers are not all looking for the same thing. They are looking at spectrum through different lenses and for different applications. What they have in common is that they are placing a very high value on access to a resource that cannot simply be manufactured when demand increases.

There is a tendency to treat spectrum as though a megahertz is a megahertz. It is not.

Low-band spectrum is a good example. Below 1 GHz, signals travel farther and penetrate buildings, foliage and other obstacles more effectively than higher-frequency spectrum. That matters when you are trying to connect equipment spread across a large geographic area, reach into buildings or maintain connectivity in environments where coverage is difficult.

You cannot simply substitute another frequency and get the same result. The physics do not work that way.

There are only so many opportunities to acquire meaningful amounts of high-quality low-band spectrum. Once those opportunities are gone, creating more spectrum with the same characteristics is not an option. ​Wireless operators need spectrum for terrestrial networks. Satellite companies are pursuing direct-to-device connectivity and looking at how terrestrial and satellite networks can work together. Our company and Lynk Global, for example, are testing satellite direct-to-device service on our 900 MHz spectrum under an FCC experimental license. Beginning with Ameren in 2020, utilities are using 900 MHz to connect more devices, automating more of the grid and asking their communications networks to do more.

What I find most interesting about the transactions we have seen recently is not the dollar value; it’s the diversity of buyers and what they are trying to accomplish.

A satellite company may see terrestrial spectrum as part of a broader connectivity architecture. A critical infrastructure operator may value spectrum because it can provide control over a network that supports operations where communications cannot be treated as an afterthought. Those are very different investment decisions, but they point to the same market reality.

A spectrum auction can tell you what the market was willing to pay under a particular set of circumstances. A strategic acquisition can tell you something different.

For an infrastructure operator, the value of spectrum may have very little to do with whether it could be sold tomorrow. It may be reflected in what the network enables every day.

Consider what is happening on the electric grid. Utilities are deploying intelligent devices, sensors and automated equipment across increasingly distributed networks. The grid is becoming more digital and more dependent on the ability to move information quickly and reliably.

Take a power line that breaks and begins to fall. Sensors can detect the break and de-energize the line in about a second, before it reaches the ground. In dry country, in high wind, that second is the difference between an outage and a wildfire. But the detection only matters if the information reaches the system quickly and reliably enough to act on.

The value of the spectrum supporting that connection is not captured by the price of the license. It is reflected in the capability of the network: better visibility, faster response, greater automation and more control over critical operations.

For any infrastructure provider, spectrum is not simply a communications asset. It becomes part of the infrastructure itself.

There is another part of spectrum’s strategic value that is harder to quantify: optionality.

Consider satellite connectivity. Direct-to-device technology is creating the possibility of satellite connectivity extending the reach of terrestrial networks and providing another layer of coverage and resilience. For a critical infrastructure operator, terrestrial connectivity could remain the primary network while satellite provides an additional layer when and where it is needed. Owning spectrum can create those options. It can allow an organization to build a network today while preserving flexibility around how that network evolves tomorrow.

It is also one reason spectrum is different from many other infrastructure assets. A physical asset can depreciate as it ages. Spectrum does not wear out. Its usefulness can increase as more devices, applications and technologies depend on connectivity.

There is no single formula that captures the value of spectrum. Comparable transactions matter. Auctions matter. But they need to be considered alongside the characteristics of the spectrum itself, its scarcity, what it enables and the alternatives available to the potential user.

Strategic value belongs in that discussion as well.

Demand is expanding across terrestrial wireless, satellite and critical infrastructure, while the supply of high-quality low-band spectrum remains limited. As more industries depend on connectivity, the more consequential that scarcity becomes. Blocks of high-quality, low-band spectrum rarely become available. If you pass on one, you are not deferring the decision. Likely you are making it permanently.

​For organizations that depend on spectrum, value is measured not by what it can be sold for but by what it enables. That is a different way of thinking about an asset that has traditionally been measured primarily in megahertz. Spectrum is finite. The demand for what it enables is not.

#3058. The Austin Powers steamroller: How to trade CoreWeave's slow moving crisis

In Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, a Virtuocon guard famously stands in front of a commandeered steamroller, screaming "No!!" three times before being run over. The joke, of course, is that the hazard moved so slowly he had ample time to step out of the way.

For months, equity traders holding CoreWeave (CRWV) have played that guard. Despite credit markets flashing warnings, equity holders essentially just stood there. Now, after a shocking 27.5% drop from last Friday's close to this Thursday morning's 52-week lows, followed by a whiplash 17% rebound, equity investors, if not squashed like Dr. Evil's henchman, are dazed and confused. Shares are down another 5% today.

With earnings just a few weeks away, massive leverage, a heavily split sell-side, and 15.4% short interest, the stock remains primed for explosive volatility.

The hazard approaching CRWV equity wasn't hidden. The AI cloud infrastructure platform essentially didn't exist five years ago and has accumulated $51.6 billion in debt (~$46 billion net of cash) against a backdrop of zero historical profitability. That was well known, but the CEO's comments that the company aspired to be investment grade so it could borrow "unlimited sums", even as investors already anticipated nearly another $60 billion in debt in the next 18months, spooked folks. (Trick or Treat!) Especially since the debt issued only in June had already fallen 20% since.

From an options trader's point of view, it was hard to reconcile deteriorating credit and rising leverage with falling options premia; as recently as last week, they were in the 6th percentile, 1.5 standard deviations below the one-year mean. At 72%, options weren't cheap in absolute terms, but given everything going on, they should have been higher. The stock also looked somewhat complacent, with the equity chopping around historical support levels dating back to May 2025. The credit side was on tilt:

Because CRWV is levered by more than 2:1, a 10% move in enterprise value translates to a nearly 22% swing in equity value.

Despite the dire credit picture, equity sentiment remains fiercely divided, driving this week's 17% bounce from the lows. For example, HSBC maintains a Sell rating with a $39 price target, essentially calling for the stock to be cut in half. Conversely, banks like BNP and Cantor Fitzgerald (my former employer) suggest these fears are overblown and the stock should more than double from here.

It's not just bankers defending the company either. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang downplayed systemic concerns, and ARK Investment stepped in to buy 192,000 shares. BofA argues that CRWV's ability to bring active power online at scale, combined with higher pricing from Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin deployments, will drive faster-than-expected revenue growth. They described execution risk as a bigger concern than financing; I'm not sure those who bought the 2032 8 1/2s at par would agree.

With CRWV's credit heavily distressed but its equity heavily defended by high-profile dip-buyers, going outright long or short into earnings carries excessive directional risk. A November/January Call Diagonal, currently trading for just under $6 per spread. Almost 9% of the current stock price. Normally, that's a lot, but given this stock has fallen 27.5% and then gained 17% in the past 5 sessions, it isn't.

#3057. Too Late to Buy CrowdStrike Stock? Here's the 1 Thing to Watch.

CrowdStrike is riding AI-driven demand for cybersecurity, but the stock is richly valued. Here's the one number that will show whether the valuation can be supported.

CrowdStrike (CRWD -1.50%) stock has climbed about 83% over the past year as of Nov. 2, 2026, and that's after a recent 10% slip from its October high. Whether it's too late to buy may come down to one number: how fast it adds new subscription revenue.

This was the year cybersecurity became a must-have for companies adopting artificial intelligence (AI). CrowdStrike's Falcon platform protects devices and cloud systems, and its advantage lies in its data. It analyzes about 7 trillion security events a day, a "data moat," as CEO George Kurtz calls it, that trains its AI.

"The world's adoption of AI is rapidly expanding the attack surface," Kurtz said. Net new annual recurring revenue (ARR), the yearly subscription value CrowdStrike added in the latest quarter, hit a record $333 million, up 51% -- a meaningful acceleration over the 32% growth reported in the previous quarter.

CrowdStrike now expects to reach $10 billion in ARR by fiscal 2030 (ending January 2030). From the roughly $6.6 billion expected by the end of this fiscal year, that implies about 15% annualized growth.

Competition is one risk, with Microsoft its biggest rival. But in the near term, the bigger risk for investors is valuation. The stock trades at about 198 times forward earnings estimates, the cash left after investing in the business, while analysts expect long-term earnings growth of roughly 29% a year.

That makes net new ARR the one thing to watch. It drives future cash flow, and at this price, investors need it to not only rise but accelerate. If AI demand drives a sharp acceleration in net new ARR, the valuation could prove justified; otherwise, the share price may be hard to support. The next check is the quarterly report expected around the end of November.

#3054. AI Will Make Code Cheap, But It Won’t Shrink Most Engineering Teams

As a leader in a technology company or role, you may be asking yourself: If agents are writing code, we’ll need a fraction of the engineers, right?

It’s a fair question. But my honest answer, for most enterprises, is probably not. Here’s why, and where I could be wrong.

In 1865, the English economist William Stanley Jevons published The Coal Question. Britain feared running out of coal, and many assumed more efficient engines would solve it. Jevons pointed out the opposite: As coal-powered work got cheaper, it spread into more industries, and the total coal use kept climbing. In his words: “It is wholly a confusion of ideas to suppose that the economical use of fuel is equivalent to a diminished consumption. The very contrary is the truth.”

That’s the Jevons paradox. Make something cheaper to use, and if enough demand is waiting, you end up using more of it.

I think code is going through the same thing.

It’s already happening one layer down. This summer, AI token prices fell by more than one-third while GPU rental prices held, according to market data compiled by Citadel Securities. Cheaper inference didn’t mean less compute. People used more of it.​​

Every enterprise I’ve worked with has two backlogs of projects. There’s an official one. Then, there’s a much bigger one that never got written down because nobody thought these were worth the money or time​.

• Needed Internal Tools That Were Put On The Back Burner: When you have approvals that run through a chain of emails or reconciliations that someone does by hand every month-end, you need a better process. But everyone is used to the manual fixes, so they make do.

• Modernization Efforts That Are Always Pushed Back To “Next Year”: You might have a core system on a database that’s full of stored procedures written by people who left a decade ago, but nobody wants to touch it.

• A Long Tail Of Spreadsheet Workflows: The operations analyst pulls reports, fixes them up in Excel and keys them into another system. There are thousands of these, but each are too small to justify a project.

The benefits are clear, but these needs didn’t justify the cost and the risk, so the business case was never made.

That’s changing. Across the modernization programs we’ve delivered over the last 18 months, engineering effort has come in about 70% lower than it used to. Not all of that is the tooling; good teams matter a lot. But modernization also changes which programs make sense.

And the demand is growing. At one of our clients, an agentic order-entry system built for one division worked well enough, and cheaply enough, that a second division funded its own program soon after. Work that used to be “nice to have, can’t justify” turns into “Why haven’t we started?”

That’s the Jevons moment for software: The forgotten backlog starts showing up as real demand, and someone has to build and run it.

Every piece of software you build is something you now have to maintain, secure and operate. That’s more access to manage, more dependencies to patch and more to monitor and support. The operations side doesn’t shrink because the build side got cheaper. It grows with it.

Much of that work will be agentic too. But someone still has to design those loops and decide what counts as an exception.​

If writing code isn’t the expensive part anymore, what is? It’s two things: deciding what’s worth building, and judging whether what got built is right.

Earlier this year, I wrote about how, once engineers start directing agents, value moves upstream to intent and downstream to validation. The danger is shipping more things nobody validated.

So, the work I see growing is specification, validation and architecture. Someone has to know the business rules well enough to write them down. Someone has to decide how a new service fits with the 20 others around it. Someone has to own it when it breaks at 2 a.m.

Agents can generate the code. They can’t be accountable for it.

Jevons isn’t a law of nature. It only holds when demand grows faster than the cost falls.

And the bar is high. If a program takes 70% less delivery effort, a company has to build more than three times as much software just to keep the same number of build hours. A backlog proves there’s demand. It doesn’t prove there’s three times more of it.

My bet is that most enterprises will clear that bar. But some will build the same portfolio with a smaller team, and that’s a legitimate choice.

The other caveat is about people. Total demand for engineering can grow while specific roles shrink. Coal use rose in Jevons’ time, but that didn’t help every worker tied to the old way of doing things. More software doesn’t automatically mean a better job for every engineer.

Back in 2023, I wrote about skills with different half-lives. Some are perishable, such as a specific framework or syntax. Others are durable, like understanding how a business process works and judging quality. The durable ones are exactly what companies need.

When a CIO asks me how many engineers they’ll need, I ask a different question first: What would you build if building were cheap? Most have been carrying that list for years. Go back through the ideas you turned down, and give each one an owner who’ll run it, not just build it.

Cheap code doesn’t shrink the work. It shows you how much you left undone.​

#3052. How to Make a $50 Holiday Gift Feel Like $100

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Trade time and a little extra thought to enhance gifts this holiday season.

Each month, NerdWallet suggests one wallet win to help you feel more confident about your money. This month’s topic is making holiday gifts feel more valuable, and we’re going to show you ways to elevate a gift without overspending.

Making an inexpensive gift feel fancy is a winter challenge I relish.

As a relatively frugal person who often gets sticker shock when shopping for gifts, I’m always looking for creative ways to save money without diminishing the present. Over the years, I’ve developed a few strategies to make a $50 gift feel like it’s worth at least double that.

In the spirit of the season, I’m sharing these strategies with you. I hope you — and your recipients — find them as celebratory as I do.

What does your gift recipient love to do? It helps if they have a favorite hobby, sports team or other interest.

Let’s say your recipient likes to fish. Giving a gift card to a niche fishing store makes it feel far more valuable than the standard Amazon card because it shows that you considered who they are. And there are specialty stores for every hobby these days.

Maybe gift cards aren’t your go-to. You can easily enhance other gifts, too.

Paying $5 extra to engrave or embroider their name on the gift — whether it’s stationery, jewelry or a backpack — makes the item feel far more valuable than its price tag because it’s customized to the individual.

If you choose a gift that couldn’t have been given to anyone else, it increases its value.

Time required: A few extra minutes to think about your recipients’ preferences and apply them when shopping.

A vintage or thrifted scarf can be a wrapping paper alternative that also functions as a gift. Similarly, you could wrap a gift in tea towels, artwork or online prints that can be reused by the recipient.

Another idea: Wrap a gift in printed sheet music that contains a special meaning for the recipient.

Customizing the presentation of the gift elevates it without adding much to the expense.

Time required: Since you have to wrap the gift anyway, this method doesn’t need to take extra time. You’ll just need to find the cloth or paper you plan to use.

One of my favorite gifts in recent memory involved turning a family photograph into a Jane Austen-era image set on a bucolic English estate with the empire-waisted gowns to match. My mom is a big fan of Jane Austen, so I knew she would appreciate seeing the family in a Regency-style photo.

I hired an Etsy artist to transform my original image, but you may be able to do it yourself with a photo app. Similarly, you could create a custom song, illustration or other form of art made specifically for your recipient.

Adding your own creative spin on a gift shows you spent extra time thinking about the recipient to make something extra special for them.

Time required: Applying your own creativity can be time-intensive, but the process is enjoyable so it goes quickly.

I like to call this technique the hybrid gift approach: You buy something, then get crafty to transform the gift into something one-of-a-kind.

One of my favorite ways to do this is with a photo. I’ll buy a nice but inexpensive frame and then put a photo of the recipient, or the recipient alongside loved ones, inside it.

If the person you’re buying for posts on social media, you might not even have to ask them for a photo in advance. Instead, you can find a favorite one that they already shared and surprise them.

The options are endless, especially with online tutorials to help hone your crafting skills. Adding your own customization to a purchased gift makes it feel special, but doesn’t have to cost much.

Time required: Baking, crafting or creating can take several hours, but again, it’s an enjoyable process.

Experiential gifts tend to go over well, and you may even get to have some fun, too.

One year, I gave my mom a membership to a nearby art museum and tacked on an offer to attend an exhibit with her. We had something on the calendar to look forward to together, and she got the option to visit more times throughout the year.

My parents have given me memberships, too. More recently, they gave me one to a local nature center. It’s great because I can visit on my own or attend kid-friendly events at a discounted rate. It makes me feel part of the community, and I love supporting an organization that helps kids learn more about nature.

Another option is to donate to charity in a loved one’s name and then make plans to volunteer at the organization together.

Experiential gifts help create more family memories together, which is one of my favorite ways to celebrate the holidays.

Time required: Setting aside time to visit a museum or other destination can take an entire day, but it’s time well spent.

The bottom line is that giving a highly personalized gift adds value without eating too far into your own budget. Spend $50. Make someone feel like a hundred bucks.

If you’re following along with us on this monthly financial challenge, start by testing out the tips we shared today over the next few weeks. We’ll be back again next month to learn about setting money goals for the new year. And if you missed last month’s edition, take a look back at how to shop the holiday sales.

#3051. Top Wall Street analysts are bullish on the growth potential of these 3 stocks

Fears around the artificial intelligence trade and higher pressure on oil prices are weighing on global markets, but a few stocks offer investors solid growth prospects even in choppy times.

Investors with a long-term horizon can look beyond the ongoing volatility and track the recommendations of top Wall Street analysts to pick attractive stocks with strong long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Health insurer UnitedHealth delivered better-than-expected results for the third quarter of 2026. The company also raised its full-year earnings outlook, reflecting continued progress on its turnaround plan.

Following the Q3 print, Morgan Stanley analyst Erin Wright reiterated a buy rating on UNH stock with a price target of $529. "UNH's beat & raise reinforces turnaround momentum, with improving MA [Medicare Advantage]/Optum Health supporting a higher '26 EPS baseline & upside to '27 consensus," said Wright.

The five-star analyst added that better-than-expected performance in the UnitedHealthcare and Optum Health businesses supported another upgrade to the company's 2026 adjusted earnings per share outlook to at least $20.50. Wright noted that UNH raised the earnings guidance despite incremental investments planned for the fourth quarter of 2026.

Furthermore, Wright highlighted management's view that the consensus 2027 EPS of $22.63 was too conservative. Reaching even the low end of the company's 13% to 16% long-term EPS growth target would imply an EPS of $23.17.

Wright raised her 2026 EPS estimate to $20.65 from $19.82 and 2027 EPS to $23.24 from $22.54, reflecting the latest upside and an improving 2026 medical loss ratio to 87.4% from 88.1%. Overall, she believes that UNH's operational performance continues to improve, increasing her confidence in its UHC strategy and Optum Health turnaround execution.

Wright ranks No. 264 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See UnitedHealth Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Social media giant Meta Platforms has been making headlines since the launch of its Muse AI agent, which is seeing solid traction. Investors look forward to updates on the company's AI strategy when it announces its third-quarter results on Oct. 21.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Guggenheim analyst Michael Morris maintained a buy rating on Meta stock and increased his price target to $850 from $700, reflecting higher estimates for 2027. He expects Muse usage momentum and engagement levels to shape investor sentiment into the Q3 earnings call.

Specifically, Morris highlighted that, according to Apptopia, Muse reached 1.3 million daily active users in five weeks versus 300,000 in the first week. Given that Muse's current adoption represents less than 0.05% of Meta's 3.6 billion daily active user base, the analyst expects management to prioritize boosting usage over near-term monetization.

"Over time, we believe Muse monetizes primarily through businesses paying to reach consumers through their agents, consistent with the economics of Meta's core advertising business, rather than consumer wallets," said the five-star analyst. He added that the checkout integrations with Shopify and PayPal reflect this framework.

While there are concerns that a rival could overtake Muse or the recently launched Muse Wonder and push Meta into a prolonged cycle of overinvestment, Morris remains bullish due to the company's strong record in scaling WhatsApp and competing strongly with TikTok via Reels as well as free distribution to an extensive user base.

Next is semiconductor company Marvell Technology. Earlier this month, Marvell held its Investor Day, where it raised its total addressable market estimate to $400 billion by 2030, reflecting solid AI-led demand tailwinds.

After hosting a non-deal roadshow with Marvell's senior management following the Investor Day, Stifel analyst Tore Svanberg reiterated a buy rating on the stock with a price target of $370.

The five-star analyst said that a major focus of the roadshow was the XPU and XPU Attach mix, as Marvell's Custom business expands toward its FY31 revenue target of $30 billion. In this regard, management reiterated that it expects a balanced mix of XPU and XPU Attach revenue in FY31, though it noted that either segment could grow rapidly enough to shift the mix toward 60/40 or 40/60.

#3050. Could Buying Micron Stock Today Help Set You Up for Life?

The memory market's impressive prospects make Micron Technology stock worth buying and holding for the long run.

If you'd invested $10,000 in shares of Micron Technology (MU -7.00%) three years ago, the value of your investment would now be worth almost $118,000, suggesting that this semiconductor specialist has made investors significantly richer in a short period.

Importantly, Micron isn't done growing yet. The company is on track to benefit from the multi-year growth in the memory market. In fact, buying Micron stock as part of a diversified portfolio could help investors achieve their long-term goals of retiring comfortably or becoming millionaires.

Micron's terrific surge in recent years has been triggered by the incredible demand for memory chips from artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. AI chips are equipped with specialized memory, known as high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which helps transport enormous amounts of data in AI chip clusters and data centers.

HBM plays a critical role in AI data centers by feeding data sets quickly to graphics cards and custom processors. As a result, these accelerators don't sit idle, wasting time and power. Not surprisingly, the HBM market's revenue could hit a whopping $641 billion in 2030, according to Bloomberg Intelligence. For comparison, the HBM market was worth just $4 billion in 2023.

What's more, Bloomberg has significantly increased its HBM estimate for 2030. The firm was anticipating $130 billion in HBM revenue for 2030 in January 2025. This massive uptick in HBM growth estimate points to a long-term tailwind for Micron. That's because HBM is manufactured by stacking multiple conventional dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) chiplets

According to one estimate, HBM consumes around 3x the wafer capacity of conventional DRAM, suggesting that the ongoing memory shortage won't be going away at least until the end of the decade. Moreover, Micron is poised to capitalize on additional AI-related applications, such as humanoid robots and self-driving cars.

These markets can substantially improve Micron's total addressable market (TAM), ensuring that the healthy financial growth the company has been enjoying continues.

Micron will release its fiscal 2027 first-quarter results next month, according to Yahoo! Finance. The company expects non-GAAP earnings per share (EPS) of $38.15 on revenue of $61.5 billion. Those numbers point to a massive jump over the year-ago period's revenue of $13.6 billion and EPS of $4.78.

Micron trades at just 12 times earnings and 8 times sales despite the phenomenal growth it is poised to deliver. Moreover, we have already seen the reasons why Micron is built for robust long-term growth. So, I won't be surprised to see shares of this memory specialist trade at a premium valuation in the future, which could pave the way for significant upside in the stock given its exponential earnings growth.

So, investors looking to buy a long-term winner that trades at an attractive valuation should consider adding Micron to their portfolios, as its upside potential could make them significantly richer.

#3049. The CIO Playbook That Worked For 20 Years Is Breaking

Sue Odle is CEO of StorMagic, where she helps organizations simplify on-site virtualization for distributed IT environments.

​For years, infrastructure planning was predictable. CIOs knew their vendors, understood licensing models and could plan around standard hardware refresh cycles. That predictability has changed as hardware costs and availability fluctuate, vendor models change and AI creates new infrastructure demands while organizations continue to manage centralized and diverse distributed IT operations.​

Many CIOs are slowing down, not because they lack urgency but because they understand that the way IT planning has been governed for the last 20 years is no longer reliable. The old playbooks assumed a level of stability that many organizations don’t have anymore.​

​Hardware is one of the clearest examples of how infrastructure planning has changed. Many organizations historically followed a three-to-five-year refresh cycle and treated it as a standard part of IT planning. Now, CIOs have more reason to question whether every scheduled refresh is really necessary.​

Hardware is more dependable today, while costs and supply are harder to predict. According to a July 2026 report from TrendForce, server DRAM contract prices were expected to rise 13% to 18% quarter over quarter in the third quarter, while there was still a hardware shortage. As a result, some organizations are extending the life of existing hardware and looking more closely at what they own before committing to a replacement.​

That decision isn’t only about preserving budget. Hardware cost has a trickle-down effect on modernization plans, software choices and the pace of innovation. It’s a risk factor, not just a line item. Refresh cycles should increasingly be driven by workload and business requirements rather than simply by the calendar. If existing hardware still supports the business, keeping it in place often makes sense.​

​When conditions are difficult to predict, long-term commitments can carry more risk than they once did. A longer agreement may create cost certainty, but it can also limit flexibility if pricing, licensing, support or business needs change before the contract ends.​

That doesn’t mean long-term planning should disappear. It means CIOs need to be more deliberate about where the business can comfortably make a long-term commitment and where a shorter scope gives the organization more room to adjust.​

Vendor history, stability and behavior are now a part of infrastructure risk. CIOs aren’t only evaluating whether a platform works today. They’re also evaluating whether the licensing model, support experience and vendor relationship can be trusted over time.​

​Cloud-first strategies have shaped IT modernization for years, but a one-size-fits-all approach is becoming harder to justify as infrastructure and workloads spread across more locations. The cloud remains important, but some workloads need to operate closer to where data is created and where the business is running.

Retail locations have different requirements than centralized data centers. Many retailers run transaction, inventory and security applications locally, where connectivity and onsite IT support vary. Relying entirely on centralized infrastructure can increase operational risk.

Healthcare, manufacturing and other distributed industries face similar challenges. Healthcare organizations may run systems locally to support patient care, while manufacturers may keep applications onsite to maintain production when connectivity fails. Latency, availability, regulatory requirements, data sovereignty and data movement costs can determine whether workloads run in the cloud, at the edge or across both.

This is where CIOs need to be careful not to apply data center assumptions to edge environments. The edge isn’t simply a smaller data center. It has different constraints around space, staff, connectivity, cost and uptime. Treating those environments the same can lead to unnecessary complexity or infrastructure that exceeds what the location actually needs.​

AI is creating new pressure on infrastructure decisions, but AI readiness isn’t only a GPU issue. Before committing a significant budget to new compute resources, CIOs need to understand where AI will be used, what data it depends on and whether the workload needs to run centrally, at the edge or both.

Some AI use cases may require specialized infrastructure. Others may be supported by existing CPU-based servers, especially in early-stage or edge environments where the objective is to process data closer to where it’s created. The point is to avoid assuming every AI use case requires the same infrastructure strategy.

CIOs should connect AI infrastructure planning to data maturity, workload placement, governance and operational requirements. AI investments should be tied to what the business can truly use, support and scale.

​There’s still pressure on CIOs to move quickly as the C-suite pushes for modernization, AI efforts and measurable returns. Taking more time can be interpreted as hesitation, but a slower decision isn’t always a weaker one.​

CIOs are weighing rising costs, changing vendor models and infrastructure needs before committing resources. Some projects can move forward now, while others may be better phased or delayed.​

CIOs also need to explain that reasoning to the rest of the C-suite. If a delay reduces unnecessary cost or operational risk, that context matters. Careful sequencing can protect the business from overcommitting to technology, contracts or hardware before the requirements are clear.​

​CIOs need to build more flexibility into the decisions they’re already making. That means looking more closely at whether existing hardware can continue doing the job before refreshing it, choosing vendors and contracts that leave room to adapt as conditions change and matching infrastructure to the workload rather than defaulting to one environment.

​The old playbook assumed more predictability than CIOs have today. Hardware cycles, vendor models, cloud strategies, data sovereignty and AI requirements are all changing at once. CIOs can’t control what the market does next, but they can build infrastructure strategies that give the business more room to adapt.​

#3048. 3 Stocks Yielding Triple the S&P 500 to Buy in November

Not every dividend stock's yield has been pared back amid the broad market's moves.

A fund or ETF that mirrors the performance of the S&P 500 Index (^GSPC +1.58%) is almost always a smart, all-weather growth investment.

There is one exception, however. That is, if you specifically need income. With a trailing dividend yield of only 1.1%, the S&P 500 just doesn't generate much of it.

There are still great alternatives, though. Here's a rundown of three dividend payers with yields that are not only at least three times bigger than the S&P 500's current yield, but yields based on dividends that have been paid and raised like clockwork for years now.

For most investors, beverage giant Coca-Cola is the go-to choice as an income holding from the consumer goods space. And it's still a good one to be sure. That's certainly not been the case for rival PepsiCo (PEP +3.75%) of late, however, which is down 28% from its 2023 peak mostly due to the company's struggle with inflation.

Both camps have arguably overplayed their hands, however. KO stock is up 50% for the past two years as investors clamored for the safety it offers, dragging its forward-looking dividend yield down to a multiyear low of 2.2%. Conversely, PepsiCo shares' prolonged weakness has pumped its dividend yield up to 4.2%.

A strong yield alone isn't necessarily enough reason to purchase a stock, even as high as this one may be. PepsiCo also brings all the rest of what it needs to bring to the table, though, including an impressive dividend pedigree as well as evidence that it's finally on a turnaround track.

Not only has this beverage (and snack) outfit now raised its per-share dividend for 54 consecutive years, but it's looking for full-year organic revenue growth of around 3% following Q3's top-line improvement of 3.1%, accelerating last year's tepid growth of only 1.7%. It's evidence that initiatives like its prebiotic cola and protein-enriched snack chips are getting traction.

Just don't tarry if you're interested. PEP stock has bounced 12% since reporting its third-quarter numbers in early October. The crowd's starting to believe in it again.

There will come a time when the tobacco business is no longer a tenable industry. Blame/credit successful smoking-cessation efforts, mostly.

That end isn't on the near-term horizon, however. Although the Center for Disease Control reports more than two-thirds of U.S. smokers say they want to kick the cigarette habit, only a little more than half actually tried to quit in the past year, while less than 10% successfully did so. That leaves 11.6% of a still-growing (albeit slowly) U.S. population that continues smoking. Meanwhile, the use of vaping continues to rise as means of delivering nicotine to craving consumers, offsetting much of the progress made on the tobacco-smoking cessation front.

Enter Altria Group (MO +1.39%), parent to U.S. cigarette company Philip Morris (which makes Marlboro cigarettes), but also vaping brand Njoy and oral nicotine pouch maker Helix Innovations. Although the company's sold nearly 3% fewer cigarettes through the first three quarters of 2026 than it did through the first nine months of last year, organic revenue is still up more than 3% thanks to a combination of higher prices and growth of its other product lines.

Perhaps most important, per-share earnings of $4.33 through the first three quarters of 2026 are up 5.1% from last year's comparison, supporting and extending 61 increases in its dividend payment over the course of the past 57 years.

Again, it can't last indefinitely. It's likely going to last longer than most people might expect it to, however, making this stock's forward-looking dividend yield of nearly 5.8% well worth it even without knowing exactly when in the future will be the right time to make your exit. That will become clearer as the time approaches.

Last but not least, add oil and gas pipeline owner/operator Enbridge (ENB -0.33%) to your list of high-yielding dividend stocks to buy while you can step into its yield of 5.6%.

Like the tobacco industry, there will come a time when the world just doesn't need fossil fuels like crude oil and natural gas. Also like the tobacco business, though, that time is well into the distant future. The International Energy Agency's latest outlook suggests demand for oil will continue rising every year all the way through 2050, from a little more than 100 million barrels per day now to 113 million per day then. There's plenty of money to be made in the business in the meantime.

And Enbridge is perfectly positioned to turn this demand into reliable dividends regardless of the price of oil or natural gas. That's because it gets paid a flat fee for the usage of its 18,586 miles of crude pipelines and 19,373 miles' worth of gas pipelines. As long as demand for both remains robust -- and it is -- this company will continue reliably collecting cash. That's why it's not only been able to pay a quarterly dividend like clockwork for decades, but raise its annual payout for 31 consecutive years -- and counting.

That being said, the company is being proactive about preparing for its eventual future, even if the industry's inevitable change is years down the road. Namely, Enbridge is investing in power-related projects like an offshore wind farm in Courseulles, France, and a solar farm near San Antonio, Texas. While these may be outside of the company's wheelhouse right now, it's smart to establish roots that position Enbridge for any and all possible future scenarios.

#3047. How AI Is Changing The Playbook For Venture-Backed Companies

Nada Usina is CEO & Co-Founder of NU Advisory Partners.

​The question I hear most often in VC circles is whether the AI investment boom is a wave that will eventually crash. Will the flood of capital and climbing valuations prove to have sustainable traction and revenue? I’ve been at the forefront of several major technology shifts, from leading digital media companies through the dot-com era to working at the leading edge of mobile. Today, I’m building an AI-native, high-growth business. I’ve seen firsthand what happens when excitement gets ahead of fundamentals.

AI investment will continue well beyond 2026, but what interests me most is how AI is changing the way companies are built and led. Technology allows them to move faster with fewer people, challenging assumptions about what an executive team should look like.

The enormous amounts of capital being poured into AI make the market appear more mature than it is. Commercially, it is still early. A breakthrough in technology does not automatically create distribution, customer trust or a sustainable business.

AI can shorten that timeline considerably. We are seeing companies go from zero to $100 million in revenue at speeds that would have seemed extraordinary a decade ago. When a company can accomplish in a few years what once took 10, investors naturally start looking for the next one.

That speed can also lead to bad bets. Some companies will be swallowed by larger platforms while they are still small. Others will discover that an impressive product does not solve a problem customers urgently need to solve. It also raises a practical question for investors: What kind of leadership does a company need when it can grow this quickly with a much smaller team?

For years, companies approaching a new stage of growth often responded by adding people. Layers of vice presidents, senior vice presidents and functional leaders came in as the organization became more complex. With AI, companies can accomplish more with smaller teams, which means the people at the top have to be much closer to the actual business.

Leaders need to understand the product, the customer, the economics and how the business actually operates. They need to make decisions quickly, work across functions and know when technology can replace a process rather than simply adding another person to manage it.

As AI reduces the need for some layers of middle management, the expectations of the C-suite are getting higher. We are seeing investors look for leaders with the judgment and operating experience to work effectively in much leaner organizations. With fewer people between the C-suite and the work itself, the people at the top need to be able to run the business, not just oversee it.

For a portfolio company, I would ask: Is AI actually changing the business, or has it just been added to the product? The strongest companies are using it to improve the customer experience, make the product smarter through proprietary data or change the economics of the business. Calling something “AI-powered” does not tell an investor very much if the underlying business still operates the same way.

That can also point to a talent decision. A company may need a more commercially minded CEO, a different product leader or an executive who has already navigated a similar technology shift.

Public markets will make it easier to see which AI companies have built durable, profitable businesses and which have benefited primarily from the private-market environment. Investors will scrutinize revenue quality, retention, margins and the cost of maintaining the technology. They will also look at who is running the company.

I have seen strong technology companies lose momentum because their leadership team was built for invention rather than growth. The executives who made sense at $10 million in revenue may not be the right people at $100 million. Waiting too long to recognize that can cost a company valuable time.

My experience with frontier technology goes back to the early days of the internet and mobile media. At broadcast.com, I worked at a company that was among the first to stream live content over the Internet. Later, at Nokia, I worked with the music industry to bring music, games and video to mobile phones.

Both experiences showed me what happens when technology opens up a market before the infrastructure, business models and consumer expectations have caught up. AI presents a similar challenge: Leaders have to figure out what the technology makes possible while building a business that can actually take advantage of it.

We are applying the same thinking at our company, where we have built an AI-native executive search firm. We use AI throughout the search process while relying on human judgment to assess leadership, experience and fit.

We ask ourselves many of the same questions we ask our clients: Where can AI make a meaningful difference? Where does judgment still matter? And how do we make the best use of our team’s expertise for the complex advisory work our clients rely on us for?

AI investment will continue, but investors will become more selective. Companies will have to prove that their products solve urgent customer problems, their economics improve with scale and their growth can survive outside a generous funding market.

Technical credibility can earn a company its first check, but building a lasting business requires operating experience and commercial judgment. AI may allow companies to operate with fewer people and fewer layers, but that does not make talent less important. It puts more responsibility on the people at the top.

Investors should be asking not only whether a company has the right technology but also whether it has the right people to make the most of it.​

To save money on holiday gifts this year, Americans are using these 5 strategies that require coordination with friends and family.

Gift giving can bust a budget, so some Americans plan to have conversations with friends and family this year about setting limits around holiday gifting.

This isn’t as Scroogey as you might think: 55% of holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy that likely involves coordinating with loved ones, according to a new NerdWallet survey conducted online by The Harris Poll.

Money can be a taboo subject, especially among family and friends. But a focused discussion on gift boundaries could be the difference between staying within your budget and piling up debt this holiday season.

What other Americans are doing: 28% of holiday spenders plan to set a per-gift dollar limit with family or friends.

Why this works: It’s simple and easy to remember. Unlike some other ideas on this list, you can probably coordinate this one over text.

For best results: If you’re the one bringing up the topic, you should come with a dollar amount that would be reasonable for everyone in your gift exchange group, so no one feels excluded or overextended.

Your circle of friends and family has a lot of kids.

What other Americans are doing: 23% of holiday spenders plan to buy gifts for children in a family, but not the adults.

Why this works: Cutting out adult gifts altogether can rescue a gift budget that has undergone major “kidflation” as new children join the family.

For best results: If you still want to include adults, give a gift that’s fun for the whole family, like a board game or an experience. And make sure your kid-free loved ones are on board.

You traditionally exchange gifts one-on-one with a friend, but the last few gifts you’ve given — and received — were duds.

What other Americans are doing: 18% of holiday spenders plan to skip exchanging gifts with at least one friend or family member.

Why this works: If you’re feeling gift fatigue, there’s a chance they are, too.

For best results: Frame this as an improvement to the gift-giving tradition rather than a scaling back. Propose an alternative way to celebrate your friendship, like swapping out the $40 gift that’ll probably get shelved for a $7 coffee together.

What other Americans are doing: 16% of holiday spenders plan to do a secret Santa gift exchange, or another game that requires purchasing only one gift.

Why this works: 15% of holiday spenders list buying gifts for more people than they originally planned for as among the reasons they’re most likely to overspend this holiday season. This strategy keeps your list in check, even if the number of people playing grows.

For best results: There are bound to be people in your group for whom the rules to the game are important. If you’re the one organizing, be ready to answer questions — can you trade or steal gifts, for example, and, if so, how many times? Also, this works best for family or friend groups who aren’t likely to go rogue and buy extra gifts anyway.

You have no idea what your college friend’s kids (or spouse) are into.

What other Americans are doing: 12% of holiday spenders plan to give one shared gift per family instead of individual gifts.

Why this works: In addition to saving money, this avoids the awkwardness that comes with uninformed gift giving.

For best results: Presentation is key. Don’t sheepishly give an UNO game you clearly bought on the drive over. You may be cutting back, but enthusiasm is free.

Talking about the holidays and talking about money can be stressful conversation topics. About four in five Americans avoid discussing some money topics with family and friends, according to a 2026 survey by the CFP Board. So discussing both at once may seem daunting. But without a doubt, you’re not the only one thinking about them.

Nearly 9 in 10 (86%) holiday spenders plan to use at least one money-saving strategy this holiday season. Start with an icebreaker: “Hey, have you noticed how expensive everything is lately? Would you be open to talking about how we can do gifts this year while keeping spending under control?” This conversation might be the thing that’s secretly on everyone’s wish list.
