#3045. What Midterms Mean for Your Stocks

Fool analysts weigh in on how Democratic control of Congress could affect your portfolio.

Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, and you may be wondering what such a reshuffle means for your investments. We asked our analysts how a Democratic Congress could affect the parts of the market they follow most closely, from healthcare and energy to artificial intelligence (AI) data centers.

For quick background, Republicans will keep the White House for another two years while Democrats will take majority control of both the House and the Senate. When power splits this way, major legislation becomes harder to pass, so investors face fewer surprises from Washington. Markets usually welcome this stability, which helps explain why stocks rose Wednesday morning.

So what happens once the new Congress gets to work? A few themes stand out across our analysts’ answers:

Stocks of the major cloud operators rallied on Wednesday, after the Democratic Party swept control of both the House and the Senate and its candidates won important gubernatorial races. Amazon (AMZN +6.12%), Microsoft (MSFT +6.68%), and Alphabet (GOOG +3.25%) gained 7.2%, 6.5%, and 4.1%, respectively, as of this writing.

That reaction might seem counterintuitive, since there’s been a groundswell of public opposition to data centers. Furthermore, there were an eye-opening 50 data-center-related ballot measures across 10 states, with many supporting moratoriums or stricter regulations in the space.

Gina Hinojosa, the new Democratic governor-elect for Texas, championed freezing data center construction until the state’s lawmakers can assess the impact on water, electricity, air quality, and property rights. This could delay further development until mid-2027.

According to research firm SemiAnalysis, Texas will make up roughly 41% of new data center capacity slated for 2028. Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona also elected Democrats to top offices, and each is a hotbed of data center construction and could face similar hurdles.

Hyperscalers might benefit from stricter regulations, as it could hinder additional competition. It could also serve to slow the massive capital expenditures that have big tech investors on edge.

Democrats just got some political capital, but only a few places to spend it. Drug and biotech companies have largely thrived under Trump 2.0 while healthcare more broadly has been a mixed bag. Investors were initially fearful of huge tariffs and “most-favored nation” pricing, but ultimately realized that the policies mostly allow for business as usual. Don’t expect big changes there–Democrats are unlikely to unwind the price cuts Trump has negotiated. Instead, they will use MFN as a bargaining chip for other goals.

What goals? “Medicare for All”–the favored approach of some left-leaning Democrats–is a non-starter. The most likely goal of Congress will be to restore ACA subsidies and maybe provide some Medicaid relief. It will be a careful dance, though, since any proposals will have to overcome a veto threat.

For investors more interested in development-stage biotech, a bigger issue than policy will be interest rates, since plentiful, patient capital is required to make new drugs. That’s largely outside the hands of lawmakers. Stabilizing the grant process of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) may be an achievable goal, however.

Every election, investors try to pick winners and losers based on who’s in charge. Energy stocks show why that rarely works.

U.S. oil production boomed after Barack Obama took office in 2009—the shale revolution didn’t wait for Washington. Yet energy was the worst-performing sector of his presidency, partly because the industry was so successful it pumped too much oil and prices collapsed in 2014-2016.

Pro-energy Donald Trump took office in 2017. Energy was the worst-performing sector of his first term.

Joe Biden took office in 2021 and signed the Inflation Reduction Act, packed with clean-energy incentives, into law. Oil & Gas stocks were the best-performing sector of his presidency. Clean energy stocks plummeted more than 60%.

Trump returned in 2025 ready to “Drill, Baby, Drill.” Energy was the worst performer in his first year back, then surged in 2026 as the war in Iran sent oil prices soaring. We’ll see where it ends up.

The point is that business fundamentals, valuations, and macro trends matter far more than who’s in office. That’s true for energy, and probably most industries. If presidents can’t steer a sector, a new Congress probably won’t either.

Gaming publisher Take-Two Interactive (TTWO +7.13%) reports results on Monday, but most casual observers are looking out to the week after. That’s the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that fans have been speculating about for well over a decade.

Take-Two is a three-time Rule Breakers recommendation, going back almost two decades, and all three are beating the market by triple digits. But Take-Two has been lagging the broader market for over five years, and the stock is down around 25% year-to-date. If you think you’ve missed the new GTA cycle, it’s perhaps worth another look.

Our successes came from two distinct theses, both of which proved correct.

GTA 5 is proof that revenue from game IP can continue long after depreciation and amortization charges push down reported earnings. Expectations for GTA 6 aren’t low, but investors may still not fully appreciate the potential for long-term cash flow.

Now that post-midterm market moves are underway, do you plan to buy or trim any stock, or wait for the market to cool down?

#3044. Five Connectivity Requirements For The Intelligent Edge

Michael De Nil is the CEO and cofounder at Morse Micro—reinventing Wi-Fi for IoT.

​The first wave of connected infrastructure was built around a simple assumption: Devices would collect data, networks would transport it and most of the intelligence would live somewhere else, normally in the cloud.

Edge AI changes that architecture. Cameras, building systems, industrial equipment and energy assets are increasingly becoming intelligent endpoints capable of analyzing data and responding locally. As that happens, the network is no longer simply a transport layer. It becomes part of the system that allows distributed intelligence to function.

That means organizations need to evaluate connectivity differently. The question is no longer simply, “How fast is the network?” The more useful question is whether the network can support intelligence reliably across the environments where it will actually operate. That comes down to five requirements.

Intelligent infrastructure is often distributed well beyond traditional indoor coverage. Cameras may sit at property edges. Smart meters and home batteries may be installed in garages or utility rooms. Industrial equipment may operate across large facilities. Energy devices may be located outdoors or behind multiple physical barriers.

In those environments, adding more access points, gateways or cabling can significantly increase cost and complexity. The network therefore has to be designed around where devices actually need to operate, not around where connectivity happens to be easiest to deploy.

Edge AI devices already have to budget power for their sensing activities and the local processing. If connectivity consumes too much of that budget, the overall system becomes more difficult to deploy and maintain.

This is especially important for battery-powered cameras, sensors, meters and other devices expected to operate for extended periods without frequent maintenance. The right question is not whether a wireless technology can deliver maximum throughput; it is whether it can deliver the performance the application needs without overwhelming the device’s energy budget. That makes power efficiency part of the architecture, not simply a component specification.

At the other end of the spectrum, many low-power networks were designed around simple telemetry: a meter reading, sensor value or periodic status message.

The intelligent edge increasingly moves richer information. A camera may transmit images, event metadata or diagnostics. Industrial equipment may send more detailed operating data. Devices may require software or model updates. Energy systems may need to coordinate multiple distributed assets.

That creates a middle ground between high-throughput conventional networking and narrowband sensor connectivity. Organizations may not need maximum bandwidth everywhere, but they increasingly need meaningful bandwidth, enough to support richer data and evolving workloads without abandoning power efficiency or range.

As more intelligence moves into physical infrastructure, the consequences of a compromised endpoint increase. A simple sensor reporting temperature is one thing. A network of cameras, access systems, industrial equipment or energy assets making local decisions is another. Strong authentication, encryption, secure update mechanisms and established network-management practices therefore need to be considered from the beginning.

The same applies to network complexity. Adding proprietary gateways or isolated networking layers may solve a short-term coverage problem but can create additional systems for IT and operations teams to secure, integrate and maintain. The simpler the architecture, the easier it becomes to manage security consistently.

The intelligent edge will not be built around one device type, one vendor or one networking technology. Buildings may combine security cameras, HVAC systems, occupancy sensors and energy equipment. Industrial environments may bring together machines, sensors and monitoring platforms. Utilities may need to connect meters, batteries, solar systems and EV infrastructure. Those systems need to work within broader IP-based architectures rather than becoming isolated connectivity islands.

Standards-based networking becomes increasingly important because it allows intelligent endpoints to integrate more naturally into existing infrastructure and management systems. Newer approaches such as Wi-Fi HaLow, based on the IEEE 802.11ah standard, illustrate how the Wi-Fi ecosystem itself is evolving toward this model by combining sub-GHz reach, lower power operation, IP networking and sufficient bandwidth for richer edge applications.

The broader point is not that one wireless technology will replace every other option. Traditional Wi-Fi will remain critical for high-throughput local networks. Cellular will continue to serve mobility and wide-area applications. Other low-power technologies will remain useful for simple sensing.​

The shift is architectural. Organizations building Edge AI systems should stop evaluating connectivity around a single headline specification and instead design around the workload. Where will the device operate? How much power can it consume? What information must it exchange? How will it be secured? And how will thousands of endpoints fit into a larger network?

The intelligent edge is changing how computing is distributed across the physical world. Connectivity needs to evolve with it. For leaders designing the next generation of intelligent infrastructure, the network should no longer be treated as an afterthought. It should be designed as part of the intelligence itself.

#3043. Greif: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Greif is shutting its Sweetwater mill to exit coated recycled board, pulling capital toward higher-margin polymer containers and closures.

On its fourth-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Greif (GEF -5.60%) announced that structural cost reductions drove higher profitability in fiscal 2026. Long-term shareholders benefit as management converts these operational gains into reliable cash flow and balance sheet strength. Three takeaways stand out for long-term investors.

Management completed its original $100 million run rate cost reduction target a year ahead of schedule. The company raised its goal to $150 million by the end of fiscal 2027 to expand profit margins through the economic cycle.

The company shut its Sweetwater mill to exit coated recycled board, which is paperboard made from recycled fibers. This decision follows prior divestitures in containerboard and timberlands as management concentrates capital on higher-margin polymer containers and closure products.

Industrial demand dropped across major product categories like metal and polymer containers during the fourth quarter. Greif countered this market contraction by capturing new customer accounts across growth sectors like data center chemicals and cosmetics.

Industrial activity remains depressed across major regions, forcing a conservative baseline for the coming fiscal year.

That said, low debt levels and global scale give Greif a durable foundation to expand high-return packaging lines. Management is prioritizing network efficiency and pricing discipline to compound value regardless of where the broader economy goes.

#3042. This Janus Henderson fund manager owns CoreWeave debt — here's why he's sticking with it

CoreWeave can overcome the market's skepticism about its debt.

That isn't the consensus view — some Coreweave debt remains deeply distressed with yields above 15%. But Coreweave should power through this tough stretch, according to John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson.

"It's a little bit of overreacting," Lloyd tells CNBC, referring to the sell-off in Coreweave bonds, which have tanked along with its equity.

Lloyd owns Coreweave 9.75% bonds due in 2031 in the firm's Multi-Sector Income Fund. The yield to maturity on the debt is now 15.97%, a more than 70% jump since its issuance in April. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"Bond prices are lower, spreads are wider, yields are wider, and I don't see a huge fundamental change in the ecosystem right now that would warrant that, other than their higher cost of financing, which I think they can get creative with," Lloyd added.

CoreWeave has taken on a massive amount of debt to fund its data center buildout. The company has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans.

The market is getting nervous about how CoreWeave will be able to keep financing its data centers, and at what cost. Its stock has tumbled 20% over the past week, while the spread on its five-year credit default swaps is nearly 1,081 basis points — lower than earlier in the session but up 13% week over week. Spreads of 1,000 basis points and above are generally a sign of credit distress.

CoreWeave shares moved roughly 2% higher on Tuesday, after tumbling over the past several days and hitting a 52-week low earlier in the session. Its bond yields and spreads remain highly elevated.

Lloyd believes the selloff is a bump in the road for the neocloud company.

The market has been spooked by the jump in Treasury rates, which pushes up funding costs for companies, he explained. The focus largely turned to companies like CoreWeave that have refinance risk when rates move higher, he said.

CoreWeave leverage is high with a debt-to-equity ratio of 702%, up from 290% a year ago. Moreover, CoreWeave will spend an estimated $36.4 billion on capital expenditures this year against Ebitda of $7.5 billion, according to consensus estimates.

Revenue and Ebitda will ramp up next year, hitting $26.5 billion and $16.7 billion respectively, analysts estimate. But capex will hit $47.9 billion, indicating the company may need to finance its data center buildout with more equity issuance and/or debt.

Lloyd isn't necessarily worried about CoreWeave's ability to finance its capital expenditures, despite the fact that its capex outweighs its free-cash flow.

"Next year … they're going to be generating operating free-cash flow that'll support some of that capex need," he said.

The company can also turn to other methods of funding, like more GPU financing, which will allow it to borrow against its graphics processing units or rental contracts, he noted. In addition, CoreWeave could ask its biggest customers — including Microsoft, Meta Platforms and OpenAI — to increase their prepayments, he added.

"They can probably get creative enough where they don't even need to come to the high-yield market," Lloyd said.

The company also doesn't have any near-term maturities, which means it isn't facing a refinancing risk anytime soon, he added.

Meanwhile the supply/demand dynamic should remain tight across the AI compute landscape. Overall adoption rates within the ecosystem are running above consensus demand curves, he said. Add to that a bottleneck in supply, with chips and memory power sold out, and it's a nice set up for CoreWeave.

"All data point to the business model functioning very, very well," Lloyd said. "CoreWeave is one of the best-in-class at getting data centers up and actually running them," he added, noting that CoreWeave's financials have been improving throughout the year.

Another turning point could come if Anthropic goes forth with an IPO, expected in November, followed by OpenAI. Successful IPOs for the frontier labs could soothe market nerves and help support the neocloud operators.

"You just need more of those data points where people become more comfortable with the AI demand side," Lloyd said.

CoreWeave still needs to convince markets it can handle higher market rates and get through the financing bottlenecks.

Lloyd sees the company making it, albeit with some bumps along the way. The bonds should recover, he says, "just not in that straight line."

#3041. American Express vs. PayPal: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

American Express commands premium margins and a closed-loop advantage, while PayPal trades at a significant valuation discount despite stronger profitability metrics.

The payments landscape is evolving rapidly as traditional financial giants face off against digital-first innovators. Investors must decide if the premium resilience of American Express (AXP +2.18%) or the digital reach of PayPal (PYPL +3.42%) offers better value today.

American Express caters to high-net-worth individuals and corporate clients through a unique integrated model. PayPal remains a leader in online transactions and mobile payments, processing trillions in volume. Comparing their growth and risk profiles helps clarify which fits a 2027 investment horizon.

American Express operates a unique integrated payments model, acting as both the card issuer and the network operator. This closed-loop system allows it to capture the full value of every transaction while gathering proprietary data on high-spending consumers and businesses. A key pillar of its growth strategy is its partnership with Delta Air Lines (DAL +7.16%), which serves as its largest strategic partner. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business, but it also provides a steady stream of premium, loyal cardholders.

Financial performance remains robust as the company expands its merchant network and refreshes its card offerings. In fiscal 2025, revenue reached nearly $80.5 billion, representing growth of approximately 8.4% compared to the prior year. The company reported net income of roughly $10.8 billion for the period, resulting in a net margin of 13.5%. These figures highlight a consistent ability to generate profit from its high-fee credit products and merchant discount revenue.

The balance sheet reflects the specific requirements of a large financial institution. As of Amex’s December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio -- which measures total debt divided by shareholder equity -- was roughly 1.7. Its current ratio, a metric that tracks the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, was approximately 0.3. In fiscal 2025, the company generated roughly $16 billion in free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

PayPal maintains a massive two-sided network that connects roughly 439 million active accounts across more than 200 global markets. The company provides essential digital tools for both consumers and merchants, including its namesake checkout service and the popular Venmo app. It is a dominant player among fintech stocks, focusing on making digital money movement simple and personalized. Its merchant solutions include branded and unbranded checkout options that help businesses of all sizes accept global payments.

Top-line growth has continued as the company prioritizes high-margin transaction services and cost discipline. In fiscal 2025, revenue reached approximately $33.2 billion, reflecting nearly 4.3% year-over-year growth. The company delivered net income of close to $5.2 billion, achieving a net margin of roughly 15.8%. While its revenue growth rate is lower than some younger competitors, its high net margin indicates a mature and profitable business model.

PayPal maintains a healthy liquidity position to support its global operations. According to its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carried a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.5. Its current ratio was roughly 1.3, suggesting a comfortable cushion for meeting its immediate financial obligations. For fiscal 2025, the company produced close to $5.6 billion in free cash flow, providing ample capital for share buybacks or further product innovation.

American Express faces intense global competition from other payment networks like Visa (V +3.84%) and Mastercard (MA +3.94%), as well as emerging alternative payment providers. It deals with significant dependence on key business partners, particularly its co-branded relationship with Delta Air Lines. Geopolitical instability and trade wars also pose risks, as these events can disrupt global travel and reduce the billed business volume from its premium cardholders. Additionally, as a highly regulated financial institution, it must manage ongoing compliance costs and strict data protection requirements.

PayPal must navigate a landscape of sophisticated cybersecurity threats and potential system outages that could damage its reputation and lead to financial loss. The company faces stiff competition from established tech giants like Amazon (AMZN +6.12%) and new disruptive technologies that could change how consumers pay. Extensive global regulatory and licensing requirements add complexity to its operations, particularly regarding anti-money laundering laws. Furthermore, its credit product offerings expose the company to potential borrower defaults and legal challenges regarding how it manages those receivables.

PayPal currently appears significantly cheaper than American Express based on both earnings and sales multiples, suggesting the market is pricing in slower growth for the digital payment pioneer.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

PayPal's valuation is clearly lower than Amex's; investors evidently don't see the former growing much from here. While I don't think historical stock performance necessarily dictates future stock performance, I kind of understand why investors are willing to give American Express a premium valuation relative to PayPal.

Over the past 10 years, Amex has outperformed PayPal by more than 250 percentage points. Worse yet, PayPal hasn't even kept pace with the broader market, trailing the S&P 500 badly in that time frame. Indeed, PayPal's returns barely outpaced inflation over the past decade. The payments specialist has been a pretty terrible investment.

I concede that Amex's single-digit revenue growth is not super exciting in and of itself. Its net margin is also just fine. But I will take a good-enough company over a stagnating stock any day. American Express gets my vote for 2027.

#3038. Financial Language AI In The Cloud: Matching The Model To The Job

Srinivas Chippagiri is a technology leader with over 15 years experience in cloud computing and distributed systems across multiple domains.

Financial firms process enormous volumes of text every day, from news wires and regulatory filings to earnings commentary and social media posts. Large language models (LLMs), the systems behind modern chatbots, offer new ways to analyze this information at scale. But putting these systems to work raises questions that go beyond model performance: Where will the model run, how much will each request cost and who is accountable for its output?​​

In my experience building enterprise AI and cloud systems, teams that settle those questions early tend to ship more dependable systems than teams that start with the model alone.

​Sentiment analysis labels a passage as positive, negative or neutral. It compresses a long document into something a dashboard or an analyst’s queue can use. It is also a narrow signal. A sentence can be upbeat in tone and still say little about a company’s prospects. Reading sentiment is not forecasting markets, and a sentiment label is not a prediction.​

Bigger is not automatically better. Models adapted to financial text, such as FinBERT, a language model pretrained for financial sentiment analysis, illustrate how domain adaptation can make a compact system competitive on focused reading tasks, even with limited labeled data.​

​That matters most at cloud scale. Cloud computing, as NIST defines it, offers “on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable computing resources” that can expand and contract quickly. Inference (running the model on new text) may be billed per request or token through managed services, or per instance-hour when self-hosted. Either way, a compact model that performs comparably can meaningfully reduce the bill across millions of daily headlines. I’ve seen organizations find that a smaller model works best for handling routine sentiment analysis while reserving a larger model for more complex passages where the meaning is less clear or depends on additional context.​

Fine-tuning, which means continuing a model’s training on specialized text, makes this practical. Efficient techniques such as QLoRA compress the base model and train only a small set of added parameters, lowering the hardware needed to adapt large models and bringing experimentation within reach of smaller teams.​

Neutral and hedged language is often the hardest case. Financial writing often uses cautious language to describe results that meet expectations or outlooks that remain uncertain. These statements can be difficult to classify because they convey neither clearly positive nor clearly negative sentiment. ​

A single headline accuracy score can conceal this. A model may look strong overall while quietly mishandling the ambiguous middle, which is where analysts most need care. Teams that examine errors across each sentiment category and test models on real-world financial text, including ambiguous or inconsistently worded passages, can identify weaknesses that overall accuracy scores and clean benchmark datasets may overlook. This helps them catch classification errors before those errors carry through to downstream reports.​

A live feed of news and filings arrives in bursts around earnings season and market events. Autoscaling, which adds or removes servers as traffic changes, can absorb those bursts, but only once a latency budget (the longest acceptable wait for a result) is defined. Without one, scaling decisions become guesswork and costs drift upward.​

Data location matters, too. Managed AI services reduce operational work, while self-hosting open models inside a private cloud network may suit organizations handling regulated or confidential data, or those with data-residency obligations. The trade-off is between convenience and control.​

Cloud-native tooling can support governance. Audit logs record who ran what, and access controls limit who can change a model. Monitoring can flag drift, meaning a gradual mismatch between the text a model was tuned on and the text it now sees. Human review queues can route low-confidence or neutral-looking cases to an analyst. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, a voluntary guide for identifying and managing AI risks, offers a useful anchor for organizing these practices.​

Organizations that build oversight into the architecture from the start, rather than adding it after launch, tend to find audits and incident reviews far less painful.​​

I expect AI for financial text to become less about running the largest model and more about matching a model to each job. Compact, domain-tuned systems may handle high-volume reading while larger ones may take on difficult reasoning, and people will supervise both. Evaluation and monitoring tooling will probably matter as much as the models themselves.​

When it comes to AI for financial text, the best infrastructure choice is often the model that is accurate enough, affordable at scale and explainable enough to oversee, rather than the largest one available.​​​

#3036. If You'd Invested $1,000 Alongside Warren Buffett in Coca-Cola, Here's How Much You'd Have Today

Coca-Cola has stood the test of time as an investment, and remains one of Berkshire Hathaway's largest stock holdings.

Coca-Cola (KO +1.05%) is one of Warren Buffett's most famous investments. By the time he stopped picking up more shares of the beverage company in 1994, the position had grown to dominate Berkshire Hathaway's (BRKA +3.93%) (BRKB +3.95%) marketable equity portfolio, accounting for more than a third of its value. Today, Coca-Cola remains one of Berkshire's largest stock holdings, though it has been more than 30 years since the conglomerate last bought shares.

Everyday investors had the opportunity to invest right alongside Buffett. He disclosed the purchases in the company's quarterly SEC filings and detailed his reasoning for them in his annual shareholder letters. If you had invested just $1,000 in Coca-Cola at around the time Buffett started accumulating shares, your position today would be worth a nice chunk of change.

Buffett first bought Coca-Cola for Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio in 1988. That year, he paid a total of $592.5 million for just over 14 million shares. His average purchase price was $41.81 per share. He added to the position the following year, paying an average of about $47 per share to bring Berkshire's total share count to 23.35 million. Over the following years, Coca-Cola split its shares twice, bringing Berkshire's share count to 93.4 million by the end of 1993. In 1994, Buffett made his final purchase of Coca-Cola shares, adding another 6.6 million shares at an average price of $41.66 to bring Berkshire's total share count to a round 100 million.

If you'd invested $1,000 in 1988 at the same price as Buffett, you'd end up with 24 shares (assuming you were willing to invest just a few bucks over $1,000 to get that final share). Since then, Coca-Cola has split its stock four times, moves that would have turned those original 24 shares into 384 shares. Those shares would be worth nearly $37,000 at today's price.

But that understates the total return of the investment by a wide margin. Among the factors that attracted Buffett to Coca-Cola are its strong free-cash-flow and earnings growth, which have supported its reliable annual dividend increases. An investor who bought 24 shares of Coca-Cola in 1988 would have collected $7.20 in dividends each quarter from the company. Last month, that investor would've collected a total of $203.52 in dividends. Since 1988, the total value of the dividend payments on that original $1,000 investment would add up to $12,581.76.

Adding the value of the shares and the total dividend payout would bring your total return on investment to about $49,500. But if an investor had opted to reinvest the dividends into Coca-Cola stock, they'd now own over 960 shares worth over $92,000. Either way, that's a fantastic return on a $1,000 investment.

Coca-Cola has what Buffett calls a wide moat: a competitive advantage that protects its business against both rivals and macroeconomic forces. In this case, the moat stems from its strong brand portfolio, which has enabled it to continue raising prices and maintain a dominant market share in the soda business for decades. Management has strategically added to the company's beverage brand portfolio via acquisitions and product development, and it now sports 32 brands with at least $1 billion in annual sales. Those strong brands enable it to charge premium prices and maintain margins even amid periods of high inflation or macroeconomic turbulence.

The company's scale also gives it leverage to drive down bottling costs and control more shelf space in grocery aisles. The latter advantage allows it to easily introduce new products or boost the visibility of newly acquired brands. The result has been steady revenue growth and margin expansion. Coca-Cola's organic revenue climbed 7% in the third quarter while its comparable operating margin expanded by 1 percentage point to 32.9%.

Coca-Cola's stock price has climbed significantly in 2026. Its strong operating results and steady free cash flow may have attracted investors looking to diversify away from cash-burning AI stocks. Trading near 28 times expected forward earnings, the stock looks somewhat expensive, so investors looking to put $1,000 to work in Coca-Cola stock may be better off waiting for a better entry point. That said, there's nothing about the company's recent results or management's outlook that should give investors any reason to sell the stock.

#3033. ​The AI Advantage Hiding In The Foundation Of Your Drupal CMS

Jon Stewart is the President of ZenSource, an open source platform combining CMS, enterprise level cloud hosting and support.

Through my work helping organizations build and manage Drupal websites, I know that Drupal has never been the loudest name in content management. While newer platforms often competed on simplicity and flash, Drupal kept investing in something less glamorous: structure, governance and clean data. Now, as AI changes how people find information, those quieter investments are paying off.

Search is shifting from ranking pages to being understood. AI assistants and answer engines don’t just index your site; they also extract, summarize and cite it. A buyer researching vendors increasingly gets an AI-generated answer before visiting a single website. Whether your organization appears in that answer depends less on keywords and more on how clearly your content can be interpreted. Platforms built on structured, well-governed content are the ones best suited to help companies succeed.

If you’ve been on Drupal for years, you’ve likely been doing AI optimization without calling it that.

Semantic URLs: Clean, human-readable paths signal topic and hierarchy to crawlers and language models, telling an AI system what a page is about before it reads a word.

Structured Content: Content types, fields and taxonomies break information into labeled pieces. An event has a date, a location and a speaker. That is exactly what retrieval systems need to answer questions accurately instead of guessing from a wall of text.

Machine-Readable Metadata: Schema.org markup, metatags and sitemaps help AI identify entities, authors and relationships.

API-First Architecture: Content flows through standard APIs to AI applications, agents and new channels without rebuilding.

Accessibility And Multilingual Support: Semantic markup built for screen readers is also easier for machines to parse, and structured translations extend your visibility across markets.

Governance: Revisions, workflows and permissions keep content accurate. When AI quotes you, accuracy is your brand.​​

​When I help long-time Drupal organizations prepare for AI-driven discovery, there are two key points I focus on: making structured content easy to maintain and introducing AI capabilities without sacrificing control. ​​

In my work, one of the most common reasons content models break down is that editors bypass structure when it slows them down. In higher education, for example, I regularly see program pages rebuilt as free-form layouts, with deadlines and tuition tucked into tables or images rather than maintained in dedicated fields. The information is available to human readers, but it becomes harder for AI systems to retrieve and interpret reliably.

This is why the authoring experience matters as much as the underlying architecture. For Drupal users, visual editing tools like Drupal Canvas can help bridge the gap between editorial flexibility and structured data, but it’s also important to design content templates that give editors flexibility while keeping key information in dedicated, reusable fields.

AI can help organizations retrieve information, answer questions and identify opportunities to improve existing content. But the ability to generate a plausible response does not establish that the response is accurate, current or appropriate to publish.​

In practice, this means grounding AI applications in trusted organizational content, making their sources visible and establishing clear approval requirements for consequential changes. It also means considering how easily an organization can change AI providers as capabilities, costs and requirements evolve. An architecture that separates content management from model selection gives technology leaders more flexibility without requiring them to surrender governance.​​

These principles can ultimately apply regardless of which content management system an organization uses, and the objective is to make reliable information easier for both people and machines to use while preserving the controls that keep it trustworthy.​​​​

Here are some additional changes that I’ve seen make the greatest difference:

• Audit your content model. Years of quick fixes often leave important information buried in body text. I regularly find event dates, locations and eligibility rules written into paragraphs, which AI assistants then misread or skip. Usually the fields to hold that information already exist and simply went unused, so the fix is migration and editorial discipline, not a rebuild. Moving key details into dedicated fields makes them visible to AI.

• Expand structured data. Make sure organizations, people, events, articles and FAQs carry consistent Schema.org markup.

• Clean up URLs and redirects. Consistent alias patterns and resolved redirect chains help crawlers and AI systems map your site.

• Retire stale content. Archive or update outdated pages so AI isn’t summarizing information you no longer stand behind.

• Add an accuracy check to governance. Most workflows ask whether content is ready to publish. For high-stakes content such as pricing, eligibility and policy, also ask whether you’d stand behind it if AI quoted it out of context.

• Stay current. Running a supported version is the gateway to the AI capabilities arriving now.

• Is content structured or trapped in page-sized rich text fields?

• Can AI tools and agents access it through open APIs and standards?

• Can you switch AI models as the market changes?

• Do humans stay in control, with review, audit trails and permissions?

• Do you own your data and hosting choices?

A “no” to any of these points is a sign that it might be worth further developing your strategy.

Many long-time Drupal organizations are approaching a major version upgrade, a consolidation or a redesign. Treat it as a content modeling exercise, not a lift-and-shift. Moving messy content to a newer version simply relocates the mess. The AI value comes from restructuring as you go: defining content types around how your audiences ask questions, establishing consistent taxonomies and setting governance rules from day one.

AI is also changing the economics of this work. It can help map legacy content to new structures, flag duplicates, suggest tags and clean up inconsistencies that once required extensive manual effort. Discovery, stakeholder review and QA still take real time, but the heavy lifting in between is faster than many organizations expect.

The organizations that win in AI-driven discovery won’t be the ones with the most AI features. They’ll be the ones whose content is easiest to understand, trust and reuse.​

#3032. Could $10,000 Invested in ASML Set You Up for Life?

It could, but how profitable that position could be for you will likely depend on your time horizon and commitment.

ASML Holding (ASML -3.60%) has a competitive moat of a type that most companies can only dream about. It might be one of the best stocks to own in the world, given its competitive advantages.

But can an investment in just one company, no matter how dominant it is in its field, set you up for life?

Getting that sort of return on investment from a stock is a tall order, and to do so would require a strong commitment. Even then, it's a long shot. But if one stock could do that, ASML might have the best chance.

ASML is a Dutch company that is a major equipment supplier to the semiconductor industry. It makes the lithography machines needed to manufacture semiconductor chips, and it's by far the dominant player in its niche, with roughly 83% market share.

But more specifically, it is the only company that has the technological capability to produce extreme ultraviolet lithography (EUV) machines, which in turn are the only machines able to make today's high-performance AI chips. It literally enjoys 100% market share in EUV lithography machines, which are used by leading foundries such as Taiwan Semiconductor and Samsung.

In the third quarter, ASML's revenue increased by 26% to 11.7 billion euros from the previous quarter, not year over year. Net income was 5 billion euros, up 72% from Q2.

In Q4, it anticipates revenue of 14.2 billion euros and 15.2 billion euros, up 26% from Q3 at the midpoint. Net sales for fiscal 2026 are forecast to land between 44 billion euros and 45 billion euros, up 36% at the midpoint over fiscal 2025. Its gross margin is projected to be 56%, up from 52.8% in 2025.

And demand for its systems is only increasing as we head into 2027 and 2028 -- and beyond. The supply of machines it currently plans to manufacture in both 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand, so the company is looking to boost its own production capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase already planned, ASML President and CEO Christophe Fouquet said.

"We are increasingly receiving orders for 2028, and customers are also expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030," Fouquet added.

ASML is so well positioned because of its technological advantages.

Due to the complexity of making an EUV lithography system, ASML had to spend 30 years developing the technology before it was able to bring it to market. At this point, considering the state of the competitive landscape, it would take perhaps 10 to 15 years of development for a would-be rival to match the EUV machines that ASML currently has, according to analysts -- and by then, ASML -- which has continued to push the technology forward with its latest high-numerical-aperture (high NA) EUV machines -- will doubtless be working on even more advanced iterations.

Plus, ASML is a supplier to the entire industry, so it doesn't matter if foundry or manufacturer names change, or if new chipmakers gain ground; they all will have no choice but to come to ASML for equipment.

There aren't many stocks that have performed better than ASML has since it went public in 1995. The stock is up by about 47% over the past year.

It has a 10-year average annualized return of 32%, and over the past 20 years, it has posted an average return of 23%.

Since the company went public, ASML stock has averaged a 20% return.

So, assume that dominance continues for at least the next two decades, due to the unfolding AI boom, which Fouquet said could last 10 to 15 years, and ASML's massive technology advantages.

Suppose you invested $10,000 in ASML stock right now, reinvested your dividends, and held on for 20 years. If the stock matches the 23% average annualized return it has delivered over the past 20 years, you would have a stake worth about $628,000. And if you contributed $100 per month to that initial investment, in 20 years, you would have a stake worth about $983,000.

And if you held it for 30 years and averaged a 20% return, you would have about $2.4 million. With $100 per month contributed, that would jump to $3.9 million.

So, yes, investing in ASML could set you up for life. But you'd have to buy the stock, hold it for at least 20 years, and also be diligent about adding to your position every month. You would also be assuming returns similar to those it has had in the past. Given its strengths and the AI cycle that we are in, those high long-term returns are certainly in play.

Dave Kovaleski has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends ASML and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

» Is now a good time to buy? See NerdWallet’s analysis

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit.

The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#3030. The Profitability Play: Pricing Strategy For What's Next

​When markets become less predictable, pricing decisions can determine whether a company can sustain revenue growth. Government policy shifts, supply chain and energy disruptions, and aggressive competition can quickly change what customers are willing to pay and what it costs to serve them. Pricing strategies built around yesterday’s conditions can leave businesses reacting too slowly to protect profitability.

At the heart of every business lies an engine that drives revenue, profitability and customer engagement. And at the heart of that engine is the balance between the thing you build and the value it delivers, defined by the price.

Getting pricing right increases customer satisfaction while creating an agreement of value. In other words, it produces the profit that powers your future. Yet, many businesses fail to fully leverage this advantage.​

Unprofitable growth occurs when companies sacrifice too much margin to win business. Heavy discounting may help meet short-term revenue targets, but it leaves less profit to invest in product development and other building opportunities, all while competitors are supporting sustainable market position.

Much of the unpredictability is beyond the capacity of traditional planning since it comes from broad macro trends and the action of external parties. Organizations must embrace an economic and business landscape that’s defined not by punctuated periods of change but rather by systemic unpredictability that’s a permanent aspect of the global economy. The pricing strategy must become more responsive, more situationally aware and more resilient to sudden changes.​

Companies can no longer rely on expansion alone to succeed—pricing is the only business function that directly translates the value you create into the revenue you keep.

Yet, according to a Simon-Kucher global study, “only 40% of companies rank pricing as their top profit lever.” At the same time, the price realization rate (when businesses can actually get the prices they set) has fallen to 43% as buyers push back on pricing models and demand higher discounts and competitors compete aggressively for customers.​​

The gap between intended prices and realized prices is where businesses can lose profitability without fully understanding why. A company may have a well-defined pricing strategy on paper, but if sales teams routinely discount to close deals, pricing guidance arrives too late or changes go unnoticed, the intended results may never materialize.​

AI-based pricing technology can help companies respond more quickly, but its value depends on the quality of the information behind its recommendations and how effectively those recommendations reach the people making commercial decisions.

Data-driven pricing guidance can make a measurable difference in how sales teams negotiate. According to a 2024 study from Bain, 74% of sales representatives and managers with data-driven deal guidance said they were confident negotiating prices with customers.

For those businesses that are able to fully engage AI in their pricing approach, the results can be significant: In the same Bain study, businesses utilizing AI in this way reported a 12% higher win rate.

​​This need to engage pricing with business operations applies in both directions. Feeding pricing guidance to sellers at the point of interaction with a buyer helps drive up margins. And feeding win/loss data into your AI model creates pricing models that meet customer and market changes as they occur.

Building a pricing strategy that can provide profitable growth in even the most turbulent macroeconomic landscape is clearly a powerful competitive and financial tool.

There are, fundamentally, three key elements to achieving such a pricing strategy:

1. Businesses should start by identifying where price realization breaks down. Compare planned prices with actual transaction prices, then examine discount patterns by product, customer segment, sales team and deal outcome. This helps distinguish between discounts that are necessary to remain competitive and those that are eroding margins without meaningfully improving win rates.​​​

2. Use AI to accelerate pricing agility but do so with a clear view on data quality and provenance. Before deploying AI-driven pricing, assess whether the underlying data is accurate, current and representative of the customers being served.

3. Ensure the pricing strategy is operationally integrated into go-to-market functions. Assign clear ownership for reviewing that feedback and updating pricing guidance so the strategy evolves alongside the market.​

An effective and enabled pricing function is an essential part of a company’s overall commerce engine. This approach embeds pricing as part of a clear chain of commerce data and processes, helping businesses respond to changing markets and winning deals without sacrificing profit.​

#3029. Champion Homes: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Factory-built housing is winning first-time buyers, but material cost inflation is squeezing margins before price increases catch up.

On its second-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, Champion Homes (SKY +11.35%) reported net sales growth of 6.2% over the prior year. For long-term investors, the company's expansion into company-owned sales centers provides higher average selling prices and direct access to homebuyers. Three key takeaways from the call highlight how management is steering the business.

Management is expanding captive retail, which refers to company-owned sales centers that sell directly to homebuyers rather than through independent dealers. Controlling these outlets lets Champion Homes capture higher retail margins and strengthen customer engagement across its footprint.

Input costs for steel and petroleum-based materials accelerated late in the quarter. Management is using targeted price increases and sourcing efficiencies to offset those expenses. But price realization tends to lag raw material cost hikes, so margins feel the squeeze in the near term.

Elevated mortgage rates and expensive site-built housing are pushing new buyers toward factory-built alternatives. Champion Homes is meeting that demand by updating home aesthetics and expanding digital marketing leads to reach buyers who might not have considered manufactured housing before.

Orders are expanding across multiple channels, and management expects third-quarter revenue growth of 8% to 10% year over year despite persistent macroeconomic inflation.

The business relies on its captive retail scale, backlog lead times, and cash position to navigate input cost swings. And management continues to execute on strategic acquisitions alongside organic growth.

#3027. BlackRock's Rick Rieder sees 'historic' opportunity in high-quality bonds

Investors may be wary of the volatility hitting parts of the bond market right now, but they have an "historic" opportunity to grab attractive yields in high-quality credit, Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Hypothetically, it's now possible for investors to build a diversified portfolio that yields more than 7% with less than three years of duration and an average credit quality of A-, he said. Duration is a measurement of a bond's price sensitivity to fluctuations in rates, and issues with shorter maturities tend to have lower duration.

"Not only is it historic in that these yields are where they are, but the only time these yields are ever here is when there's some problem, like an economic problem or default problem," Rieder said in an interview about his fourth-quarter outlook, released Wednesday.

That isn't the case now, where the economy remains strong, he said. "So you don't really have to worry about defaults of any significance."

While Rieder didn't specifically identify the credits in the aforementioned portfolio, the iShares Aaa - A Rated Corporate Bond ETF (QLTA) has a 30-day SEC yield of 5.68% and an effective duration of 6.48 years — higher than Rieder's low duration focus.

The iShares Flexible Income Active ETF (BINC), which is managed by Rieder, has a 5.66% 30-day SEC yield and three-year effective duration, but its portfolio extends beyond investment-grade credit.

Rieder sees the best opportunity right now in investment-grade corporate bonds — which he pointed out he hasn't said "in a really long time." Investment grade bonds are rated AAA through BBB- by S&P and Fitch, while Moody's rates them Aaa through Baa3.

That includes hyperscaler bonds, which have flooded the market with issuance this year as they ramp up their AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have issued a total of about $228.4 billion in bonds year to date, as of Oct. 20, according to LSEG.

"They're very low leverage. They have tremendous amounts of cash flow coming in," Rieder said of the hyperscalers in general. "You're now getting to buy these entities which are higher quality, paying you a very attractive yield to get it."

Rieder's iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has upped its allocation to investment-grade corporates to 14.3% of its portfolio. In July, that stood at 8.5%.

That said, investors need to be patient and sit tight since rates could still move higher from here, he advised.

"Your starting point is by far your best barometer of what your return is going to be," he noted. "So if you get seven and a quarter, maybe you get eight, maybe you get six, but ... if your holding period is a year or longer, you're going to get that yield."

Caution should also be exercised outside of investment-grade credit, which requires more selectivity and deep research, he warned. That includes AI names.

"There's parts of the data center supply that's not hyperscaler guaranteed or hyperscaler backed," he said. "That we've been more cautious around, and we'll continue to be."

The bond market, particularly high-yield credit, has been rocked as investor concern grows over the massive amount of debt some companies are taking out to fund their artificial intelligence build-out.

Junk-rated CoreWeave has become the poster child, seeing its stock drop, bond yields jump and credit-default spreads widen. Oracle, which is sitting in the lower end of investment grade and is seen as a bellwether on the broader AI market, has also taken some hits.

Rieder is also keeping an eye on the Federal Reserve, which is expected to raise its federal funds rate again in December to combat inflation. The market is currently pricing in a nearly 90% probability that the central bank will hike at that time, according to the CME Group FedWatch tool.

The money manager expects that to happen, although he does not agree with it. Higher rates are hurting parts of the economy, like housing, while not having much of an impact on other areas — such as tech companies' capital expenditures, which have become a big driver of growth, he said.

"They're not borrowing off the overnight funds rate," Rieder noted. "There's a lot of floating rate finance in housing, credit card, auto loan finance, and you're seeing those areas already under pressure."

Instead, the market is and will continue to price the AI supply coming into the market, he added.

Rieder sees a number of possible risks ahead, including rising levels of government debt across the globe. In the United States, the budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026.

"The more the central banks raise the rates, the cost of debt to these to already indebted governments is something we've got to be careful about over time," he said.

Bond supply coming from AI companies should also be watched.

"With the amount of supply that's coming — data center, hyperscaler — there's some crowding-out effect that's taking place," he said. "With government rates moving higher, that is something that we just got to keep an eye on."

In the meantime, Rieder would just continue to reap the rewards of high investment-grade yields "and smile a lot," he said.

#3026. 20 Must-Have Security Controls When Outsourcing Sensitive Workloads

As companies rely more heavily on third-party providers for infrastructure and computing capacity, they’re increasingly placing sensitive applications and data in environments outside their direct control. When workloads involve confidential information or critical business operations, relying on outside providers creates additional security and oversight challenges. A provider’s security assurances alone aren’t enough to guarantee that company data and systems remain protected.

Before moving these workloads outside their own environments, organizations need to consider which safeguards will help them maintain visibility and control while protecting sensitive information. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council share the controls companies should insist on before entrusting sensitive workloads to third-party providers.

Companies should work to ensure they are clear on the contractual terms associated with the use of these external computing environments, especially as they relate to access to environments and data, usage terms remaining exclusive to the owner/operator, and provisions about backups and other redundancy practices and methods. These practices have a history but require some modernization to ensure risk is managed in the current era of external reliance. - Charlie Sanchez, Black & Veatch

Insist on verifiable control over where data and models run and who can touch them. Before moving sensitive workloads, require customer-managed encryption keys, no training on your data, and audit logs you can inspect. In healthcare, that means a HIPAA-compliant BAA and proof that PHI never leaves your approved environment. Trust, but verify continuously. - David Talby, John Snow Labs

Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?

Ensure that there is a tested ability to revoke third-party access, rather than just a contractual obligation. Implement a gate for QE acceptance by ensuring that revocation denies access to sensitive information by active sessions and automated processes, even when the support team of the provider cannot be reached. - Kavitha Thiyagarajan, Newrez LLC

Always insist on holding your own encryption keys outside the provider’s environment. Contracts and certifications describe what a provider promises, but key custody is something you can verify and enforce yourself. If you control the keys, a provider breach, a legal demand or a change of jurisdiction is far less likely to expose your data without you. This is especially important in a sovereign compliance context. - Paul Speciale, Scality

Organizations must insist on absolute data sovereignty and immutable auditability, not just basic access controls. With AI-driven processing, companies need explicit zero-data-retention guarantees, customer-controlled encryption keys, and complete traceability over how data is processed. Sensitive workloads must never be used for background model training or vendor analytics, with real-time audit logs and instant access revocation built in by default. - Chris Brown, Sngular

Insist on a way to run without the vendor. The system should run inside your own cloud or an isolated environment so that personal identifiers arrive scrambled and the vendor never holds the key. Then, add source code in escrow with an independent agent and a license that keeps you running if the vendor fails. If the vendor can switch you off or read your data, the workload is not really yours. - Vivek Thomas, AISensum

Before moving sensitive workloads, require proof that the provider can isolate your data and limit privileged access. Review independent testing, access logs and remediation practices—not just policy documents. If the provider cannot demonstrate that those controls operate effectively and are retested after material changes, the workload should not move. - Brian Harmison, Corsica Technologies

Insist on an architecture that minimizes data movement. Sensitive data should stay in the company’s environment whenever possible, with only the metadata or security findings needed by the provider shared externally. Every additional copy creates another retention, residency and access problem that has to be secured. - Asaf Kochan, Sentra

Before moving sensitive workloads to a third party, companies should insist on continuous visibility and policy enforcement. It’s not enough to trust security certifications. Organizations need real-time insight into where data resides, who accesses it, how it’s used and whether it meets compliance requirements. Strong controls, auditability and zero-trust principles ensure risks are detected and managed before they become business or regulatory issues. - Hemant Soni, CAPGEMINI AMERICA INC.

Demand a clear “kill switch.” If a vendor is hosting sensitive workloads, your company should be able to quickly cut off access, revoke credentials, and move or isolate data if something goes wrong. Trust is useful, but control over your own exit is what really protects you. - Margarita Simonova, ILoveMyQA

I’d want a very clear understanding of access. Who can reach the workload, what can they do, and how quickly can that access be removed? As systems become more connected, small gaps in permissions can create much larger risks. Clear ownership and tightly managed access are worth establishing before sensitive workloads move anywhere. - Deniz Gezgin, Eightpoint

Security and assurance mean knowing a provider won’t misuse your data or intellectual property to build a competing product. This was a major concern when AWS, Azure and Google entered the cloud market. Companies feared providers would learn from what they built and compete with them. The cloud companies were careful not to cross that line. With AI, we’re seeing the same concern return, and some frontier AI companies are crossing it. - Srinivas Mukkamala, Securin Inc.

Strong vendor management is essential, but if I could only ask for one thing, it would be a SOC 2 report. It’s not a complete security assessment, but it provides some of the best security and control visibility available from a single document—provided you actually review it. - Shane O’Donnell, Centric Consulting

Companies should insist on legally binding agreements requiring third-party providers to comply with their data processing governance framework. These agreements must define data ownership, permitted processing activities, security standards, access controls, audit rights and accountability for breaches. Outsourcing infrastructure should not mean surrendering control over sensitive data or responsibility for its governance. - Eranda Maldeniya, Enterprise Analytics

Insist on the right to audit and the right to get your data back, in usable form, on exit. Performance SLAs are table stakes; the real control is what happens when the relationship ends or the provider is breached. In regulated work, you answer to the regulator for data you don’t hold. If you can’t inspect it and can’t leave with it, you don’t control it. - Mayur Khandelwal, EXL

Ask for the list of non-human identities on their side that can touch your workload. Every provider talks about which humans have admin access. Nobody volunteers the service accounts, monitoring agents and automation inside their environment that read your data as part of normal operations. If they can’t produce that list, the control conversation hasn’t started yet. - Nidhi Jain, CloudEagle.ai

Make remote attestation a go-live requirement for sensitive workloads. Before deployment, teams should verify that the workload is running in an approved environment, with the expected code and access controls intact. If that proof cannot be produced, the workload should not move outside the enterprise. - Dr. Chiranjiv Roy, C5i.ai

Know exactly what happens to your data once it leaves your environment. Before adopting a third-party service, require clear documentation on where data is processed, how long it is retained, who can access it, and whether it can be used for secondary purposes, including AI model training. Make these requirements enforceable through contractual terms. - Anastasia Georgievskaya, Haut.AI

Insist on a joint incident drill before anything moves. The contract and the SOC 2 report tell you what is supposed to happen. A tabletop with the provider’s on-call team shows you who actually picks up, how fast you get logs, and who can isolate your workload. If a provider won’t rehearse with you, find out why before you sign. - Ganesh Ariyur, Transform Smarter

Insist on a specific incident notification timeline written into the contract before any sensitive workload moves. Most third-party agreements include breach notification language that is vague on timing and structured to protect the vendor. A contractual obligation to notify within a defined window, regardless of whether the provider has finished its own investigation, determines whether you can respond or can only react. - Dan Haiem, AppMakers USA

#3024. China's Rare-Earth Export Pause Expires Nov. 10. Here's What It Means for USA Rare Earth and MP Materials.

The U.S. government is making major investments to rebuild domestic rare-earth mining and processing capabilities, marking a sharp break from decades of Western dependence on China.

After decades of aggressive state subsidies and undercutting competition, China has taken control of rare-earth mining and processing. According to research from The Motley Fool, China controls 70% of rare-earth element extraction and 90% of processing.

This strong position has given China the upper hand in trade negotiations and has been a strong point of contention between the two countries. In October 2025, China's Ministry of Commerce significantly tightened control over rare-earth supply chains.

In November 2025, the U.S. and China came to a bilateral trade truce that put these measures on pause for about a year. The sides announced an extension of the broader trade truce in late September, extending the deadline to Jan. 10, 2027. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the extension covers China's broader rare-earth controls. However, China has yet to publish a formal notice, and the legal suspension on rare-earth will end on Nov. 10 without it.

The U.S. is taking steps to reestablish a domestically controlled supply chain for mining and processing rare-earth elements, with companies like MP Materials (MP -5.08%) and USA Rare Earth (USAR -5.86%) leading the way. Here's what the export pause means for these miners and what comes next.

The U.S. government is investing heavily to reestablish rare-earth mining and processing, a fundamental shift that reverses decades of Western reliance on China for these elements.

MP Materials was naturally among the first companies to benefit from U.S. spending to establish rare-earth supply chains. The company owns the Mountain Pass mining and processing site in California, the only large-scale rare-earth mining and processing facility in North America.

Last year, MP entered into a historic partnership with the Department of Defense. As part of this, the DOD provided a 10-year, 100% magnet offtake commitment and a 10-year price floor mechanism guaranteeing $110 per kilogram for all neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) products. The DOD also agreed to purchase 100% of magnets produced at MP's upcoming 10X facility.

USA Rare Earth has a bigger uphill climb. Late last year, it acquired Less Common Metals, a U.K.-based company that can convert separated rare-earth oxides into refined metals and specialized strip-cast alloys. Earlier this year, it secured up to $1.6 billion in funding from the CHIPS and Science Act to establish its own "mine-to-magnet" supply chain.

The company also acquired Serra Verde Group in September 2026, a Brazil-based rare-earth operation and the only one outside Asia that produces all four critical magnetic rare-earth elements. On top of this, it is investing heavily in the resource-rich Round Top mine in Texas and expanding its manufacturing and processing capabilities.

China's potential export restriction on Nov. 10 doesn't change the story for rare-earth miners like MP Materials and USA Rare Earth. While the two sides could extend the truce, China's export controls are fundamentally bullish for domestically based rare-earth miners in the long term.

For investors considering these stocks, USA Rare Earth is establishing itself, integrating its acquisitions, and expanding its production capabilities, and is a more aggressive long-term play in reestablishing U.S. supply chains. Meanwhile, MP Materials is the top domestic rare-earth miner, is actively fulfilling customer agreements, and has government backing that others cannot match.

#3021. Casey's General Stores Has Fallen 10% Since Reporting Earnings. Is It a Buy in November?

Casey's General Stores' same-store sales disappointed, but that didn't change the big problem with the stock.

Casey's General Stores (CASY +1.42%) is a fast-growing convenience store chain, but investors weren't particularly excited by its fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings results. Even after regaining some ground, the stock is still down 10% from its pre-earnings level as of this writing. That's probably not enough of a decline to make this stock worth buying as November gets underway. Here's why.

Casey's General Stores' business didn't fall off a cliff in the fiscal first quarter of 2027. Earnings rose 27% year over year, with same-store sales (excluding gasoline) up 3.2%. That's not exactly bad, given that consumers are increasingly watching their budgets, but the same-store sales growth rate was lower than a year ago and the lowest in five quarters. Meanwhile, gallons of gasoline sold fell slightly year over year, which is notable because fuel sales are what get people into a Casey's store.

But a 10% price drop may still seem a bit extreme. Until you take valuation into consideration. Even after that drop, Casey's General Stores' price-to-sales ratio is 1.3x compared to a five-year average of roughly 0.8x. Its price-to-earnings ratio is 32x, compared to a five-year average of 26x. Basically, this retailer's stock still looks expensive, suggesting the drop was driven more by investor sentiment than anything else.

So the bigger issue is really that investors clearly have high expectations for Casey's General Stores. Falling short in the slightest way can turn into a negative event in such situations. That dynamic was on clear display when the company reported its fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings. Perfection is often the only way to keep an expensive stock moving higher, but perfection is an impossible expectation of any company. Casey's is still growing its business, with plans to open or acquire 120 new locations in fiscal 2027. However, it is clear that investors are increasingly concerned that too much good news has been priced into the stock.

Casy's General Stores' yield is a paltry 0.4%, so income investors won't be interested. As noted above, the stock looks expensive historically, so value investors won't like it either. That leaves growth investors, but the post-earnings price drop suggests even they are getting worried that the company's growth prospects won't live up to expectations. In other words, only the most ardent fans of Casey's General Stores will probably want to step into this stock in November.
