#3017. Should You Buy C3.ai Stock After Its 93% Decline? The Answer Might Surprise You.

C3.ai is proof that not every artificial intelligence stock is a winner.

C3.ai (AI +3.64%) went public in December 2020, and its stock quickly set a record high of $177. It has trended lower ever since, with the downside reaching a crescendo after its founder and chief executive Thomas Siebel announced he was stepping away to deal with health issues last September.

Siebel always played a central role in the sales and customer relationship management processes, so his departure led to a dramatic decline in C3.ai's revenue. Fortunately, he returned to lead the company in May, and he's now trying to right the ship.

C3.ai stock remains 93% below its all-time high, so could this be a buying opportunity as Siebel puts his turnaround plan in place? The answer might surprise you.

Developing AI software from the ground up requires a considerable amount of financial and technical resources, which the average business simply doesn't have. C3.ai developed a portfolio of turnkey applications covering a range of different industries, and they can be tailored for the specific needs of almost any customer, giving enterprises a more practical way to tap into the power of AI.

However, C3.ai is expanding its addressable market by becoming a platform provider. It launched the C3 Agentic AI Platform last year, which builds a deep understanding of every existing process, relationship, and data set within the enterprise, allowing managers to create powerful agents that can make operational decisions and even automate tasks. In essence, it serves as an intelligent operating system for the enterprise.

The C3 Agentic AI Platform integrates with leading cloud platforms like Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, so it can ingest operational data from across the entire enterprise in real time.

C3.ai's decision to become a platform provider will be critical to its future success because AI will eventually be at the center of every enterprise, so catering to those deploying just one or two applications was simply the wrong strategy for the long term.

C3.ai delivered $250.3 million in revenue during its 2026 fiscal year (ended April 30), a 35% decline from the prior year. The company then delivered $52.4 million in revenue during its fiscal 2027 first quarter (ended July 31), a 25% decline from the year-ago period.

The negative results were directly attributable to Siebel's departure, but better times might be ahead now that he's leading the company again. According to management's latest guidance, C3.ai could generate up to $240 million in total revenue during fiscal 2027, which would represent a much smaller decline of 4% compared to fiscal 2026. Plus, Siebel thinks a return to sales growth could be in the cards within the next two quarters.

C3.ai has significantly cut costs across the board to right-size the business in light of its shrinking revenue. It was a necessary step, because the company lost a staggering $470.4 million at the bottom line during fiscal 2026, an increase of 63% from the prior year. It lost a further $92.8 million during the first quarter of fiscal 2027, but that was a 20% improvement from the year-ago period, so things are starting to move in the right direction.

Shortly after C3.ai went public in 2020, its price-to-sales (P/S) ratio briefly climbed to over 100, which was a ludicrous valuation. For some perspective, the technology-heavy Nasdaq-100 index has a P/S ratio of just 6.3. Investors were expecting rapid revenue growth from C3.ai that simply never came, hence the prolonged decline in its stock over the last six years.

The stock is now trading at a more reasonable P/S ratio of 7.2, which is a steep discount to its average of 14.1 since going public. However, given the company's revenue is expected to decline in fiscal 2027, its forward P/S ratio is actually slightly higher at 8.3.

In other words, C3.ai is more expensive when valued against its future potential financial results, whereas a healthy, growing company would actually look cheaper on a forward basis. Shrinking businesses tend to destroy shareholder value over time, which is exactly why investors try to avoid them.

With that said, C3.ai saw a 73% quarter-over-quarter increase in its gross bookings during the third quarter, which typically reflects the value of signed contracts for services that haven't been delivered yet. Bookings can be a good predictor of future revenue, so this supports Siebel's expectation of a return to sales growth in the next two quarters.

However, I wouldn't buy C3.ai stock right now. I would prefer to wait until the company actually does start delivering consistent revenue growth, because any further declines could leave shareholders exposed to steep losses.

#3015. AI Is Agriculture's Next Big Opportunity. But Which Decisions Has It Actually Changed?

Aidan Connolly, President, AgriTech Capital, is a food/feed/farm futurologist and author of the book The Future of Agriculture.

​In a new survey of nearly 2,000 agri-food professionals, I asked where they see the greatest opportunities for AI and how they are using it today. The respondents were primarily agribusiness executives, consultants, technology providers and researchers, so the findings reflect industry perspectives.

Overall, their answers were unsurprising: 67% identified better decision-making as a major opportunity, and 65% pointed to productivity. However, the picture became more interesting when we asked about specific applications. Just 5% identified autonomous equipment and robotics as potentially the most significant application, while 31% selected decision support and recommendations.

These findings raise an important question: How does agriculture move from recognizing AI’s potential to using it in ways that genuinely improve business performance? The answer may have less to do with choosing the right technology than with identifying the decisions worth improving.

Twenty-nine percent of the respondents say that they have used AI features built into software they already owned, compared with 9% who had used a tool developed specifically for agriculture. That number suggests two things: First, it may undercount actual usage, as AI features are now tightly bundled into office software. More importantly, it indicates an opportunity for increased use of AI tools in both commercial and production decision making, and that the biggest AI opportunity for agribusiness right now may be in purchasing, inventory, scheduling or other commercial decisions.

McKinsey’s 2026 global survey, The State of AI: On the Road to ROI, found that 80% said AI had improved their individual productivity, while 37% attributed at least some EBIT impact to AI use. Although only 6% were classified as AI “high performers,” nearly 75% of those had fundamentally redesigned workflows because of AI (versus 25% of the other respondents).

Using AI to perform an existing task faster is different from redesigning how work gets done, but the latter is much more closely associated with meaningful returns. It also gets harder when the recommendation affects a biological or operational outcome in food and farming.

Generating recommendations about feed, treatment or nitrogen timing is very different from creating a document. The recommendation has to be specific enough to act on, providing the right information, at the right time.

Over the past two months, I’ve moderated conference panels in China, the U.K. and the U.S. At each, I’ve asked a simple question: Has AI actually changed a task or a decision in your business? Very few people have been prepared to say yes.

That gap between AI’s potential and actual impact matters particularly in agriculture. Saving time drafting an email is useful. Changing a nutrition, treatment or crop-management decision is a different test: Someone must act on the recommendation and live with the result. The University of Wisconsin-Madison asked 44 independent soybean experts to evaluate AI-generated management plans and found that the recommendations missed important regional differences. The conclusion was that agricultural AI needs to move toward tailored, field-specific advice before farmers can just trust it.

Adoption will partly depend on the user trusting recommendations enough to act on them. McKinsey’s Global Farmer Insights 2026 survey of 5,500 farmers across 10 countries found that just 17% are using AI for farm-related tasks, and only 6% cited generative AI or AI search as a trusted source for decision-making. Our respondents raised similar concerns: Integration with existing systems and accuracy were cited as serious concerns by 32% of respondents. Only lack of knowledge or training was seen as a more serious obstacle, at 52%.

McKinsey’s The State of AI in 2025 survey found that inaccuracy was the most common AI-related risk, and that high-performing organizations were more likely to have defined when model outputs need human validation. Our survey did not ask who should have the final say, but my view is simple: If an AI recommendation can affect an animal, a crop or the bottom line, somebody still needs to own the decision. Trust shouldn’t depend on how confidently AI delivers a recommendation. It should depend on how consistently those recommendations perform against the alternatives, and on knowing when human judgment is still required. Its track record should determine how much responsibility it earns.​

So where should an agribusiness begin? With the decisions, not the software. I’ve argued before that AI pilots should address specific business challenges, and the same principle applies here. Which recurring decisions have the greatest impact on margins: feed rations, treatment protocols, input purchasing, production scheduling? Who makes those decisions today, what information do they use and what would a wrong call cost? That last question really matters.

Start with a decision whose outcome can be evaluated relatively quickly, rather than one you can only judge at harvest. Choose one where the available information is reasonably good and the cost of error is manageable. Test the AI recommendation against the existing approach, identify who has authority to accept or override it and keep a record of what was recommended, what was done and what happened.

Then evaluate the results. Was the recommendation accurate? Was it used? Did it improve the outcome compared with the existing process? Building confidence will generally take repeated testing, but this is how experimentation becomes evidence.

Our survey respondents identified lack of knowledge and training as the biggest barrier to adoption. Their open-ended responses reinforced the need for practical training, better integration, confidence in accuracy and clearer evidence of value.

Before you ask which AI tool your business needs, ask which decision you most want to improve. What does it need to know, and how will you tell a season from now whether the recommendation was right? If you cannot answer those questions about the decision, buying another AI tool will not solve the problem.

#3013. Apple Stock Is Up 22%, but 1 Slowing Business Could Test That Valuation

Apple stock has outperformed the market this year, but the growth of its services business is slowing.

Apple (AAPL +5.31%) stock is up about 22% this year through Nov. 3, roughly double the S&P 500's (^GSPC +1.58%) 11% gain. That run has pushed the stock to a valuation of about 38 times earnings. One reason Apple has deserved that premium is steady growth in its high-margin services business, making the recent slowdown worth a closer look.

In Apple's fiscal 2026 fourth quarter, which ended Sept. 26, services growth slowed to 10% year over year, down from about 12% the prior quarter, and management said it expects 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027 Q1, citing headwinds from third-party licensing and shifts in foreign currency exchange rates. Notably, in Apple's annual report for fiscal 2026, it did not describe the App Store as a driver of services segment growth, listing only advertising and cloud services.

The slowing growth of the services business matters because it is Apple's profit engine. Services revenue came with a 76% gross margin last fiscal year, nearly double its 39% gross margin on products. And services accounted for 40% of Apple's gross profit.

Earnings grew 13.5% year over year in fiscal Q4, but analysts are modeling for annual growth of less than 11% over the long term. If growth in services continues to weaken, investors may re-rate the stock to a lower earnings multiple, which could limit its upside potential.

The rest of Apple's business looks strong. Revenue rose 15% in fiscal 2026 to a record $479 billion as iPhone sales grew 17% last quarter and Mac sales jumped 24%. Apple expects the current holiday quarter to be "the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company," as it will be the first full quarter of sales for the iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable smartphone.

With the stock trading at about 38 times earnings, investors are paying for a lot of anticipated growth. The one thing to watch is whether the next quarter's services growth lands within or above the 8% to 9% forecast range. If it falls short, the stock's current premium valuation could become harder to justify.

It feels natural to protect your pet’s health with insurance in the same way you protect your loved ones with health insurance. After all, fur babies are part of the family.

But if you’ve shopped for pet insurance recently, you might have cringed at the cost. Should you really pay hundreds of dollars every year for something you might not use? For some pet parents, the answer is yes, even if their pet is young and healthy. And that’s partly because of how pet insurance handles pre-existing conditions.

A pre-existing condition is any illness or injury that shows symptoms before your pet insurance policy takes effect. Pet insurers usually won’t cover these conditions.

Dr. Rebecca Greenstein, chief veterinarian at Kleinburg Veterinary Hospital and veterinary expert for rover.com, says she’s seeing an increase in claim denials based on pre-existing conditions. “The whole point of insurance is you want broad spectrum coverage for a variety of things,” she says. “By the time they're excluding major organ systems and anything related to that, you may be paying monthly for coverage that doesn't actually help you when you need to go make a claim.”

If you’re considering pet insurance, it’s best to buy a policy before your pet needs it.

Your pet’s pre-existing conditions will determine which treatments and procedures insurers cover down the road.

Say your dog has a history of allergies. If you buy a policy after your four-footed friend has shown symptoms, pet insurers typically won’t pay for allergy shots or other treatments. The exclusion might also apply to related problems like itchiness or ear infections, says Dr. Michael Goldstein, medical director at Billerica Veterinary Hospital and Thrive Pet Healthcare.

He offers the example of a dog who goes to the vet for a hotspot one year and an ear infection the next. If you got pet insurance for your dog between those visits, the insurer might deny your claim because both issues could be caused by underlying allergies.

The best way around this type of scenario is to buy coverage when your pet is young, before any symptoms develop.

» MORE: The best pet insurance for pre-existing conditions

It’s tricky to figure out if pet insurance will actually save you money in the long run. The most common type of plan covers accidents and illness. It costs an average of $836 for dogs and $435 for cats each year, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association (NAPHIA). You could pay these premiums for years before an emergency surgery or chronic illness makes its way to your financial doorstep.

It’s impossible to know for sure whether your pet will stay healthy or run up sky-high vet bills. But you can assess the potential value of pet insurance by looking at common chronic conditions that pets develop with age and how much it costs to treat them.

For instance, “cats generally, as younger animals, don't have a lot of problems,” Goldstein says. “But as they get older, there are definitely common issues. Older cats in particular get chronic kidney disease.”

In cats over age 10, the Cornell Feline Health Center estimates that as many as 40% have chronic kidney disease. The annual cost to treat this condition can top $1,200.

Another example is atopic dermatitis from skin allergies, a common ailment affecting as many as 15% of dogs, according to the Cornell Richard P. Riney Canine Health Center. A single vet visit to address these itchy, persistent symptoms can cost $250 or more. And while that’s a fraction of what you might pay for pet insurance, costs of chronic conditions can add up over your pet’s lifetime.

Vet bills can also balloon quickly if chronic conditions require surgery. One example of this is hip dysplasia, a genetic disorder that can cause arthritis and pain in large-breed dogs. Depending on the procedure, you could pay up to $10,000 for hip surgery.

Many pet insurance plans cover treatments for hip dysplasia, including surgical costs, as long as it's not a pre-existing condition. However, some policies have waiting periods of six to 12 months for orthopedic issues like hip dysplasia. If symptoms develop during that waiting period, the condition will be considered pre-existing. That’s another argument for buying your pet’s coverage earlier rather than later.

Most importantly, having insurance means you can choose the best treatment for your pet no matter the cost. “It's really tragic when it's a life and death decision that is needed and it’s based on someone's financial constraints,” Greenstein says. “What is best and what's affordable often are not on the same side of the spectrum.”

One option to keep pet insurance affordable is to buy an accident-only plan. This type of coverage is usually much cheaper, costing about $190 annually for dogs and $112 for cats, according to NAPHIA. These plans cover injuries resulting from accidents, which include not just wounds and broken bones but also objects or toxins your pet might swallow.

However, an accident-only plan won’t help with some of the most common vet expenses. Illnesses, not injuries, are behind most claims submitted to pet insurer Lemonade, the company said in an email. In the past year, more than 60% of Lemonade's pet insurance claims stemmed from illnesses. That’s twice as many as the next-largest claim category, which was preventive care. A similar trend can be found in data from Nationwide, where chronic diseases make up a clear majority of pet insurance claims submitted to the company in 2025.

If you opt for an accident-only plan or no coverage at all, it’s still smart to set aside some savings for those inevitable pet emergencies and illnesses. This pool of funds can keep you from having to make difficult decisions about your pet’s care based solely on the cost of treatment.

#3010. Biotech stocks are surging. How investors can play the new drug innovation boom

Moderna gave investors a scare as its stock plunged on Thursday. But it's still one of the hottest biotechs this year. And it's hardly alone – the sector is on a roll and looks poised for more gains.

The iShares Biotechnology ETF (IBB) is up 24% through October 23, building on a 28% gain in 2025. Two dozen of the ETF's 233 holdings have more than doubled year-to-date. Moderna leads the pack with a 587% surge — even after an 18% decline following a leak of clinical data for its cancer vaccine (which was actually positive).

Analysts say a new biotech cycle is underway, fueled by clinical trial results, M&A activity, and promising technologies such as genomics, mRNA — and AI.

"We're in the midst of a powerful innovation cycle," said John Hall, portfolio manager of the T. Rowe Price Biotechnology ETF. "What's super exciting is we're seeing newer modalities start to make it to market." Companies "understand the disease biology better," he adds, and that could ultimately lead to more novel drugs making it to market.

Investors are excited about technologies like mRNA and genomics, along with a steady stream of new drug approvals. The FDA approved about a dozen novel biologic drugs in 2025, out of 46 approvals in total. Roughly 66 novel drugs are in the pipeline for FDA approval, including potential blockbusters like Moderna and Merck's cancer drug for melanoma, and a next-generation obesity drug from Eli Lilly.

Analysts say AI could also lead to more approvals as companies deploy the software to speed up drug development.

"Biotech is a phenomenal application for artificial intelligence and machine learning," says Piper Sandler analyst Ted Tenthoff. "You can set up exciting predictive models that, frankly, can do things that we've never been able to do in the space in terms of novel drug discovery."

Granted, the industry is recovering from a fallow period. The sector's last strong performance was during the Covid era when ultra-low interest rates encouraged investment in early-stage drug developers, and mRNA vaccines fueled a revenue surge for companies like Moderna, Pfizer and Biontech.

The sector then went cold as many early-stage companies fizzled. Demand for Covid vaccines evaporated, and surging interest rates put a chill in IPOs and M&A.

The risks haven't evaporated – this is still a sector whose products take years to develop, resulting in far more failures than successes. But analysts say the outlook is healthier now. While that's reflected in strong performance and richer valuations, there's still good reason to invest.

Recent clinical trial results are stoking excitement that novel drugs in the works could tackle some of the toughest problems in medicine.

Moderna and Merck's melanoma drug, for instance, uses mRNA to trigger an immune response in patients, targeting tumors that have been surgically removed and genetically analyzed. It's not a preventive vaccine, but it uses a similar immunology mechanism and showed a 42% reduction in cancer recurrence or death (used in conjunction with Merck's cancer drug Keytruda).

While the Phase 3 results disappointed Wall Street, oncologists say the outcomes were still highly positive. And they see the technology as a potential game changer, ushering in an era of personalized treatments for cancers. Moderna and Merck have said they aim to submit the drug for FDA approval and get it launched in 2027.

Inflammation treatment is another promising area. AstraZeneca and Amgen recently released positive Phase 3 results for another use for their drug Tezspire, an injectable approved for nasal polyps and asthma. In clinical trials, it showed that it successfully relieved swallowing symptoms and healed microscopic and visual tissue damage in patients with severe throat inflammation.

Roche, meanwhile, notched a win after the FDA approved its drug Enspryng, a therapy to treat rare inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. It became the first and only at-home injection for adults with thyroid eye disease.

Obesity drugs are also advancing beyond the first generation of GLP-1s. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple agonist" targeting three different hormone receptors, cleared two more clinical trials over the summer. The drug produced 28%-30% weight loss at the highest doses in the study, Lilly said. The company plans to submit the drug for FDA approval in the first quarter of 2027.

Much of the innovation isn't just happening in drug-making – it's also in areas like gene sequencing, mRNA, and high-tech instruments.

Illumina has more than doubled this year. The DNA and gene sequencing company is seeing accelerating demand for its NovaSeq X high-end sequencing platform. Pharmaceutical companies including Bristol-Myers Squibb, Merck and Kura are working with Illumina to develop precision oncology solutions.

Another big winner is 10x Genomics, up more than 300%. The biotech firm offers its lab instruments to help scientists research cancer, immunology and neuroscience. The company's Atera platform is helping produce data sets to train AI models, a process that helps accelerate personalized therapies.

On the AI front, companies are using the technology for more efficient drug discovery, says Shreefāl Mehta, president of Guidant BioTherapeutics. Using AI, "you can now bring a drug to clinical trials with less capital. More investment is also going into companies that are demonstrating that," he said.

Global AI in drug discovery will grow from a $20 billion market in 2025 to more than $160 billion by 2035, according to forecasts by Towards Health, a research and consulting firm.

One other catalyst for the sector could be M&A. Dealmaking for biopharma hit $134 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $112 billion for all of 2025, notes Jeet Mukherjee, biotech analyst at BTIG. That's a positive signal, indicating more drugs in development are showing clinical promise.

It also helps that Big Pharma has a "patent cliff" ahead. Products representing $180 billion of revenue will lose exclusivity by 2030, according to research firm RTW Institute. Companies with looming expiries "are looking for novel products and innovative products to put into their pipeline," Mehta says.

GLP-1 blockbusters have also left some companies flush with cash for acquisitions. Eli Lilly alone has completed 10 acquisition deals in 2026 worth $25 billion.

ETFs can capture the investing theme, though they aren't all alike. The iShares Biotech ETF is one of the lower cost funds. It tracks a market-cap weighted index of biotech stocks, led by companies like Gilead Sciences, Amgen, Vertex Pharmaceuticals, and Moderna.

The State Street SPDR S&P Biotech ETF holds stocks in equal weight, offering more exposure to small- and mid-cap names. Its top holdings are Moderna, Natera, Twist Bioscience and Halozyme Therapeutics.

Piper Sandler calls Illumina and 10x Genomics the "primary infrastructure plays" in the life science arena, saying their technologies are "driving the next generation of precision medicine."

Piper analyst David Westenberg has a buy rating and $305 target on Illumina, implying 14% gains from recent prices around $267. He has a hold rating on 10X with an $80 target, above recent prices around $70.

Twist Bioscience is another name to consider. The company makes customized synthetic DNA and sells DNA sequencing tools. Twist has partnered with Eli Lilly's AI and machine-learning platform and linked up with Anthropic in August to start testing its AI model, Claude, for protein development.

Twist isn't expected to turn an EPS profit until 2029, according to consensus forecasts. But revenue is expected to go from $572 million in 2027 to $833 million in 2029. Analysts have an average target of $168 on the stock, implying 21% returns from recent prices around $138.

In the small-cap space, Piper Sandler's Tenthoff likes Monte Rosa Therapeutics, a pioneer in protein degradation that selectively destroys disease-causing proteins.

The firm has partnered with Novartis to develop a drug for inflammatory conditions and autoimmune diseases. The companies announced a Phase 2 clinical study in September for an autoimmune disease treatment, which has been "triggering milestones to Monte Rosa," Tenthoff said.

Tenthoff has a buy rating and $37 target on the stock, which recently traded around $10.70.

Also in the small-cap arena, BTIG's Mukherjee recommends Faeth Therapeutics.

The biotech is developing a novel two-drug regimen to treat breast cancer and other tumors. The regimen "has the potential to address safety and dosing limitations of another recently approved drug for breast cancer," he says. And it could become "a mainstay of the future breast cancer treatment paradigm and other cancers."

Faeth is a clinical-stage company that has yet to bring a drug to market. Yet the stock is up 93% year-to-date on positive clinical trial results, trading around $18. Mukherjee has a $55 target on it.

Kymera Therapeutics is worth considering too. The company is developing an oral version of the blockbuster drug Dupixent (made and co-developed by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals and Sanofi). Dupixent is an injectable, however, and oral agents "are frequently preferred by patients," Mukherjee says. "The drug has the potential to not only take share from patients taking Dupixent for numerous immunological diseases but also expanding the market to those not taking systemic biologic drugs," he tells CNBC.

Kymera has said it doesn't expect a patent fight over Dupixent because its drug is distinct, not a biosimilar or biologic copy.

T. Rowe's Hall also likes Kymera for its potential "to unlock disease targets that have been classically considered un-druggable." The stock is the second largest holding in T. Rowe's Biotech ETF, accounting for 4.2% of the portfolio.

#3009. I Love Brookfield Renewable for 1 Reason, and It’s Not the Dividend

The income draws investors in, but the growth story is what makes Brookfield Renewable so attractive.

Plenty of investors own Brookfield Renewable (BEPC +2.63%)(BEP +2.01%) for the dividend. With a 5% yield and 17 years of delivering at least 5% annual dividend growth, it's a high-quality income stock.

However, Brookfield's dividend isn't the main thing I like about the renewable energy stock. What I love about Brookfield is its high-powered growth rate, which significantly enhances its total return potential.

Brookfield Renewable recently reported its third-quarter results. The clean energy company generated $0.51 per unit of funds from operations (FFO), up 11% year over year. Meanwhile, it has grown its FFO per unit by 12% over the last 12 months. That's robust growth for a company with a 5% dividend yield.

The company has multiple growth drivers, including inflation-linked rate increases, rising margins, development projects, and its value-enhancing capital recycling strategy. Brookfield has invested about $700 million in two new businesses over the past few months (Boralex and Aypa), funded by $850 million in asset sales. Meanwhile, it has delivered 5.6 gigawatts (GW) of new renewable energy capacity so far this year. These investments should support its continued growth.

Brookfield expects to deploy more than $11 billion in capital over the next five years. It's ramping up its renewable energy development capabilities, with 10 GW expected to be delivered next year and 11 GW in 2028, while continuing to pursue M&A transactions. These and other catalysts drive its expectation of delivering more than 10% annual FFO per share growth going forward. Add that to its 5%-yielding dividend, and Brookfield's total returns could approach 15% annually.

While Brookfield's high-yielding dividend is nice, its strong growth rate is what positions it to deliver high-powered total returns in the coming years.

Matt DiLallo has positions in Brookfield Renewable and Brookfield Renewable Partners. The Motley Fool recommends Brookfield Renewable and Brookfield Renewable Partners. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3005. Why AI Inspection Accuracy Is Not Enough To Earn Factory Trust

Rajesh Iyengar, Founder & CEO of Lincode Labs and author of Teach the Factory to See.

​When manufacturing leaders evaluate AI’s inspection capabilities, the conversation often begins with a percentage: How accurate is the model? It is a reasonable question. But in my experience developing and deploying visual inspection systems, it is rarely the most useful starting point.

I prefer to ask a different question: What happens when the inspection decision is wrong?

A defective component may move into another operation, accumulating material and labor costs before anyone discovers the problem. An acceptable component rejected unnecessarily may trigger reinspection, delay production or consume an engineer’s attention. Both errors matter, but their consequences differ.

Factory trust begins when leaders understand those consequences and design the inspection system around them.

Consider a hypothetical evaluation containing 990 acceptable parts and 10 defective ones. A system that passes every part achieves 99% overall accuracy while missing every defect.

The arithmetic is correct, but the inspection is useless.

Overall accuracy can mislead when one class is rare or different mistakes carry different costs. In Chapter 13 of my book, Teach the Factory to See, I explore this distinction, but my main takeaway is as follows: A reassuring score can conceal an error profile the factory cannot afford.

Leaders should ask what sits behind the number. Which defects were tested? Did the evaluation include borderline cases and acceptable variation? Were reference decisions agreed upon by qualified quality personnel?

Track missed defects and false rejections separately, using clear denominators. Examine performance by defect type and severity. Connect those measures to the operating problem the project is supposed to solve.

An impressive average should never conceal poor performance on the defect that justified the investment.

In one manufacturing application documented by our engineering team, cylinder heads were inspected before washing. Their surfaces could carry machining oil, coolant residue, dirt and loose metal shavings. Reflections further complicated the image.

Those conditions were part of production. Treating them as unusual exceptions would have meant designing for a factory that did not exist.

Leaders need to evaluate inspection under the conditions the production process actually creates.

The challenge extends beyond the model. Camera selection, optics, illumination, computing and inspection logic all have to fit the component condition and quality requirement.

As such, before accepting a pilot, require evidence from representative conditions: different shifts, material variation, part presentation, surface finishes and expected contamination.

Confirm that the sensing method can measure the required characteristic. If acceptance depends on scratch depth, detecting a visible scratch in a conventional two-dimensional image does not establish that its depth meets the specification.

A better algorithm cannot compensate for missing measurement information.

A model cannot settle a disagreement between engineering, quality and production about what constitutes an acceptable part.

Address that disagreement before training and evaluation.

I recommend building a shared collection of examples covering clear defects, acceptable variation and uncertain cases. Record the disposition and reasoning. Identify who can approve changes to the standard.

Operators belong in this process. They see recurring conditions, handling differences and shift-specific problems that may never appear in a carefully prepared demonstration.

Their involvement creates a practical route for reporting mistakes. A recurring false rejection should become evidence for investigation rather than an inconvenience people quietly work around.

Correctly identifying a defect is only one part of a functioning inspection process.

The decision must arrive in time, reach the appropriate equipment or person and trigger the intended action. An uncertain result needs an agreed path for review. Someone must own the final disposition.

Before deployment, ask who can stop the line, authorize reinspection, override a result and approve a configuration change. Define what happens when the system becomes unavailable. Preserve enough evidence to reconstruct a disputed decision, including the relevant image, inspection result and configuration version where appropriate. These details can determine whether the technology becomes useful during a difficult shift.

Production changes after installation. Materials, tooling, lighting and processes evolve. An inspection system needs monitoring and controlled updates throughout its operating life. Post-deployment monitoring is crucial for assessing AI reliability under real-world conditions.

To address this, leaders must assign responsibility for reviewing errors, investigating changes and validating updates before wider release.

The leadership question is broader than “How accurate is our AI?” Can the factory explain its decisions, act on them consistently and recognize when performance changes? This is the evidence manufacturing teams need before they can place their trust in AI inspection.​​

This addition will significantly expand The Edit’s footprint — currently at more than 1,500 hotels and resorts — although its usefulness will depend on your travel style. The new properties are curated in partnership with Plum Guide, a vacation-rental booking platform.

Plus, when you book a stay of four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use at your vacation home.

Here’s everything you need to know about the upcoming changes to The Edit.

Eligible Chase cardholders can currently book vacation homes through the issuer’s travel portal. However, those bookings are not eligible to receive The Edit benefits. That changes Jan. 1, 2027, with select listings.

If you have the Chase Sapphire Reserve® or the Sapphire Reserve for Business℠, here’s what you can expect when you book a vacation home through The Edit:

Up to $250 in statement credits on prepaid stays of two nights or more. Chase Sapphire Reserve® cardholders are capped at $500 in credits a year, while Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ cardholders get up to $1,000 (starting Jan. 1, 2027).

$150 in-stay credit when booking a stay of at least four nights.

Early check-in and late checkout, when available.

Compared to booking hotels and resorts with The Edit, you’re losing out on perks like a $100 property credit (which doesn’t have a four-night minimum), complimentary breakfast and room upgrades.

While cardholders will be able to redeem points toward vacation-home stays, Chase told NerdWallet that these bookings will not be eligible for Points Boost at launch.

You’ll also need to book vacation homes at least seven days in advance — a requirement that’s currently in place with standard vacation homes available in Chase’s travel portal. Chase said it plans to reduce that requirement in the near future.

Chase’s addition of vacation homes to The Edit follows American Express’ recent move to add Airbnb Luxe properties to its own lodging credit for eligible cardholders.

When you book a vacation home for four nights or more through The Edit, you’ll get a $150 in-stay credit to use on services like massages, a private chef, dry cleaning and airport pick-ups.

Options vary by property, but you’ll see a list of available offerings prior to booking your stay. You won’t be able to see pricing, but you can reach out to a Reserve travel designer — a travel concierge who can help plan your trip — to get pricing estimates prior to booking. (You won’t be able to contact the vacation home host until after you’ve booked your stay.)

While it’s nice to get the credit, the four-night minimum could be frustrating for cardholders. When you book hotels through The Edit, there isn’t a stay minimum to get the $100 property credit (although you must stay two nights to use your eligible card’s $250 prepaid stay credit).

By comparison, AmEx offers a $250 Airbnb Experiences credit on the American Express Platinum Card® or The Business Platinum Card® from American Express each calendar year when you book a prepaid Airbnb Luxe property through its travel portal. Terms apply. That statement credit is good for the rest of the calendar year in which the booking is confirmed. However, you can only unlock one $250 credit a year, even if you make multiple bookings.

Booking a vacation home through The Edit makes the most sense for longer group trips.

One of the best perks of booking a vacation home is that everyone gets to stay together in a shared space — something that’s difficult to do in a traditional hotel. If you’re able to get a larger group, you’ll also have more people to split the booking cost with.

Plus, you’ll want to stay at least four nights to benefit from the $150 in-stay credit.

If you’re traveling by yourself or with a partner on a shorter trip, you might find more value staying at a hotel or resort that’s part of The Edit. You’ll get useful perks like complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit.

Ultimately, the biggest benefit of adding vacation homes to The Edit is creating more booking options. If vacation homes fit your travel style, this is a great development to look forward to. If not, you’ll still be able to book hotels through The Edit like before.

#3000. Bill Ackman Says Long-Term Investors Can Benefit From a Broken Market. Here's the Price I'd Pay for Netflix Stock.

His fund reported a stake in the streamer in August, and its shares now trade at around half their peak. Is that cheap enough?

Bill Ackman isn't impressed by how the stock market has been acting recently. On Tuesday, Nov. 3, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that markets seem broken to him sometimes, with stocks trading at prices he can't understand. But he also saw an upside for one type of investor.

Long-term investors can benefit when they get to buy shares at prices that are way too low, Ackman said.

According to CNBC, the stocks he's especially bullish on include Netflix (NFLX +4.68%), where he reported a stake in August.

And Netflix has definitely gotten cheaper. Shares are near $66 as of this writing, about half the $133.91 record close they set in June 2025 (split-adjusted, after last November's 10-for-1 stock split).

Has Netflix stock dropped that far, then?

I don't think it's there yet. But I think it's getting close.

Netflix's third-quarter earnings per share climbed 49% from a year ago, to $0.87, and operating income grew 37% to around $4.5 billion, for an operating margin of 34.6%. Granted, both numbers got help from an easy comparison. In the year-ago quarter, Netflix booked an expense of around $619 million linked to a dispute with Brazilian tax authorities, which the company said cut its operating margin that quarter by over 5 percentage points.

Yet the business grew its profits without that help. Add the Brazil charge back to the third quarter of 2025, and Netflix's operating income climbed around 15% year over year, with its operating margin about a point higher than the year before.

Buybacks are helping, too. Netflix spent $4.8 billion repurchasing 63.9 million shares in the third quarter, its biggest quarter of buybacks ever. And its diluted share count has dropped around 3% year over year.

Sales are the weak spot. Revenue growth reached 17.6% in the fourth quarter of 2025 and has slowed every quarter since, to 16.2%, 13.4%, and then 11.8% last quarter.

Management's guidance is for around 11.5% growth in the fourth quarter. Netflix also cut its 2026 ad revenue forecast to around $2.7 billion from about $3 billion, citing a slower-than-expected rollout of some ad features.

In the first quarter, Netflix got a $2.8 billion termination fee linked to its Warner Bros. acquisition that fell through. Its first-quarter earnings per share landed at $1.23, far above the company's own pre-quarter forecast of $0.76.

Through September, Netflix earned $2.90 per share, and its fourth-quarter guidance is for another $0.67. That's around $3.57 for the year. Plug in the $0.76 forecast for the first quarter's reported figure, though, and 2026 comes to around $3.10 -- a rough stand-in for what the business earned without the fee.

On average, analysts expect Netflix to earn around $3.77 a share in 2027, about 22% above this year's number without the fee.

I think the estimate is reachable if margins keep widening. But it might get tougher every quarter that revenue growth slows, because more of the earnings growth then has to come from margin gains and buybacks.

At around $66, Netflix stock costs about 18 times earnings on analysts' average estimate for 2027. For a company still widening its operating margin, the stock arguably looks reasonable. But reasonable isn't the same as a bargain.

I'd pay about 16 times the 2027 earnings estimate, or around $60 a share.

The reason is room for error. If Netflix's 2027 earnings fell 10% below the estimate, a $60 stock would still cost about 18 times earnings -- the same price-to-earnings ratio investors pay now for the full estimate.

After all, a 10% miss isn't hard to imagine for a company whose sales growth has slowed for three straight quarters.

This is a slightly tougher bar than I used last week. On Oct. 28, I put Netflix on a list of stocks worth owning through 2030, and on Oct. 30, I said I'd rather own Apple. Neither view has changed. But owning a company through 2030 and picking a price for new shares today are two different calls.

Netflix's profits keep climbing even as its stock price has been cut in half. At about $60, or around 10% under where shares trade as I write, I'd be glad to open a position and add to it slowly. At $66, the stock isn't quite there.

Daniel Sparks and his clients have positions in Apple. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Apple and Netflix. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#2995. How To Talk To Your Board About AI

Jaime Meritt is Chief Product Officer at Verint, overseeing product management for the company’s market-leading CX Automation solutions.

​CX and technology leaders face a clear AI mandate today: Move quickly without sacrificing discipline. But the gap between AI activity and business outcomes shows a problem that many leaders aren’t acknowledging. From what I’ve seen in the industry, it may be easy to see productivity gains from AI, but it’s much harder to see how that translates into revenue gains.

Technology executives must be candid arbiters of AI, even when that means tempering boardroom enthusiasm. Their role is to provide the guidance and rigor needed to ensure AI materially contributes to enterprise value.

According to industry analyst Mark Smith, the fear of missing out that many leaders face in relation to AI needs to be refactored into AI discipline. In a recent LinkedIn post, he notes, “AI is advancing quickly across enterprise applications, technology platforms, data infrastructure and productivity tools, and the potential economic impact is significant. But urgency does not eliminate the need for discipline. In fact, the faster AI evolves, the more important it becomes for an organization to determine when to act, where to focus, who should be accountable and why an investment deserves priority.”

What most boards don’t have is a clear, grounded view of:

• Where and how AI will actually create value in their business

• What AI initiatives will really cost (beyond the demo)

• How to separate hype from sustainable advantage

When I brief my own board, I focus on the key considerations required to generate a return from AI investments. The discussion often centers on outcomes, cost controls, governance and commercial safeguards.

AI must move from experimentation and pilot projects to enterprise-wide deployment with verifiable outcomes. Putting the focus on business value, IT leaders must explain how successful proofs of concept are being transformed into operational capabilities and corporate strategic plans with the necessary resources, governance, staffing and integration.

That dialogue should specify what concrete use cases are being targeted, what success will look like and the anticipated timeline for results. This can help build the organizational “muscle” of making AI a core business discipline, rather than an isolated innovation initiative. The goal is to show how each AI investment will affect revenue, costs or margins.

Every AI initiative must be tied to a quantified business case. This requires a clear, prioritized roadmap that starts with operational wins that are measurable, providing the runway to then level up to more ambitious use cases. To do this, you need defined metrics (cost to serve, NPS/CSAT, error rates, cycle times, revenue per interaction, etc.) with a clear payback period for return, ideally 12 to 24 months.

It’s essential to enact a stop-and-redirect discipline here, too. This means pilots that don’t show value should be either shut down or reshaped quickly.

This outcome-oriented discipline shifts the conversation. Stop saying, “We’re piloting multiple LLMs and experimenting with multi-agent frameworks.” Instead, tell the board, “We’re using AI to reduce average handle time by 15-20%, automate 30-40% of routine inquiries and free our employees to focus on more complex high‑value work. Here is the impact that can have on our operating margin over the next 12-24 months.”

Large, well-known companies have made headlines for outpacing their AI budgets or exhausting allocated funds for AI coding and tokens in a single quarter. Runaway usage has driven these costs upward, with one company reportedly spending $500 million on Claude licenses in one month.

The goal shouldn’t be token maximization or token minimization; it should be valuemaxxing, a term coined recently by Marc Boroditsky, the chief revenue officer of Nebius. Boroditsky says valuemaxxing focuses the conversation on where and how AI is creating business value in exchange for those tokens. It should center on a few questions:

• How much modernization work was accelerated?

• How many vulnerabilities were resolved?

Under this organizing principle, IT leaders can then institute rate limits and quotas by use case or business unit. Then they can also provide guidance on who can deploy new AI-powered workflows within the organization.

IT leaders should explain to their board why model choice matters. Lower-cost models may be sufficient for simple tasks, while premium models should be reserved for use cases that require them. Boards also need to be looking at what workforce transformation is necessary to build the hybrid human-AI organization needed over the next three to five years.

The board-level AI economics discussion should answer two questions: What will this cost now and at scale? What is the expected payback?

A recent survey shows enterprise AI use is moving faster than oversight. While 87% of senior business decision-makers encourage AI agent use, only 47% have clear governance, oversight and controls in place.

Boards must balance AI enthusiasm with a disciplined and safe adoption path. Their goal should be to pursue transformative opportunities without turning the company into an uncontrolled AI experiment.

IT leaders will know they have all the bases covered when they can tell their boards three things:

• We have governance and controls in place so we don’t violate data residency or sovereignty rules.

• We stay aligned with the regulatory regimes where we operate.

• We have a framework in place for model risk management and maintain human accountability for high‑impact decisions.

These are the elements of an outcome-driven AI strategy. By embracing these elements, leaders can turn AI enthusiasm into long-term enterprise value. That’s the reality check every board needs.​

AI and the new economy build-out dramatically impact capital flows, commerce, and ultimately risk. As a result, questions about where we are on the credit cycle have grown louder throughout the year. Expectations for interest coverage and direct lending facilities are moderating. We first expressed a more cautious view about the potential for rising private credit losses late last year. That view rested on our 20-plus history of managing private credit vehicles and recognizing that the industry was approaching the middle stages of a credit cycle.

We believe these signs can no longer be dismissed. They are clearly visible through the lens of rising defaults and realized losses. The simple average net asset value per share has declined more than 5% for public BDCs year to date and Fitch ratings recently indicated that the trailing 12-month default rate is the highest on record as of the end of the third quarter. Against this backdrop, we continue to believe investors are looking for private credit portfolios that are less exposed to areas of private credit exuberance during the past 5 years. We think the strength of our portfolio today reflects how we structure and select investments not where we sit in the current cycle or the amount of capital we need to deploy. Many of today's market participants have never underwritten through a true downturn, as rapid capital formation loosened cash flow underwriting as non-listed BDCs grew into tens of billions of dollars under management in a very short period. The stress was concentrated in the 2021 and 2022 vintages underwritten at high leverage in the low interest rate environment and are now facing a large wave of cyclicals and software loan maturities. Importantly, less than 15% of our comprehensive portfolio is invested in these vintages.

Floating rate direct lending would normally benefit from an increase in base rates. But higher financing costs, margin compression and rising credit losses are thus far offsetting this tailwind. Continued lackluster M&A activity and excess supply of capital further won the supply-demand imbalance and extend the highly competitive environment for good cash flow assets. As a result, sourcing good risk return and sponsor finance remains challenging. We expect defaults and liability management exercises to rise throughout the next year. This is a typical credit cycle downturn. Not a crisis, a la 2008. However, we believe that defaults will be higher than many expect.

Weaker documentation and unitranche structures that sit deeper in the capital structure leave less cushion beneath lenders, so loss given default rates could run higher than many assume. The current environment favors experienced collateral based lenders as sponsors of capital structures that cannot refinance in the traditional market need liquidity and working capital solutions. Our portfolio is built for this environment. It primarily consists of first lien loans against collateral that we can monitor and liquidate selective cash flow exposure and a small watch list. Our ABL teams are a countercyclical sourcing engine when liquidity and capital are scarce. In this market phase, credit dispersion is expected to widen and manager and asset selection will matter more.

#2991. Apollo to buy nearly 10% stake in Abu Dhabi-backed alternative asset manager Mubadala Capital

Investing giant Apollo Global Management is finalizing a deal to buy nearly a 10% stake in Mubadala Capital, the alternative asset manager subsidiary of Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth fund, Mubadala Investment Co., according to people familiar with the matter who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The deal is expected to be announced later Monday morning, they said. Financial terms were not immediately known.

The transaction is significant on multiple fronts. It further advances Apollo's ambitions in Abu Dhabi often called the "capital of capital." The firm has spent the past 15 years building key strategic relationships there, with both the country's investment arm and its core leadership.

Apollo already has a multibillion-dollar partnership with Mubadala Investment Co., first established in 2022 and extended two years ago. At the time of that extension, Apollo said the agreement would strengthen the firm's Capital Solutions platform by enabling the firms to jointly source and provide customized debt and equity financing to companies worldwide.

In 2023, the institutions formed a $2.5 billion joint venture designed specifically to co-invest in global private credit opportunities over a five-year horizon.

For Mubadala Capital specifically — the region's only large-scale asset manager, advising and administering more than $755 billion in assets — the deal further advances its growth strategy under the direction of CEO Hani Barhoush, and its relevance on the global investing stage. It also marks an inflection point for the company's core alternatives business, which has grown to more than $60 billion.

John Zito, co-president of Apollo's Asset Management arm, and Barhoush have worked closely together over the past several years and, according to sources, their close-knit relationship and the success of prior partnerships led to talks of deepening ties. So did the belief that scale in the asset management business matters more than ever.

"Capital as a moat is a big thing," said one person familiar with the deal.

Importantly, the deal also continues a notable shift in the relationship between American investment firms and the Middle East. While the region, and Abu Dhabi specifically, has long been a sought-after source of capital, this deal further reverses that dynamic, with Apollo making a significant direct investment in the country and its investment vision.

Mubadala Capital's international offices include London, New York, Rio de Janeiro and San Francisco.

Apollo's investment in Mubadala Capital is similar to deals the firm has done with other asset management platforms, including Diameter Capital, Thoreau, Motive Partners and others.

Spokespersons for both firms declined to comment.

#2989. LTC Properties (LTC) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

SHOP now drives 45% of NOI as the REIT recycles capital into senior housing.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

LTC Properties, Inc. (LTC +1.16%) reported a significant strategic transition as its Seniors Housing Operating Portfolio (SHOP) reached 45% of total annualized net operating income (NOI), with a target to hit 50% by year-end. Management indicated that the company is actively recycling capital from lower-growth triple-net lease assets into the higher-growth SHOP segment, which now includes 50 communities and 14 operators. The company increased its 2026 investment guidance to $1 billion following record acquisition activity and maintains a pro forma liquidity position of over $900 million. Management stated that the current strategy triples the pro forma internal growth rate of the portfolio as it moves toward a long-term goal of generating 75% of NOI from SHOP assets by 2028.

Before management begins its presentation, please know that today's comments, including the question and answer session, may include forward-looking statements subject to risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results and events to differ materially.

These risks and uncertainties are detailed in LTC Properties filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission from time to time, including the company's most recent 10-K dated December 31, 2025. We expect total acquisitions for the year of approximately $1 billion, at which point SHOP will have grown from zero communities into a $1.6 billion portfolio over 19 months.

This was offset by decreases from property sales and loan and financing receivable payoffs, and an increase in interest expense.

#2984. MFA Financial (MFA) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Rate-driven losses dominated, but succession and new loan deals now matter most.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

MFA Financial, Inc. (MFA -0.45%) reported a GAAP net loss for the third quarter as sharp increases in treasury yields and wider mortgage spreads resulted in significant unrealized mark-to-market declines on its portfolio. Management reported that the company remains focused on transitioning leadership and resolving its legacy credit book while deploying capital into a higher-yielding environment where new acquisitions are averaging coupons of 7.8%. The company reported improved underlying earnings power, with distributable earnings prior to realized credit losses rising to $0.44 per share. CFO Mike Roper noted that although near-term headwinds exist from maturing interest rate swaps, the company has options to offset these impacts through the continued recycling of unproductive capital and utilization of a balance sheet capable of supporting more leverage.

Operator: Greetings, and welcome to the MFA Financial Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your host, Hal Schwartz, General Counsel. Thank you. You may begin.

Harold Schwartz: Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. I would now like to turn the call over to MFA's CEO, Craig Knutson.

Craig Knutson: Thank you, Hal. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us for MFA Financial's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. With me today are Bryan Wulfsohn, our President and Chief Investment Officer; Mike Roper, our Chief Financial Officer; and other members of our senior management team. Before I get to the quarter, I'd like to say a few words about the announcement that we made on October 8. As you I'm sure saw, I plan to retire from my role as Chief Executive Officer at the end of June next year, and Bryan will become President and CEO on July 1, 2027.

Bryan will also join our Board on January 1 of next year, and I expect to remain on the Board after I retire, so I'm not going to disappear. This transition is the result of a deliberate succession process on which I have been working with our Board since early 2023. Bryan has run our residential whole loan portfolio since we began buying loans in 2014, and since late 2024 has overseen Lima One and our Agency MBS and BPL portfolios. Bryan has played an active and central role in shaping both the MFA of today and the strategy that guides us.

I've worked with him for over 20 years, both at MFA and previously, and I can't think of anyone better suited to lead the company than Bryan. We also announced that Andrew Kail will join us on January 1 as Chief Investment Officer. I've known Andrew for over 15 years, and he brings over 25 years of mortgage finance experience most recently as Head of Residential Lending at Starwood Capital. Andrew's arrival will let Bryan spend the first half of next year preparing to step into the CEO role, while our investment team gains the benefit of another very experienced leader with deep expertise in our target assets. Bryan will say more about this in a few minutes.

It's been a privilege to work at MFA for the last 18.5 years and to lead the company for the last 9. I'm sure I'll have more to say on that topic in the coming months. But for now, there's plenty of work to do, so let me turn to the quarter. The third quarter was a difficult one for rates, particularly in September. During the quarter, the market began to come to terms with a more hawkish Fed as inflation remains sticky and the economy and payrolls stayed strong. In September, the Fed raised the Fed funds rate by 25 basis points, their first increase since 2023, and the accompanying message made clear that more increases will likely follow.

Although the Fed left rates unchanged at their meeting last week, market expectations are overwhelmingly anticipating a hike at the December meeting. Treasury yields moved sharply higher in the third quarter. The 2-year yield rose over 70 basis points during the quarter from 4.17% to 4.89%. The 10-year rose almost 85 basis points from 4.46% to 5.29%, the highest level in 2 decades. The last time the 10-year closed this high was in 2007. Most of that move came in September and much of it in the final week.

Oil prices climbed with continued tension with Iran, rate volatility spiked with the MOVE index rising from the high 70s at the start of September to above 110 at month end, its largest 1-week jump since April of last year. Against that backdrop, credit spreads were relatively resilient, but mortgage spreads were not. Agency MBS underperformed meaningfully in September. Non-QM securitization spreads, which tightened into mid-September, widened back out to about 140 to 150 basis points on AAAs by quarter end. Mortgage rates rose above 7.25%, up about 50 basis points in September alone. We felt the impact of these moves.

Our portfolio carries interest rate risk that we hedge to an approximate 1-year duration gap, but the combination of a sharp increase in rates, wider mortgage spreads and swap rates that rose less than treasuries collectively worked against us. It is worth noting that most of the book value decline was due to unrealized losses from marks. Mike will walk through the drivers in more detail. While book value was disappointing, we continue to make progress on the operating priorities we laid out for you over the past year. First, we continue to work through our legacy credit book. Realized credit losses improved from the second quarter as we said they would.

Our overall portfolio 60-plus day delinquency rate improved again to 6.7% and our legacy multifamily portfolio shrank to under $300 million UPB and $263 million fair value. With a clear path to resolution on most of the remaining multifamily loans and most of these losses already reflected in DE, we believe our multifamily credit issues are largely behind us, particularly as we look forward to 2027. Second, the earnings power of the portfolio continued to improve. Distributable earnings rose to $0.26 per share from $0.12 in the second quarter and DE prior to realized credit losses was $0.44 per share. Third, we kept our expense base tight.

G&A for the quarter was $23.6 million, well below the $33 million quarterly average of 2024. Fourth, we continued issuing in the securitization market. We issued a new $447 million NPL securitization in September after calling our 2024 NPL deal, unlocking an additional $40 million of capital and issued a Non-QM deal shortly after quarter end. As we have discussed previously, the securitization markets are remarkably deep and resilient even in the face of general fixed income market volatility. None of this makes the third quarter book value decline easier to accept, and we still have more work to do.

We need to finish resolving the legacy credit book and turn improving earnings power into consistent results, but the same market that hurt us in the third quarter has also created opportunity. Loans that we acquired in Q3 carried an average coupon of 7.8%, and we expect returns on new investments today will produce mid- to high-teen ROEs. We will remain disciplined, but we will continue to put capital to work in this attractive investment environment. I'd like to turn the call over to Mike now to discuss our financial results.

Michael Roper: Thanks, Craig, and good morning, everyone. The loss was driven by net mark-to-market declines of approximately $153 million across our various fair value assets, liabilities and hedges as rates rose sharply and mortgage spreads widened, particularly in late September.

Net interest income, including TBA dollar roll income, was $63.4 million, up from $60.2 million in the second quarter. Our G&A expenses declined $23.6 million, attributable primarily to nonrecurring depreciation expenses in the second quarter and a nonrecurring benefit from a true-up of incentive compensation accruals in the third quarter. Moving to Distributable earnings. DE for the quarter was $26.4 million or $0.26 per share, up from $0.12 per share in the second quarter. Realized credit losses on fair value loans declined to $18.9 million, consistent with the expectations we shared last quarter. DE prior to realized credit losses was $45.3 million or $0.44 per share.

That figure includes approximately $0.05 per share of nonrecurring benefits related to a refund of disputed servicing costs and a reduction of incentive compensation accruals in the third quarter. Excluding those items, DE prior to realized credit losses was approximately $0.39 per share, an increase of 11% from last quarter and 30% from the third quarter of 2025. This marks the third straight quarter of significant growth in the underlying earnings power of our portfolio and reflects the progress of the strategic initiatives that we shared a year ago.

In light of the significant market volatility over the last few months, we also want to provide an update on how we're thinking about the path of our distributable earnings from here. Earlier this year, we shared our expectations for elevated credit losses in 2026 as we work to resolve our legacy multifamily portfolio. This has played out largely as we expected. While these resolutions have been a drag on our DE, many of our most troubled legacy multifamily loans have now been resolved or charged off, and we continue to expect realized credit losses to moderate meaningfully from here.

As we look past the near-term, the recent move in rates and spreads has added significantly more variability to the longer-term outlook for our DE. We also have some known headwinds with approximately $1.3 billion of 1.4% pay fixed interest rate swaps that mature at the end of the year and into the first quarter of next year. These swaps contribute approximately $0.08 per share per quarter to our DE today. We have meaningful options to offset this loss carry and to continue to grow the portfolio's earnings power. With new investments coming on at returns in the mid- to high teens, the continued recycling of unproductive capital and a balance sheet capable of supporting significantly more leverage.

How quickly this builds will depend in part on how volatility, rates and markets evolve. As always, our Board will continue to evaluate the dividend each quarter, taking into account our long-term earnings outlook, taxable income, market conditions and other factors. Finally, subsequent to quarter end, we estimate that our economic book value has increased by approximately 5% since the end of September, driven by a rally in interest rates. I'd now like to turn the call over to Bryan, who will discuss our investment portfolio and Lima One.

Bryan Wulfsohn: Thanks, Mike. Before I get into the portfolio, I want to add a few words to what Craig said about our announcement last month. We have a long runway to make this a smooth handoff next summer. I'm also very glad Andrew Kail is joining us in January. I've known Andrew for over 15 years. He has built and run residential lending businesses, and he knows the Non-QM business purpose and broader residential credit markets from both sides of the table.

As CIO, Andrew will lead our investment activities alongside the team that has been with us through many cycles. Despite a very volatile September, we continued to add assets, securitize loans, reduce our legacy credit exposure and make improvements at Lima One. I'll touch on each. Starting with Non-QM, which remains our largest asset class at nearly $6 billion. We acquired over $480 million of loans during the quarter with an average coupon of 7% and an LTV of 70%. These were sourced through a select group of long-standing origination partners.

Just after quarter end, we issued our 25th Non-QM securitization, successfully selling $360 million of bonds and locking in nonrecourse non-mark-to-market financing on the underlying loans. We also remain pleased with the performance of our seasoned RPL and NPL loans, which, as a reminder, were loans originated pre-GFC that were acquired at discounts to par between 2014 and 2019. The default rate in that portfolio fell to another all-time low during Q3. In September, we called our 2024 NPL securitization and issued $379 million of new bonds with an average coupon of 6%. That transaction unlocked $40 million in cash and financing capacity that we can utilize to make new investments.

Turning to our agency book, which comprises nearly 1/3 of our investment portfolio at roughly $4 billion. Though we did not sell any bonds due to volatile market conditions, we were active during the quarter, rotating lower coupon securities into higher coupon spec pools. We also continued to roll our $478 million TBA position. Agency spreads widened in September as rate volatility spiked, which hurt book value this quarter. But at current spreads, we believe agencies offer mid- to high teens ROEs and remain an attractive liquid complement to our credit assets. At Lima One, origination volume was $288 million in the third quarter, including $214 million of short-term transitional loans and $74 million of 30-year rental loans.

Although these figures were a slight drop from Q2, we have not and will not compromise the underwriting improvements we've made over the past 2 years in order to grow volume. We sold $95 million of rental loans during the quarter, generating $2.4 million of gain on sale income. We're pleased to announce that last week, Lima originated and distributed its first multifamily loans since the spring of 2024. This was the culmination of months of hard work by an entirely new underwriting regime. As with Lima's 30-year rental production, our business plan for multifamily will be originate to sell. #2982. An Agent Cannot Be A Payee

Ran Grushkowsky is CEO of MassPay, a global payout orchestration platform specializing in instant, real-time payouts worldwide.

Agentic commerce has a measurement problem, and it is worth starting there.

In September, TRM Labs went looking for agent-initiated payments on the x402 network. It found $52.7 million settled across 198.9 million transactions since May 2025. Screening out self-payments, bulk flows from one or two payers and sellers with fewer than 10 buyers left $25.62 million. Of that screened volume, TRM estimated just 0.6% to 7.5% was plausibly initiated by an AI agent, depending on how strict the test.

TRM is candid about the limits. A script and an agent leave the same record on-chain, so the real number could be higher. It cannot be shown to be much higher. Most of what gets counted as machine commerce looks like ordinary automation.

That is not a reason to dismiss it. It is a reason to notice we are early, which is useful, because there is still time to build the half nobody is building.

AP2, launched by Google in September 2025 and donated to the FIDO Alliance in April, starts from the premise that payment systems “generally assume a human is directly clicking ‘buy’ on a trusted surface.” It responds with mandates that prove a person intended the purchase.

Mastercard’s Agent Pay for Machines, launched in June 2026 with more than 30 partners including Adyen, Coinbase and Stripe, is built on credentialing, permissioning, transacting and settling.

Serious infrastructure, none of it wrong. But all of it answers questions about the sender: Is this agent legitimate, did a person authorize it, is it within its limits?

None of it answers the questions on the other side: Is the recipient who they claim to be, is the account in their name, did the money arrive? That fails differently. An authorization failure stops a payment before it moves. A beneficiary failure lets it move, to the wrong place or to nowhere.

The clearest institutional thinking came from an IMF note in April, which splits agentic payments into intent, authorization and settlement. It flags “a key tension between probabilistic AI behavior and the deterministic requirements of payment infrastructures,” and keeps authorization and settlement rules-bound to preserve legal finality.

That is correct. A payment either lands or it does not, and there is no confidence score on whether someone got paid.

But a deliberately boring rail still has to know who the money is for. None of the three layers is built around that question.

An agent can hold a credential, carry a mandate and spend against a limit. It cannot be paid. Money has to land on a person or legal entity with a bank account, a verified name, a tax status and a jurisdiction.

x402, created by Coinbase and now governed by the x402 Foundation under the Linux Foundation, skips this by design: no account setup, no sign-ups, no API keys. For a machine paying a fraction of a cent for an API call, that is right. Identity would cost more than the transaction.

But TRM found 99.6% of that volume settled in USDC. A developer in Lisbon selling API calls has a growing stablecoin balance, and at some point it has to become rent.

The identity you did not need to take the payment is the identity you need to make the payout.

Payout failures are usually caught by the person waiting on the money. They check; it is not there, they raise a ticket. That ticket is the industry’s error detection.

Machine-initiated flows delete that person. TRM’s data works out to about 26 cents a transaction. At that size and speed, a systematic failure looks like nothing. No queue fills up, nothing gets escalated, and the discrepancy waits until someone reconciles, if anyone does.

Verification does not matter less when machines transact. It matters more, because the last human error detector has been designed out.​

Establish the payee before the volume arrives. Verify name, account and jurisdiction at onboarding, while a person is present to fix a typo. Confirm the account can receive funds and collect tax status up front.

Reconcile end to end. Track every payout to confirmed credit, not just to the moment it left your system. Alert automatically on payouts unconfirmed past a set window and on failure spikes by corridor or rail. Give the silent-failure rate a named owner.

Set an aggregation policy for small balances. Sub-dollar earnings need a payout threshold, a schedule and a rule for balances that never reach it. At these sizes, that is not an edge case. It is the main case.

The underlying lesson is incentives: Whoever pays for a failed payout has a reason to prevent it. At MassPay, we made payee verification free and stopped charging for failed payouts, putting the cost on the party that can engineer it away. When nobody is watching the money arrive, providers should be measured on confirmed delivery, not volume sent.

The industry is building the send side carefully and well, and it has the luxury of doing so because the real volume has not shown up yet.

When it does, every one of those transactions will end on a person. Deciding who that person is, and proving it, is not a layer in anyone’s architecture diagram. It is what has to work before the rest of it means anything.​
