#2980. Why Rare Earth Stock MP Materials Dropped 11.9% in October

Temperatures fell last month -- so did the market's enthusiasm for this rare-earth leader.

After falling 13.6% in September, MP Materials (MP -5.08%) shares continued to tumble last month. With firms curbing their enthusiasm for the rare-earth stock, investors had sufficient cause to click the sell button.

According to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence, MP Materials stock fell 11.9% in October.

Maintaining an outperform rating, Baird cut its price target 19% to $65 from $80 on Oct. 1. Based on MP Materials stock closing at $47.29 on Sept. 30, Baird's new price target implied upside of 37%.

A few days later, Morgan Stanley adopted a similar perspective on MP Materials stock, slashing its price target to $66 from $73. According to Thefly.com, Morgan Stanley stated in a note on Americas Metals & Mining that it currently prefers precious metal stocks, recognizing "upside to spot gold and silver prices near-term and higher long-term price forecasts."

Later in October, Goldman Sachs also adopted a less optimistic stance, lowering its price target on MP Materials to $57 from $65, while maintaining a buy rating.

MP Materials is an American company that operates throughout the rare-earth supply chain. In addition to owning and operating the Mountain Pass Rare Earth Mine and Processing Facility in California, the company owns and operates Independence, a rare-earth metal, alloy, and magnet manufacturing facility in Texas.

The company has two reportable segments. The materials segment generates revenue primarily from sales of neodymium-praseodymium oxide and metal, mostly sold to customers in the United States, Japan, and South Korea. The magnetics segment includes the Independence facility, which produces and sells magnetic precursor products and rare-earth permanent magnets.

It's not only the last week of October that was challenging for MP Materials. Shares of the rare-earth specialist are currently down about 53% from their 52-week high. While the recent plunge may be alarming, the company hasn't reported anything disastrous that underpins the drop. Instead, it's simply part of a sectorwide decline in rare-earth stocks.

For those who have been waiting patiently for MP Materials stock to dip to a more attractive entry point, now may be a great time to act. Before doing so, though, investors will want to dig into the company's third-quarter 2026 financial results (expected to be released after the market closes on Nov. 5) to confirm that it's making progress with construction of its 10X facility, a large rare-earth magnet manufacturing facility located in Texas.

Scott Levine has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Goldman Sachs Group and MP Materials. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#2978. SpaceX vs. Rocket Lab vs. AST SpaceMobile: 3 Space Stocks Compared on the Only Numbers That Matter

The three companies face different cash flow challenges and valuation risks that could shape investor returns.

Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -3.81%), also called SpaceX, reported revenue of about $14.6 billion in the third quarter. However, more than half came from its Super Intelligence (SI) business, formerly known as the artificial intelligence (AI) business, rather than from its traditional space operations. SpaceX's other two businesses include Space, which manufactures and launches reusable rockets, and Connectivity, which provides satellite internet services through Starlink.

Rocket Lab (RKLB -3.79%) generated $234 million in its fiscal second quarter (ended June 30), mainly from its Space Systems segment. Rocket Lab manufactures spacecraft and satellite components through Space Systems, while its Launch Services business sends satellites and other payloads into space.

AST SpaceMobile (ASTS -4.12%) reported just $31.5 million in its fiscal second quarter (ended June 30), with no recognized revenue from its planned satellite-cellular service. AST SpaceMobile is developing a satellite-based cellular broadband network that aims to connect ordinary smartphones directly to satellites through existing mobile operators.

However, revenue alone cannot determine which stock offers better returns. The more important numbers are the companies' ability to generate future cash flows relative to their current valuations.

SpaceX's Connectivity segment earned $2.37 billion in operating profit, while the SI segment earned $431 million in the third quarter. However, SI is also accounted for about $40 billion of the company's $48.1 billion in capital expenditures during the first nine months of 2026. SpaceX also reported $13.1 billion of operating cash flow and nearly $35 billion of negative free cash flow in the first nine months of 2026.

SpaceX's profitable Connectivity business is not yet generating enough cash to offset the company's enormous AI infrastructure spending. Additionally, a single unidentified SI customer accounted for 34.5% of the company's third-quarter revenue, equivalent to roughly two-thirds of SI revenue. The high customer concentration risk makes future cash generation particularly sensitive to that customer's spending decisions.

Rocket Lab and AST SpaceMobile are also free cash flow negative. In the first six months of 2026, Rocket Lab reported about $188 million in negative free cash flow, compared with roughly $1 billion for AST SpaceMobile.

AST SpaceMobile is burning cash at a high rate mainly due to investment in its satellite components and supporting infrastructure. While Rocket Lab needs to improve cash generation from its existing businesses and future launches, AST SpaceMobile must still convert its network investments into recurring commercial service revenue.

Rocket Lab exited the second quarter with an order backlog of $2.36 billion, of which 45.5% is expected to convert into revenue by June 2027. This provides visibility into future sales, although revenue still depends on the fulfillment of launch and spacecraft contracts. The inaugural launch of the company's next-generation Neutron rocket has been pushed to 2027, potentially delaying revenue from the new rocket while development costs continue.

Rocket Lab's planned acquisition of Iridium Communications could add an established satellite-services business. Iridium Communications reported $245.7 million of revenue in the third quarter, with services accounting for 76% of the total.

However, certain risks can't be ignored. In September, Rocket Lab raised $1.94 billion by issuing 29.3 million shares, primarily to finance the acquisition. Iridium Communications' existing term loans, totaling about $1.78 billion as of June 30, are also expected to remain outstanding after the deal closes, with a guarantee from Rocket Lab's operating subsidiary.

Hence, the acquisition will create value for existing shareholders only if the additional cash flow justifies the equity dilution and increasing financial obligations.

AST SpaceMobile believes it has sufficient funding to manufacture and launch about 90 satellites. However, deploying the network is only part of the challenge. The company must also generate enough recurring revenue to cover operating costs and earn attractive returns on its investment.

SpaceX, Rocket Lab, and AST SpaceMobile traded at 57 times, 40.8 times, and 101.8 times trailing-12-month sales (as of Oct. 30), respectively. These premium valuations already assume significant ramp-up in revenue and profit in the coming quarters.

AST SpaceMobile's valuation is particularly steep. The company expects $150 million to $200 million in revenue for 2026, supported partly by U.S. government contracts. Hence, even if AST SpaceMobile achieves the upper end of this forecasts, its $13 billion market capitalization would still represent more than 61 times projected 2026 revenue.

AST SpaceMobile also expects to recognize only 6.6% of its $1.2 billion in remaining contractual performance obligations as revenue by June 2027. This highlights that a significant amount of time is required to convert contracted business into recognized revenue. With its commercial SpaceMobile service yet to generate recognized revenue, AST SpaceMobile's valuation depends heavily on future network monetization.

Rocket Lab needs to become free cash flow positive, while SpaceX must demonstrate that its substantial AI investments can deliver attractive returns.

Of the three, Rocket Lab appears to be the best pick on a risk-reward basis, although its valuation is rich. The company's established launch and spacecraft businesses provide a foundation for growth, while the Iridium acquisition could add recurring service revenue. However, the company must demonstrate that its expansion can improve per-share cash flow after accounting for dilution and financing obligations.

SpaceX ranks second. Starlink's profitability is a significant advantage, but the company's huge AI investments can't be ignored.

AST SpaceMobile ranks third for now. The company's satellite-cellular network offers substantial growth potential, but commercial service revenue and long-term profitability remain unproven.

Manali Pradhan, CFA has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends AST SpaceMobile and Rocket Lab. The Motley Fool recommends Space Exploration Technologies. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#2975. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream company operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

"As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," said Mackay.

Mackay ranks No. 569 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.9%. See Kinetik's Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving to Crescent Energy (CRGY), an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian, and Uinta Basins. With a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share (annualized dividend of $0.48 per share), CRGY's dividend yield stands at 3.56%. Earlier this month, Crescent announced an agreement to acquire Eagle Ford assets from Devon Energy (DVN).

Heading into Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reiterated a buy rating on Crescent stock and slightly lowered the price target to $17 from $18, citing dilution from new shares.

"CRGY's recent acquisition of DVN's Eagle Ford assets marks a strategic, growth-oriented move, potentially enhancing cash flow performance," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst noted that the acquisition of the Eagle Ford assets at a net purchase price of $3.85 billion will add about 68 MBoe/d of net production and over 600 net Tier 1 locations. Richardson added that a solid track record of synergies from past deals in the Eagle Ford region increases confidence about Crescent achieving efficiencies with this deal.

Additionally, Richardson noted that the financial implications of the acquisition seem impressive, with a projected increase in cash flow per share of about 9% for 2027 to 2029.

The analyst believes that Crescent is not just expanding its business through acquisitions but positioning itself as a more durable company, regardless of market conditions.

Richardson ranks No. 478 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Crescent Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

#2972. CEO Andy Jassy Just Told Investors That AWS Can Grow Revenue 40% in 2027 and 2028 and Eventually Become a Trillion-Dollar Business. Is It Enough to Get Wall Street on Board?

Despite strong guidance for AWS over the next few years, Amazon sold off following its recent earnings report.

Although investors are extremely worried about an artificial intelligence bubble and when it might pop, it's also become clear that the market has significantly raised its threshold for evaluating large hyperscaler and AI stocks. As of this writing, the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF has declined more than 6% over the past month, despite many earnings reports showing signs that AI is benefiting their businesses.

For instance, on Amazon's (AMZN +6.12%) third-quarter earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy told analysts that he expects the company's cloud business, Amazon Web Services (AWS), to grow revenue by more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, becoming a trillion-dollar business at some point in the next five to 10 years.

Is this enough for Wall Street to get on board?

Amazon CEO Andy Jassy. Image source: Getty Images.

It's hard to look at Amazon's third-quarter earnings and say AI isn't significantly benefiting the business. AWS experienced 39.3% year-over-year revenue growth, the highest level seen in nearly five years. Revenue also achieved an annualized run rate of $184 billion.

AWS benefits from AI in several ways, including selling compute capacity, renting out its custom chips, and selling access to AI models, tools, and agents.

In the third quarter, AWS accounted for nearly 23% of the company's total revenue but nearly 64% of its total operating profit, so AWS has by far the best margins of the three business lines.

AWS was Amazon's traditional cloud business, but it's clear that AI has become the big driver moving forward.

On the earnings call, Jassy told investors, "Enterprises are still very early in using inference at scale, and yet inference already accounts for well over half of AWS's AI revenue and is growing, and we have a lot of training revenue as well."

Furthermore, the AWS backlog is now $578 billion, driven by strong demand for core infrastructure and generative AI services.

The day after its earnings report, Amazon stock actually fell.

Investors remain concerned about the high spending required to achieve these growth rates at AWS. Amazon continues to guide for $220 billion in capital expenditures this year. Jassy also told analysts the company expects to spend "meaningfully more in 2027."

This intense level of spending has resulted in negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion for the company over the past 12 months, which has concerned the market.

Interestingly, Wall Street believes AWS's growth will materialize. Consensus estimates project at least 40% growth in AWS revenue in 2027 and 2028, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. On Amazon's third-quarter earnings call, Jassy also came across as increasingly bullish about AWS's ability to generate compelling returns.

"We continue to accelerate our capex payback and have even more conviction than we already had that the investment we're making in AWS will yield a much larger revenue and free cash flow-generating business than we would have imagined a couple of years ago, with strong return on invested capital," Jassy said, adding that he views AI as "a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity." "We have a compelling flywheel spinning in AWS."

One reason the earnings report may not have received the response the company was looking for is that quarterly year-over-year growth expectations had climbed as high as 44% before the quarter, according to analysts at William Blair.

The real issue may simply be the unknown. While AI shows no signs of slowing, safety concerns have mounted, leading investors to wonder what could happen to a major AI company or the AI trade if a major security breach or safety event occurs.

Furthermore, investors also worry that AI might cannibalize existing businesses. For Amazon, there are concerns about how AI agents could impact Amazon's massive e-commerce and ads business.

The concerns might be overblown, but it's really difficult to imagine what AI looks like in the future. Meanwhile, companies like Amazon are spending hundreds of billions on AI, making it a make-or-break bet.

That's why expectations are so high -- because of the risks. Surely, if Amazon executes as Jassy says, the stock will benefit. But it's hard for investors to look that far ahead right now, even if they believe in the company's ability to capitalize on AI.

Bram Berkowitz has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Amazon. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#2971. I've Been Writing About Disney Stock for 30 Years. Here's Why My Conviction Has Never Been Higher.

I've had a lot to say about Disney over the past three decades. I'm just saying it louder now.

This might not be a good time to don my mouse ears. Shares of Walt Disney (DIS +4.18%) are barely trading higher this year. The stock has lost roughly a third of its value over the past five years. I still think that now is a great time to warm up to the leading media and entertainment company.

I've been a Disney shareholder for 40 years. I have now been contributing content to The Motley Fool for 31 years. I wrote about Disney then. I'm writing about Disney now. My conviction has never been higher. The combination of Disney's pipeline across several categories and its compelling forward valuation makes it a star you can wish upon again.

Disney's business is faring a lot better than its flat stock performance over the past year. Its operations and ugly chart since peaking in early 2021 are passing ships. Disney continues to oversee the world's most visited theme parks. According to last week's TEA Global Experiences Index -- an annual third-party research report that spells out attendance trends -- Disney had nine of the 11 most visited theme parks in the world. Closer to home, it operates the only five theme parks to attract more than 10 million turnstile clicks apiece in the U.S. in 2025.

It's not just dominant in gated attractions. U.S. movie studios cranked out just six theatrical releases in 2024 and 2025 that topped $1 billion in box office receipts. Disney was responsible for all of them. On the broadcast media front, Disney has written the playbook on navigating the transition from linear to digital distribution. Disney+ -- along with Hulu and ESPN -- has been collectively profitable for two years. Growth there is more than offsetting the declines of its original cable and over-the-air broadcasting businesses.

The future is bright, pretty much everywhere you look. Even in a rare category where it's not the dominant player, Disney is coasting. Disney isn't the largest player in cruise ships, but its ability to charge a premium for its family-friendly experience has made the top dogs envious for years. No one is growing its fleet faster -- on a percentage basis -- than the Houseboat of Mouse.

The past is historic, and not just because Disney is a master storyteller. The future could be an even better tale to tell. Its theme parks worldwide are expanding, adding bar-raising experiences that will open in the coming years. It raised admission prices for its domestic attractions last month. This happens every year, but folks keep coming. The elasticity is mesmerizing.

The same thing can be said about its streaming services. Disney+ and Hulu raised their monthly subscription rates in September. The same ad-free version of Disney+ that launched just seven years ago for $6.99 a month now costs $21.49 a month. Viewers are still glued to their screens.

What about the biggest screen that Disney serves? Your local multiplex is going to get a healthy dose of Disney product in the near future. Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters next month. In a big year for exhibitors, this will be the highest-grossing movie of 2026. The spigot will keep gushing in 2027, with new Avengers, Frozen, and Star Wars movies coming out.

On the cruising front, the water continues to be inviting. Disney will add four more cruise ships in the next four years, each one with its own distinctive features that keep regulars coming back for more bon voyages.

Disney stock has been discarded like Jessie in Toy Story 2. It's expected to deliver its strongest revenue growth in more than three years when it announces its fiscal first-quarter results later this month. The bottom line will grow even faster. With momentum building and the future promising, you would expect to pay a juicy premium for your chunk of cheese in this Mickey Mouse company. Disney is cheaper than you think.

The shares are trading at less than 16 times what analysts expect it to earn for fiscal 2027, which began last month. Its 1.3% dividend yield may not seem like much, but it's approaching a historic high with its recent aggressive payout hikes.

There will always be risks when it comes to Disney. It's susceptible to a softening economy. There's a new CEO this year. There will be duds between the blockbusters. I'm comfortable with all of that. Quality matters, and there's a reason why Disney is dominant across many markets.

Rick Munarriz has positions in Walt Disney. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Walt Disney. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#2966. Warriors’ Steve Kerr compares Steph Curry to NBA GOAT in late stages of career

From being a part of one of the greatest basketball teams ever in the 1990s as a player with the Bulls to coaching one of the greatest basketball dynasties in the 2010s with the Warriors, Steve Kerr knows what greatness looks like.

The Warriors coach appeared on ESPN's "NBA Tip-off" and told longtime host Ernie Johnson how coaching Steph Curry at age 38 reminds him of playing alongside Michael Jordan.

Steve Kerr reveals watching Steph Curry during late stages of career reminds him of Michael Jordan. AP Photo/David Zalubowski

"Honestly, it really does remind me of what it was like to play with Michael Jordan back in the day," Kerr said. "Every single night you just are amazed, and you marvel at what he's capable of doing no matter what the defense does but also just the longevity of it."

Last season, Curry appeared in only 43 games for the Warriors after spending most of the season on the team's bench due to patellofemoral pain syndrome, also known as runner's knee.

This season, Curry has played in six games and is averaging 28.8 minutes per game and is looking like his regular self.

Known as one of the greatest shooters of this era, Curry is averaging 30 points per game, shooting 42.9% from beyond the arc and 46.8% from the field.

Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr compares Steph Curry to NBA all-time great. NBAE via Getty Images

In his last three games, Curry has averaged more than 30 points, including a 44-point performance against the Timberwolves on Oct. 28.

"To see night after night, defenses doing everything possible to slow Steph down like they did with Michael, and yet the love for the game, the competitiveness, the passion, the desire to put on a show for the fans — there's such great comparisons to be made there," Kerr said.

Steve Kerr says watching Steph Curry during the late stages of his career reminds him of Michael Jordan. NBAE via Getty Images

Kerr added, "You get to experience the thrill of seeing them do their thing night in and night out, and it never gets old."

Kerr has won nine NBA titles, five as a player and four as a coach. Jordan won six NBA crowns as a player.

#2960. Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling

A version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.

A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading.

Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up.

Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.

Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova, Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff.

Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies.

The ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week.

Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.

Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24.

Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.

Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year.

Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500.

Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.

Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors.

Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

#2954. Celtics survive late stampede from Bucks, win 109-102

The Celtics led the Bucks by as many as 22 points on Wednesday night before the Bucks made a big comeback and briefly took the lead in the fourth. Thankfully for Boston, Paul George and Derrick White saved the day as the Celtics held on with a 109-102 win.

Jayson Tatum did not play in this game for the Celtics and Boston started Derrick White, Sam Hauser, Paul George, Hugo Gonzalez and Neemias Queta. Devin Carter was still out with mono as well. Meanwhile, the Bucks started Tyler Herro, Brayden Burries, Kyle Kuzma, Jaine Jacquez Jr. and Myles Turner and were only missing two-way player Kam Jones.

The Celtics got off to a quick start, going up 19-8 mid way through the first quarter. After Sam Hauser hit the first two shots of the game, Paul George scored 7 of the next 13 Celtics points.

The Celtics led after the first quarter 28-14. Paul George led the way with 10 points and 3 steals while playing the entire quarter. Mitchell Robinson also had 6 rebounds off of the bench.

Boston got off to a good start in the 2nd quarter as Payton Pritchard had a few baskets. It was good to see Payton Pritchard be aggressive on his first shot as well. However, a pair of Bucks threes leading to a 6-2 run lead to Joe Mazzulla calling his mandatory timeout.

The offense picked up in the 2nd quarter, as Boston led 62-41 at the half. Luka Garza led the way with 11 points and 5 rebounds while Derrick White had 9 points, 4 assists and 3 rebounds.

It was good to see the Celtics three point shooting get going, they were 10/17 in the first half after being 30% in their last 4 games, according to the NBC Sports Boston broadcast.

Boston came out flat in the 2nd half and Milwaukee took advantage. The Bucks went on a 12-5 run to open the 3rd quarter and Joe Mazzulla called a timeout. Jamie Jaquez Jr. had 5 points and Tyler Herro had 4 points during the run for Milwaukee.

The Bucks made 10 of their first 12 shots in the quarter and cut the Celtics led to 7. Back-to-back key Baylor Scheierman threes grew Boston's lead back to 13 as Milwaukee called timeout.

Payton Pritchard left the game with an right eye abrasion and he did not return to the game.

It was Tyler Herro's quarter, he had 17 points on 6/8 from the field and 2/2 from three in the 3rd quarter.

The Celtics did lead the Bucks at the end of three but what was a 21-point game at halftime was just an 8-point lead entering the fourth. Paul George's 16 points, 4 assists and 2 steals led the way for Boston.

The Bucks opened the fourth quarter on a 10-4 run and forced Joe Mazzulla to call another timeout.

Milwaukee took their first lead with 6:50 to go in the game but Boston fought back and took a 3 point lead as Taylor Jenkins called timeout.

The Celtics struggled score as they missed Tatum and Pritchard a lot. It felt like Paul George was their only source of offense late in the game.

George then stepped up to the line with under 4 minutes left and missed both free throws in a tie game.

The Celtics were able to go on a 7-0 run thank to 5 points from Derrick White to take a 104-97 lead, which Tyler Herro cut to 104-99 with two made free throws.

Paul George hit a clutch 3 to put the Celtics up 8, Ryan Rollins hit a 3 and the Bucks had a few looks to cut the Celtics lead to 2 with just over 30 seconds to go but they missed both.

Two Derrick White free throws iced it and the Celtics hung on, 109-102. George's 25 points and White's 24 points led the way for the Celtics.

Boston shot 41% from the field and 41% from three while Milwaukee shot 41% from the field and 40% from three. The Celtics next game is an NBA Cup game in Charlotte at 7 pm EST on Friday night.

#2944. Jalen Brunson's 22 first-quarter points kickstart Knicks' 135-105 smackdown of Bulls

The Knicks took advantage of a floundering Chicago Bulls defense -- ranked 29th of 30 in the league -- Wednesday night, winning their third-straight game and their fourth in the last five with a final score of 135-105.

-- New York came out of the gate fast, stunning a young Bulls team into a state of near paralysis. Chicago surrendered 10 points off of turnovers through the first 13 minutes of play, while the Knicks, who have struggled in transition so far this season, let up none across the same span. The Bulls also faltered from beyond the arc, missing 20-straight threes in the middle stretch of the first half. Led by Jalen Brunson's 26 first-half points, New York went into the break with a dominating 32-point lead (84-53).

-- After struggling to find the basket through the first few games of the season -- and missing his first three of Wednesday's game -- Brunson looked back to peak form in the first quarter, scoring a staggering 22 points in 11 first-quarter minutes. Collectively, the Bulls only scored 21 in the opening frame.

Even with significantly decreased minutes in the back half of the contest, Brunson continued to produce, finishing the night with 33 points, two rebounds, and four assists.

-- The Knicks went 24-for-26 from the charity stripe in the first half. OG Anunoby contributed nearly half of those points.

He drew 10 free throws in the first 14 minutes of play -- marking the second-straight game in which he earned eight attempts -- and landed every one for 10 of his 18 first-half points. A third personal foul with 8:48 left in the opening half stifled his run as he sat for the next five minutes, and while he drew two more foul shots before the half wound down, he only hit one. Still, his 11 made free throws tied a career-best mark for most in the first half.

-- Karl-Anthony Towns finished the game with his eighth-consecutive double-double (17 points, 12 rebounds), completing the set less than halfway through the third despite only recording one shot from the field by the end of the first half. He opened the third quarter with two back-to-back threes and only turned up the heat from there.

Toward the end of the second frame, Towns jumped up to shoot a three but was met by Chicago forward Zach Collins, who knocked the ball out of Towns' hand. On his way down, Collins stepped on Towns' toe and knocked him over, triggering a review for a flagrant foul. However, because Collins' foot landed on top of Towns' rather than below, the move was ruled as a common foul instead, and Towns earned three free throws. He made all three.

-- With Josh Hart sidelined due to ankle soreness, Landry Shamet joined New York's starting five for the first time this season. The shooting guard more than earned the right Monday, lifting the Knicks to a win against the Brooklyn Nets with a game-leading 22 points.

Right off the bat, Shamet landed two buckets, scoring the Knicks' first four points. His production slowed down after that, but he finished with seven points, two rebounds, two assists, and a plus-21 rating.

-- For the second game in a row -- and third in the last week -- New York's bench combined for 40-plus points (53 on Wednesday). This time, Jordan Clarkson and Dalton Knecht led the way.

In his first game as a Knick, Knecht scored 10 points in 13 minutes played. His first points came from a tip-in dunk on a Shamet miss. His second -- a 25-foot step-back jump shot -- put the Knicks at 84 first-half points, tying the franchise record for most points scored in the opening 24 minutes of a game. He also added seven rebounds and an assist.

Clarkson, who also scored 10, went 4-for-9 from the field and 2-for-2 from three.

Mohammed Diawara, who first subbed in for Anunoby with five minutes left in the first, collected three points, one rebound, and one block in three first-quarter minutes. He finished with eight points, tied with James Wiseman for second-most on the bench.

Late in the third, Miles McBride leapt up for a 24-foot jumper from deep at the play clock buzzer before he was knocked over, drawing a foul and turning the sequence into a four-point play. He finished with seven points.

-- All 14 available Knicks made an appearance. Everyone except Jose Alvarado and Pacome Dadiet played 11 minutes or more. They each played nine.

The star point guard finished 10-for-17 from the field, 5-for-10 from three-point range, and 8-for-9 from the free throw line en route to a season-best 33-point performance. No other Knick surpassed 18 points.

After a few days of rest, New York will be back in action Saturday night when they take on the Cleveland Cavaliers. Tip off is scheduled for 8 p.m.

For release at 2:30 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday requested public comment on two proposals related to establishing a regulatory framework for Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers under the GENIUS Act.

The first proposal would require that Board-supervised payment stablecoin issuers fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets, such as short-term Treasury bills and certain other high-quality, liquid assets. The proposal would also establish standardized capital requirements to address certain credit and operational risks of payment stablecoin activities, as well as risk management standards, in accordance with the law. Separately, the proposal would introduce rules for Board-supervised firms that safekeep the assets backing payment stablecoins. It would also clarify the permissibility of stablecoin and related activities for Board-supervised banks.

The second proposal would establish a tailored application process for Board-supervised banks applying to issue payment stablecoins. These applicants would be required to submit a business plan and financial information, among other documents. The proposal would also create a process governing appeals, hearings, and final determinations for applications.

The comment period will close 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

#2935. Recap: Wizards plagued by familiar issues in 120-105 loss to Hawks

The Washington Wizards' 120-105 loss to the Atlanta Hawks at Capital One Arena on Wednesday followed a script similar to the team's first three defeats this season. The home team was outshot from long range and gave up far too many offensive rebounds.

Anthony Davis got off to a hot start, scoring 6 of the Wizards' first 8 points. He tweaked his ankle just over a minute into the contest after landing on AJ Dybantsa's foot on a closeout. But Davis still finished with 10 points through the first 12 minutes.

Despite Washington seemingly playing well, Atlanta stayed ahead with the three-ball. The Hawks hit 8 three-pointers in the first quarter alone to take a 37-32 lead after one.

Dybantsa had a tough night offensively. He looked out of control at times and failed to get a veteran whistle on some of his drives. He took his frustrations out on the rim with a two-handed jam in the second quarter.

A triple from old friend CJ McCollum gave the Hawks a 16-point lead with 2:13 to play. The Wizards closed the half on a 9-0 run to cut the deficit to 68-61. Davis led all scorers with 18 points, along with 6 rebounds and 2 blocks at the break.

Kyshawn George ran point whenever Young was off the floor. He evidently picked up a few things from the All-Star point guard, as he repeatedly found Davis and Deandre Ayton for easy baskets around the rim.

The defense was much improved in the third quarter, but it was the offense that lagged behind. Washington finally built up some momentum late when Trae hit a step-back three that got the team within four points of Atlanta.

Will Riley missed a clean look at a three on the following possession that would have gotten the Wizards to within one. The Hawks made it hurt as another old friend, Corey Kispert, connected on a four-point play on the other end.

George had a huge fourth quarter. He came alive with 12 points in the period but did not have much support from his Wizards teammates as the Hawks pulled away for the 15-point victory.

The Hawks more than tripled (19) the Wizards (6) in three-point makes. Atlanta already had Washington's three-point total midway through the first quarter. The Wizards also gave up 19 offensive rebounds as Dyson Daniels and Onyeka Okongwu combined to grab 33 boards.

Davis powered through his ankle injury to tally 26 points and 10 rebounds. George flashed more of his star potential with 25 points on 10-of-14 shooting, on top of his 7 assists.

Dybantsa and Tre Johnson both struggled from the field in this one. The No. 1 overall pick had his first poor outing offensively, with 9 points on a 4-of-12 clip. He also badly missed on 3 of his 4 free-throw attempts. Johnson looked rattled after his first few misses. He continued to force his shots through garbage time, making just 1 of his 9 attempts.

The Wizards get an immediate chance to avenge the loss when they head to Atlanta to face the Hawks on Friday for their second NBA Cup game.

#2931. Federal Reserve Board finalizes changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements

An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .govA .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPSA lock (LockLocked padlock icon) or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, provides the nation with a safe, flexible, and stable monetary and financial system.

Review of Monetary Policy Strategy, Tools, and Communications

Mergers, Acquisitions, and Other Applications

Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 9:00 a.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Wednesday finalized changes to enhance the transparency and public accountability of its stress test and reduce volatility in its stress test-related capital requirements. The two final rules are largely similar to the proposed rules from 2025. The Board also requested comment on a proposal to better capture differences in banks' business models to generate fee income.

The Board conducts stress tests to ensure that large banks are sufficiently capitalized and able to lend to households and businesses even in a severe recession. In December 2024, the Board announced it would modify the test to improve its resilience.

"The stress test is an essential component of our regulatory capital framework," said Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman. "Today's changes preserve its resilience by ensuring that it is transparent, granular, and risk-sensitive. The public will now have greater assurance that the risks banks take will be reflected appropriately in their stress test losses and their capital requirements."

The first final rule requires the Board to invite public input annually on the stress test scenarios and any material model changes. It also updates the framework that guides the design of the hypothetical scenarios and adopts the models that will be used for the 2027 stress test. In addition, the final rule makes several adjustments to the stress test calendar. The final rule also updates the global market shock component, which is a set of shocks to specific market components applied to banks with large trading books. These banks will now be tested against two global market shock components each year, and the Board will use the shock that produces the largest losses for each firm to calculate the firm's stress test results.

The second final rule requires the Board, when calculating stress capital buffer requirements, to average the results from the two most recent annual supervisory stress tests for firms subject to the stress test in both years. The Board will begin averaging stress capital buffer requirements in 2028 to ensure that only models incorporating public input are used in the calculation.

The proposal would request public comment on a revision to the Board's noninterest income model that would improve the stress test's ability to capture business model diversity across firms. If adopted, these adjustments would replace the current noninterest income model that projects each bank's fee income under stress. Comments are due 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Together, the changes are likely to reduce year-over-year volatility in capital requirements by approximately 50 percent and are not expected to materially affect aggregate capital requirements.

#2921. What happened to Kon Knueppel? Hornets star's season debut ends after 6 minutes

The Charlotte Hornets were eagerly awaiting the regular season debut of second-year star and Rookie of the Year runner-up Kon Knueppel.

The Hornets ruled Knueppel out for the remainder of their game Wednesday, Nov. 4 against the Brooklyn Nets with left leg soreness. This is particularly concerning because Knueppel had been sidelined with a left hamstring strain.

After the game, Hornets coach Charles Lee told the local broadcast that he did not have an update on Knueppel and said he would be evaluated once the team returned to Charlotte later Wednesday.

Although there didn't appear to be a specific play in which Knueppel got hurt, he exited shortly after he dribbled the ball off his foot. During the play, Knueppel tried to dribble the ball behind his back but it caromed off his right leg, forcing him to take a small step as he tried to recover it. Immediately after the play, Knueppel limped but tried to stay in the game before quickly heading to the bench. He eventually went into the locker room and did not return.

Knueppel scored 3 points, all from free throws, missed his only shot attempt, a 3-pointer, and committed 2 turnovers in 5:51 on the floor against the Nets. He did not record any other statistic.

"Hopefully I can contribute in a capacity similar to last year, and with all the offseason work that I put in, even more," Knueppel told the Hornets broadcast in a pregame interview. "It might take me a little bit to get to that full capability, but tonight I'll be ready to go and help us get a win."

Last season, his first in the NBA after the Hornets selected him with the No. 4 overall pick in the 2025 NBA Draft, Knueppel recorded 18.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game. He converted 3-pointers at a 42.5% clip and lost out to his college teammate at Duke, Cooper Flagg, for the Rookie of the Year honor.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: What happened to Kon Knueppel? Hornets star's season debut ends after 6 minutes

#2911. As AI becomes more fractured, one name stands out: AMD

As Anthropic rushes to takes its shares public, the AI trade is showing cracks, and they are not confined to fringe players.

We recently wrote about CoreWeave, which fell 15.5% on Oct. 14 as yields on its 2032 notes touched 15%, and its default-swap spreads nearly doubled in October. IREN is down more than 20% this year. Last Thursday, the contagion reached chipmakers, which makes sense since much of CRWV and IREN's spending is going there. AMD dropped 8.1% as Meta's financing plans and a supply warning from Lam Research exacerbated data-center fears about the pace of AI spending.

Because when you screen for factors that demonstrably generate outperformance over time, the list narrows quickly. My screen: price above the 200-day moving average; revenue growing at least as fast as the S&P 500 (5%+ per annum); EPS growing at least as fast (7%+); rating upgrades; a PEG below 3; and ROE and ROIC of at least 12%. Of the names reporting in the next two weeks, AMD is effectively the only one that makes the list. Yes, you can (and arguably should, as our staples article described) position your portfolio with slightly less tech exposure than the broad indices provide, but we can't ignore the market's biggest and most transformative sector entirely.

Especially because the growth in this case doesn't just meet my criteria; it blows past them. Consensus for Q3 calls for EPS of $1.94 on revenue of $13.06 billion, versus $1.20 and $9.25 billion a year ago. That's YoY growth of nearly 62% and 41%, respectively. The recent drawdown came from a sector selloff, not anything AMD reported, but it shows that if some names in the space get hit, even the larger players are likely to feel it. On Oct. 6, Lisa Su said AMD would substantially increase supply in 2027 because AI orders keep outrunning capacity.

So how do you balance factors we know work for a fast-growing company against a backdrop of cracks in the AI trade? Options.

Owning the stock outright means absorbing a roughly 9% to 11% implied earnings-related move (day of). Earnings are about a week out, and over the past four quarters the smallest move over a similar window was more than 9%, and the largest move, after the company reported its Q1 26 results, was 38%! Of course, that kind of volatility means options aren't cheap, and that rich premium is also a reason not to simply buy calls.

A call spread risk reversal does both jobs: it reduces risk if the cracks widen, and the short options offset the elevated volatility we would otherwise pay for. The bottom chart shows that, by sacrificing about $1,700 of upside for $5,000 in outperformance during a severe downside move, and given how jittery this trade has been lately, this is a way to stay in it with considerably less risk. $5,000 less, specifically. Of course, selling that out will tie up some cash, but less so than simply buying the stock. And selling both the out and the call reduces long call purchase by 66%

#2900. Knicks, Jalen Brunson explode in decimation of Bulls to reach .500 mark

Jalen Brunson saw red and gouged the Bulls.

Then his teammates feasted on the carcass.

Brunson dropped 22 of his 33 points in the first quarter of a 135-105 Bull-dozing Wednesday night at MSG, an emphatic victory that will, at least temporarily, quiet the criticisms of New York's sputtering offense to start their title defense.

"That was as close to a 48-minute game as our group has had yet," coach Mike Brown said.

The Knicks (4-4), winners of four of their last five games, tied a 38-year-old franchise record with 84 points in the first half, shooting 63 percent before the break — including 50 percent from beyond the arc.

The game was essentially sealed in the second quarter with New York's 37-point advantage.

Jalen Brunson, who scored a game-high 33 points, drives to the basket after getting a pick by Karl-Anthony Towns during the Knicks' 135-105 win over the Bulls on Nov. 4, 2026 at Madison Square Garden. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

"It was a really good half, in terms of doing what we believe, what we should be doing offensively as our staples," Brown said. "Everybody was really good in those areas."

Brunson shot 10-for-17 as the Knicks won his 28 minutes by 33 points.

"When you have it going, it feels good," Brunson said. "And then just trying to play off that and using my gravity to get teammates involved."

Brunson entered the evening shooting under 40 percent but had no problems hitting his attempts Wednesday.

OG Anunoby, who scored 18 points, slams home a dunk during the Knicks' win over the Bulls. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

"He's obviously missed some shots but he took the same shots tonight that he's been taking," Brown said. "And, we felt we've gotten some good shots in previous games that just haven't gone down.

"But the good part about it is, they went down tonight, and we defended. A great game by him as well as everybody else."

Karl-Anthony Towns added 17 points and 12 rebounds. OG Anunoby had 18 points with three steals and 11 converted free throws.

Karl-Anthony Towns shoots over Jalen Smith during the Knicks' blowout win over the Bulls. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

The Knicks lived at the foul line, going 30-for-37, as the refs operated as if they were paid by the whistle. The teams combined for 65 free throws.

All the Knicks starters were pulled for extended garbage time, which was the entire fourth quarter.

The landslide victory followed the Knicks' much closer win in Chicago about a week prior, when Brunson went off for 38 points. He must enjoy the matchup against the Bulls (1-7), who were a defensive calamity Wednesday and projected as one of the NBA's worst this season.

Before the onslaught, the Knicks were in a scoring rut, falling to 21st in the NBA in offensive rating — a position unbecoming of reigning champs.

Josh Hart, who sat out Wednesday's victory with ankle soreness, said the team hadn't yet recovered from a short and celebratory offseason.

New York Knicks guard Jalen Brunson (11) reacts after hitting a 3-point shot against the Chicago Bulls at Madison Square Garden in New York, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. Charles Wenzelberg / New York Post

"I think it's a tough spot. It's kinda like a little conundrum because obviously we played into mid-June. Then in the summer, obviously you're working out, you're doing that, but you also are enjoying the fruits of the labor of winning in terms of going to brand [appearances]. Off the court, it's kind of booming for you," said Hart, who was replaced in the lineup by Landry Shamet (seven points, 24 minutes). "So, you're doing all of that, so that takes a little bit of a wear on you. And then you get into it. So, sometimes the body has to kinda catch up."

The Knicks looked all caught up Wednesday. Next up is a little tougher matchup: at Cleveland (4-4) on Saturday.

The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF), which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability.

The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Financial Stability Coordination & Actions

Financial Market Utilities & Infrastructures

For release at 2:00 p.m. EDT Share

The Federal Reserve Board on Tuesday released the minutes from its recent meetings to review and determine the discount rates provided to depository institutions through the discount window. Today's minutes cover the Board meetings that occurred on August 17, September 9, and September 16, 2026.

The Board's process for setting the discount rate is distinct from the process the Federal Open Market Committee follows in setting the target range for the federal funds rate.

The Federal Reserve Board on Friday announced the termination of the enforcement actions listed below:

Gardner Bancshares, Inc., Lenexa, Kansas and Small Business Bank, Lenexa, Kansas Cease and Desist Order dated September 1, 2023 (PDF) Terminated October 13, 2026

Small Business Bank, Lenexa, Kansas Cease and Desist Order dated November 13, 2024 (PDF) Terminated October 13, 2026

Small Business Bank, Lenexa, Kansas Prompt Corrective Action dated June 29, 2026 (PDF) Terminated October 13, 2026

Additional enforcement actions can be searched for here.
